Asymptotic bounds and input-sensitive running-time analysis · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: method

Uses eventual inequalities, encoding size and tight best/worst-case examples to compare algorithmic costs.

Asymptotic bounds and input-sensitive running-time analysis

For nonnegative functions, f=O(g) means f(x)≤Cg(x) beyond some threshold with fixed C>0; f=Ω(g) reverses the inequality, and f=Θ(g) requires both. Ratios establish or disprove these relations. For f(n)=n2+10n and g(n)=n3/3+n, f/g→0, so f=O(g) and not Ω(g). Their logarithms both have order logn, even though the polynomials have different degrees. Similarly 3n=Ω(2n) but not O(2n), while log(3n) and log(2n) are both Θ(n). The solution's nested logarithm in its polynomial-log comparison is a typographical error; leading logarithmic terms are 2logn+o(1) and 3logn−log3+o(1).

Count elementary operations such as arithmetic, comparisons and assignments, and state the size parameter. Binary encoding of an integer a uses O(1+log(1+|a|)) bits, including sign; numeric magnitude is not its bit length. A bound polynomial in a large numeric value need not be polynomial in the encoded input length. Growth rates explain why a constant-factor hardware speedup has limited benefit for exponential or factorial algorithms.

The sheet's insertion-sort pseudocode inserts L[j] into the already sorted prefix by shifting larger entries. It maps [4,7,9,2,1] to [1,2,4,7,9]. In decreasing order, iteration j shifts j−1 entries, for ∑j=2n(j−1)=Θ(n2) work, proving a tight worst-case bound rather than merely an upper bound. Already sorted input performs no shifts but still traverses the outer loop and checks each insertion, giving Θ(n) best-case time. The official solution swaps the names of its loops in the best-case explanation; the outer loop still executes n−1 times.

Dijkstra labels and unit-edge maze path reconstruction · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: algorithm

Relates minimum-distance vertex selection to a supplied Python grid-maze implementation and its unit-weight assumptions.

Dijkstra labels and unit-edge maze path reconstruction

Dijkstra initializes d(s)=0 and all other labels to infinity, repeatedly selects an unvisited vertex with the smallest finite label, settles it, and relaxes its outgoing edges by d(v)←min{d(v),d(u)+c(u,v)}. Nonnegative costs justify finality of settled labels. In a general weighted graph, stop when the target is settled, or when no finite unvisited label remains; first discovery alone does not establish a weighted shortest path.

The supplied Python exercise implements the special case of undirected unit-weight grid edges. Vertices are consecutive integer indices; a dictionary maps endpoint tuples to weight 1, and adjacency is tested at either endpoint. random_graph.py samples each horizontal/vertical edge with parameter p, seeding from the current timestamp. Despite “weighted” names, this generator does not sample varying edge costs.

The missing minDistance routine is a linear scan of all vertices for the smallest finite unvisited distance, returning −1 if none exists. Both provided solution files implement that scan. The surrounding algorithm initially marks the source visited, initializes its neighbors to distance 1, and repeatedly relaxes edges by adding 1. It stops as soon as dist[t] becomes finite. That early-discovery rule is supported here by equal edge lengths and increasing distance layers; extending it to arbitrary nonnegative weights would be incorrect. Isolated or disconnected targets terminate with infinite distance.

The returned pair contains discovery/relaxation edges and a distance array, rather than the dictionary of shortest-path edges claimed in a comment. maze.py traces backward from the target along recorded edges whose opposite endpoint has distance one less, then draws the route separately from explored edges. Grid coordinates map vertices to every other square and edges to their midpoint squares; the displayed square count is 2(d(t)+1), which differs from graph edge distance. The driver exposes grid dimensions, block size and sampling probability; it prints timings but supplies no fixed measured benchmark.

The renderer explicitly imports processing_py, a visualization dependency named by the sheet as processing-py. The starter and completed routines are supplied instructional code, not evidence of personal authorship. Their list scans and repeated full edge filtering do not implement the lecture's Fibonacci-heap complexity.

Feasible network flows and cut-capacity bounds · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: theorem

Derives net flow identities by cancellation and bounds throughput by every source-sink cut.

Feasible network flows and cut-capacity bounds

A network consists of a digraph, distinct source s and sink t, and nonnegative rational arc capacities u. A feasible flow satisfies 0≤f(e)≤u(e) and equal incoming/outgoing totals at every other vertex. Its value is net source outflow, not gross outgoing flow. Summing vertex balances cancels internal arcs and proves equality with net sink inflow.

For any S containing s but excluding t, write S¯=V⧵S. The directed cut contains only arcs from S to S¯. The same cancellation gives

val(f)=f(δout(S))−f(δin(S))≤u(δout(S)).

The reverse crossing flow is subtracted; it is not part of cut capacity. Equality holds exactly when every outgoing cut arc is saturated and all incoming cut arcs carry zero flow. Such a matching feasible flow and cut certify maximum throughput and minimum cut capacity.

The notes eliminate antiparallel original arcs by subdividing them through auxiliary vertices, assigning the original capacity to each segment. Conservation at the new vertices forces equal segment flows and preserves the original feasible transfers and objective. This is a representational convenience for distinguishing original arcs from later reverse residual arcs. Zero flow is always feasible in this model; lower bounds or prescribed supplies would change that claim. The lecture's final example has source-side set {s,1,2}, cut capacity 1+2+3=6, and a flow of value 6. The 10 May annotation instead shows an earlier, weaker cut of capacity 7; a valid upper bound need not be tight.

Graph incidence, cuts, paths and cycles · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: concept

Defines the graph structures and boundary notation used by path, tree, flow and matching problems.

Graph incidence, cuts, paths and cycles

A simple undirected graph G=(V,E) has nonempty vertex set and edges that are two-element subsets of V. A simple digraph uses ordered pairs of distinct vertices as arcs. Thus both exclude loops and parallel copies; opposite directed arcs are distinct and can coexist. Set n=|V|, m=|E|. Graph structure is independent of the chosen drawing.

For an undirected vertex subset S, the boundary δ(S) consists of edges with exactly one endpoint in S. In particular δ(v) denotes edges incident to vertex v; the notes' expression intersecting an edge with v is read as membership of the vertex, or intersection with its singleton. Edges wholly within S form E(S). A subgraph on S may choose only some edges of E(S); the vertex-induced subgraph retains all of them. For a digraph,

δin(S)={(u,v)∈E:u∉S,v∈S},δout(S)={(u,v)∈E:u∈S,v∉S}.

An internal edge does not belong to either directed boundary.

The course uses “walk” for an edge-nonrepeating sequence of incident vertices and edges, allowing repeated vertices; this corresponds to a trail in other conventions. A closed walk returns to its starting vertex. A path has no repeated vertices. A cycle closes such a sequence with all other vertices distinct and no repeated edges; direction must be respected in digraphs. A digraph is acyclic when it has no directed cycle. These conventions distinguish a path from a general traversal and a graph's cycles from cycles created merely by a drawing.

Kruskal forests and component merging for grid mazes · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: algorithm

Builds a minimum spanning tree by sorted edge acceptance and relates cycle tests to a supplied Python component-set implementation.

Kruskal forests and component merging for grid mazes

Sort edges in nondecreasing cost order and start with the forest (V,∅). Accept an edge exactly when its endpoints belong to distinct current components; merge those components. This condition is equivalent to not creating a cycle. For a connected graph the result is a spanning tree.

A rejected edge already has a path between its endpoints made from earlier edges of no greater cost. That path remains in the final tree. Hence every rejected edge satisfies the fundamental-cycle MST certificate, proving optimality. Prim keeps one growing connected component; Kruskal can grow several components before joining them. Ties may give different optimal edge sets.

The elementary analysis sorts in O(mlogm) and tests each prospective edge by a search in the current forest, taking O(n) per edge and O(mn) overall for the simple-graph setting. The notes also state the improved O(mlogm+mα(m,n)) bound using an advanced component data structure; the provided Python code is not that implementation.

In Sheet 2, a rectangular grid contains every horizontal/vertical edge with independently sampled integer costs from 0 to 99. The completed code sorts dictionary entries by cost, represents components as a set of immutable frozenset vertex sets, finds the two endpoint components by scans, and replaces them with their union when distinct. It returns a dictionary of selected endpoint tuples and original weights. The starter instead returns the entire input edge dictionary, leaving all grid cycles present.

The grid tree defines a maze with exactly one graph path between every pair of cells. maze.py maps vertices and edge midpoints to display squares, labels costs and offers incremental or final rendering through processing_py. The driver exposes dimensions/block size and prints total selected cost and timings. The supplied screenshots illustrate full-grid and tree mazes; they provide no fixed benchmark or personal implementation result.

Linear programs, integer restrictions and the integer hull · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: concept

Separates continuous linear optimization from integer-feasible solutions through their convex hull.

Linear programs, integer restrictions and the integer hull

A linear program optimizes cTx over real variables subject to finitely many affine inequalities or equalities. A common maximization form has feasible polyhedron P={x∈Rn:Ax≤b,x≥0}. Adding x∈Zn produces an integer linear program; simply solving the continuous relaxation can yield a fractional optimum.

The integer hull is PI=conv(P∩Zn). Linear objectives over the integer points and their convex hull have the same supremum, since every finite convex combination has objective equal to the corresponding combination of objectives. However, the original relaxation P can be strictly larger. The class diagram illustrates a triangle with a fractional maximizing vertex and an integer hull with a different boundary and optimum.

The prerequisite theorem states polynomial-time solvability of linear programming, naming the ellipsoid method. For the algorithmic statement, coefficients must have finite rational encodings and the input size includes their bit lengths; this does not assert a polynomial-time method for arbitrary integer programs or the availability of an explicit small description of every integer hull. No ellipsoid algorithm construction is developed in this introductory block.

Independence systems, matroid augmentation and basis exchange · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: theorem

Characterizes matroids by augmentation and equal-sized bases in every restriction, with graphic, linear and uniform examples.

Independence systems, matroid augmentation and basis exchange

An independence system on finite E is a family I⊆2E containing ∅ and closed under taking subsets. A basis of F⊆E is an inclusion-maximal independent subset of F, not automatically one of largest cardinality. A circuit is a dependent set all of whose proper subsets are independent.

A matroid additionally satisfies augmentation: if I,J∈I and |I|<|J|, some e∈J⧵I makes I+e independent. It suffices to check cardinalities differing by one, by restricting the larger independent set. Equivalently, for every F⊆E, all bases of F have the same size. Augmentation rules out two different-sized maximal sets; conversely, a failed augmentation makes I a basis of I∪J while J extends to a larger basis there. The quantifier over every restriction matters.

Examples include the free matroid 2E, the uniform matroid {I:|I|≤k}, and a matrix's indexed columns with linear independence. Their bases have sizes |E|, min(k,|E|), and the column rank. In the graphic matroid independent edge sets are forests, circuits are graph cycles, and bases are maximal forests (spanning trees for connected graphs). For its augmentation proof, if no edge of the larger forest J joins separate components of I, each component of J lies in a component of I. The forest count |F|+#components=|V| would force |J|≤|I|, a contradiction.

All matroids have at least one basis: extend the empty set maximally on finite E. For any two bases B1,B2 and specified y∈B2⧵B1, some x∈B1⧵B2 satisfies B1−x+y is a basis. Start from (B1∩B2)+y and augment using elements of B1 until reaching their common rank. Exactly one element of B1⧵B2 remains excluded.

Sheet 3 illustrates loops and restrictions: {∅} is a rank-zero matroid, and all subsets of {a,b,c} of size at most two form a matroid even when the ground set has other elements that never occur. Missing required subsets or the empty set invalidates an independence system immediately. The family of sets disjoint from some basis of the rank-one uniform matroid on eight elements is all proper subsets, the rank-seven uniform matroid. In the sheet's uniform-rank-three proof, augmentation needs |Y|+1≤|X|≤3, correcting the reversed printed inequalities.

Greedy optimization characterizes matroids · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: theorem

Proves that descending-weight feasible insertion is optimal for every nonnegative weighting exactly for matroid independence systems.

Greedy optimization characterizes matroids

Sort elements of a finite independence system by nonincreasing nonnegative weight. Begin with G=∅ and insert each element if the result remains independent. This algorithm finds a maximum-weight independent set for every nonnegative rational weighting if and only if the system is a matroid.

For sufficiency, the greedy set is a basis. An optimum can also be extended to a basis without lowering its weight, including when some weights are zero; thus both can be compared at the common rank r. Write their elements in descending weight order as g1,…,gr and f1,…,fr. If the optimum were heavier, some index q would have w(fq)>w(gq). Augmentation of {g1,…,gq−1} by the independent prefix {f1,…,fq} supplies a feasible element of weight at least w(fq). That element was considered before gq and was feasible then by heredity, so greedy could not have skipped it. This contradiction proves optimality.

For necessity, a nonmatroid has a restriction F⊆E with bases B1,B2 of different sizes, say |B1|>|B2|. Give elements of B2 weight 1+ε, those of B1⧵B2 weight 1, and all others weight zero. Greedy takes all of B2, and its maximality in F prevents later weight-one additions. The feasible B1 is heavier for sufficiently small positive rational ε, since its cardinality advantage dominates the premium on B2⧵B1. Zero-weight additions outside F cannot repair the objective gap. The restriction is essential: a nonmatroid need not have different-sized bases on the full ground set, although the printed converse proof starts there.

The system is accessed through an independence oracle rather than an explicit list of all feasible subsets. Sorting costs O(|E|log|E|) comparisons and the algorithm uses |E| independence tests; actual runtime must include each oracle's implementation. The abstract constant-time oracle assumption does not make graph cycle detection free. Kruskal follows by applying this greedy structure to the graphic matroid after converting minimum spanning-tree costs to nonnegative maximization weights.

Residual reachability and the max-flow/min-cut certificate · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: theorem

Proves that absence of an augmenting path yields a saturated outgoing cut with zero incoming flow.

Residual reachability and the max-flow/min-cut certificate

A feasible flow is maximum exactly when its residual network has no source-sink path. If such a path exists, augmentation by its positive bottleneck increases the value, contradicting optimality.

Conversely, suppose no path exists and let S be all vertices reachable from s by positive-capacity residual arcs. Then s∈S and t∉S. Every original arc leaving S is saturated, otherwise its forward residual arc would reach another vertex. Every original arc entering S carries zero flow, otherwise its reverse residual arc would leave S. Therefore

val(f)=f(δout(S))−f(δin(S))=u(δout(S)).

The cut upper bound proves both maximum flow and minimum cut optimality. This also gives the max-flow/min-cut equality: the maximum feasible flow value equals minimum source-sink cut capacity. For rational capacities, terminating Ford-Fulkerson constructs both witnesses; the reachability argument certifies any feasible flow without requiring knowledge of how it was obtained.

The proof must distinguish outgoing saturation from incoming zero flow. The printed proof changes set letters and loses complement marks in some expressions; using the explicit incoming/outgoing boundaries above retains the cancellation and reachability argument unambiguously.

Tree structure and cut/cycle certificates for minimum spanning trees · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: theorem

Characterizes minimum spanning trees through local exchanges across fundamental cuts and cycles.

Tree structure and cut/cycle certificates for minimum spanning trees

A forest is cycle-free; a tree is a connected forest. On n vertices, a tree has n−1 edges and a unique path between every pair. Conversely, connectivity together with n−1 edges, or acyclicity together with n−1 edges, characterizes a tree. Removing any tree edge disconnects it into two components; adding a non-tree edge creates exactly one cycle. A forest with p components has n−p edges.

For a connected undirected graph with rational edge costs, a minimum spanning tree minimizes the sum of its n−1 edge costs. Given a spanning tree T, the following are equivalent:

  • T has minimum weight.
  • For every non-tree edge e={u,v}, all edges of the unique u-to-v path in T have cost at most c(e).
  • Each tree edge is cheapest across the cut formed by deleting it from T.
  • Its edges can be ordered so that each is cheapest across a cut crossed by none of the preceding chosen edges.

The exchange arguments explain necessity: replacing a more expensive tree edge on a fundamental cycle, or reconnecting a fundamental cut with a cheaper edge, improves the tree. For sufficiency of the ordered-cut criterion, choose an optimum agreeing with the proposed tree for the longest initial edge prefix. Add the first missing edge to this optimum. Its cycle must cross the certifying cut again; that other crossing edge is not in the agreed prefix. Exchanging it preserves optimal cost by the cheapest-cut property and increases the agreement, a contradiction. The fundamental-cut condition supplies such a certificate for any ordering of T.

The MST formulation permits negative costs even though the algorithm boxes restrict inputs to nonnegative costs: shifting every cost by the same constant leaves the ordering and every spanning-tree comparison unchanged, since all trees have n−1 edges. Likewise c′(e)=M−c(e), with M>maxec(e), turns minimization into positive-weight maximization because c′(T)=(n−1)M−c(T). This fixed-cardinality argument does not apply to arbitrary feasible sets of different sizes.

MST uniqueness and membership in the union of all optimum trees · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: method

Uses fundamental-path maximum costs to identify all edges that can occur in a minimum spanning tree.

MST uniqueness and membership in the union of all optimum trees

Distinct costs on every pair of edges imply a unique minimum spanning tree. For a precise exchange proof, suppose two optimum trees differ and select the cheapest edge in their symmetric difference, say e∈T1⧵T2. Deleting e from T1 gives a cut. The cycle in T2+e contains another edge f crossing that cut; f∉T1 and thus c(f)>c(e). Replacing f in T2 by e improves it, a contradiction. Selecting this cheapest differing edge supplies the ordering that the sheet solution leaves implicit in its “without loss of generality” step. Equal costs permit multiple optima but do not force them.

To find the union of the edge sets of all MSTs, first compute any one optimum T. Every edge of T belongs to the union. For a non-tree edge e={u,v}, let Me be the maximum cost along the unique u-to-v tree path. Optimality gives c(e)≥Me.

  • If c(e)=Me, exchange e with a maximum-cost path edge. The result is another optimum containing e.
  • If c(e)>Me, no optimum can contain e. Otherwise deleting it from that optimum gives a cut crossed by some edge f on the original tree path; c(f)≤Me<c(e), giving a strictly improving exchange.

A tree search computes Me in O(n). Testing all non-tree edges plus the initial O(mn) MST construction therefore takes O(mn). This computes edges appearing in at least one optimum, rather than edges common to every optimum. The official solution's concluding “every” wording must be read in light of its stated union task and exchange construction.

Augmentation failures in knapsack, matching, clique and tour systems · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: concept

Exhibits concrete hereditary feasible families whose lack of augmentation prevents general matroid greedy guarantees.

Augmentation failures in knapsack, matching, clique and tour systems

Hereditary feasibility does not suffice for matroid structure. Counterexamples identify an independent I smaller than J, with no element of J⧵I addable to I.

For knapsack with capacity 10 and item weights 9,5,5, the singleton weight-nine item and the pair of weight-five items are both maximal feasible sets with different cardinalities. Neither weight-five item can augment the singleton. This shows the knapsack family is not a matroid in general; special capacities/weights can still define matroids.

For matching on a four-vertex path a−b−c−d, take I={bc} and J={ab,cd}. Each proposed addition shares an endpoint with bc, violating matching feasibility. For clique vertex sets, a disjoint triangle and edge give maximal cliques of sizes three and two, again violating augmentation.

The traveling-salesman independence family consists of edge sets contained in some Hamiltonian cycle of a complete graph. It contains the empty set and is hereditary, but need not be a matroid. A concrete four-vertex instance has I={12,23,34} and Hamiltonian cycle J={12,24,34,13}. The set I is contained in the cycle closed by edge 14; adding either edge of J⧵I={24,13} creates a vertex of degree three, impossible in any Hamiltonian cycle. Thus |I|=3<4=|J| but no augmentation is possible. This makes explicit the sheet's two-edge tour-switch obstruction.

These failures concern the displayed feasible-set systems. They do not say every instance lacks a greedy optimum, only that the matroid theorem cannot promise success for every objective weight.

Partition quotas and bipartite matching through intersected constraints · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: concept

Models disjoint-block quotas by a matroid and bipartite matchings by two endpoint-partition matroids.

Partition quotas and bipartite matching through intersected constraints

Partition a finite ground set into disjoint blocks E1,E2 and impose nonnegative integer quotas d1,d2. The family

I={F⊆E:|F∩E1|≤d1, |F∩E2|≤d2}

is a partition matroid: it contains the empty set and is hereditary; when |J|>|I|, some block contains more elements of J than I, and an element in that block can augment I without exceeding its quota.

For a bipartite graph, partition its edge ground set once by left endpoint and once by right endpoint, giving every block quota one. Each constraint family is a partition matroid, but a matching must satisfy both. Thus matchings form their intersection; that intersection need not itself be a matroid, consistent with the four-vertex-path augmentation counterexample.

The lecture also encodes bipartite matching as flow: add a source linked to each left vertex, direct graph edges left-to-right, and link every right vertex to a sink, all with unit capacities. An integral feasible flow selects graph edges carrying one unit, and the source/sink unit capacities enforce at most one selected edge at each endpoint. Conversely, each matching gives such a flow of the same cardinality. Integrality is essential for reading a flow directly as a matching; a fractional flow is not itself an edge subset. The later matching chapter can develop the algorithmic consequences of this encoding.

Prim growth across a cheapest boundary edge · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: algorithm

Grows one connected tree and maintains cheapest connecting edges to obtain a quadratic-time MST algorithm.

Prim growth across a cheapest boundary edge

Start with an arbitrary vertex v0 of a connected undirected weighted graph. While the selected vertex set S is not all of V, add a cheapest edge of δ(S), together with its exterior endpoint. Exactly one vertex joins at each step, so the partial graph stays connected and cycle-free and finishes as a spanning tree after n−1 additions.

Each selected edge is minimum on a cut crossed by none of the earlier selected edges. The ordered-cut optimality certificate therefore proves minimum total weight. Ties can be resolved arbitrarily, but can lead to different optimum trees; the initial vertex can also change the selection order. The worked eight-vertex lecture example has optimum weight 14. Sheet 2's separate execution graph has stated MST cost 23; neither figure asserts a unique edge order without a starting point and tie rule.

For an O(n2) implementation, store for each exterior vertex the cheapest edge connecting it to the current tree, or infinity if none exists. Scan these keys to choose the next vertex and update keys using edges incident to the newly added vertex. Each iteration uses O(n) work with suitable adjacency access, over n−1 iterations. The notes also state O(m+nlogn) using a Fibonacci heap, without developing that data structure. Connectedness ensures a crossing edge exists until completion; a disconnected input requires separate component forests rather than one spanning tree.

Residual augmentation and Ford-Fulkerson termination · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: algorithm

Updates forward and reverse residual arcs and distinguishes integral, rational and irrational capacity behavior.

Residual augmentation and Ford-Fulkerson termination

For a feasible flow in a network without antiparallel original arcs, each original e=(v,w) contributes a forward residual arc of capacity u(e)−f(e) if positive, and a reverse arc (w,v) of capacity f(e) if positive. A reverse traversal cancels previously sent flow; it does not add flow to a new original connection.

On a residual source-sink path, let γ be the smallest residual capacity. Increase original flow by γ on forward traversals and decrease it by γ on reverse traversals. The bottleneck guarantees capacity feasibility, while one incoming and one outgoing path adjustment preserve each internal balance. Net source outflow increases by γ>0.

Ford-Fulkerson starts from zero and repeats arbitrary residual-path augmentations until none exists. With integral capacities every flow and bottleneck remains integral, each augmentation increases the value by at least one, and cut bounds force finite termination. In particular an integral maximum flow exists. Rational capacities reduce to this argument by multiplying by a common denominator and scaling back. This proves termination, not a polynomial bit-complexity bound.

In the four-vertex example, four outer arcs have capacity N and the middle arc capacity 1. Choosing the two outer paths attains value 2N in two augmentations. Alternating paths using the middle arc forward and backward can instead require 2N unit augmentations. Since N takes only logarithmically many bits, arbitrary path selection can be exponential in input length. The notes further state that irrational capacities can cause nontermination and even convergence to a suboptimal limiting value; no explicit irrational construction is developed on these pages.

The worked six-vertex sequence illustrates cancellation on reverse residual arcs and ends with the capacity-six cut certificate. It is evidence of algorithm execution on that diagram, not a runtime benchmark.

Choosing shortest-path algorithms by graph and weight assumptions · tum-combinatorial-optimization · Type: method

Matches acyclicity and edge-cost restrictions to linear-time DAG, Dijkstra and Bellman–Ford bounds.

Choosing shortest-path algorithms by graph and weight assumptions

The shortest-path problem seeks an s-to-t path minimizing the sum of its arc costs; an unreachable target has no such path. The prerequisite results distinguish three regimes, with n vertices and m arcs:

  • In a directed acyclic graph, use a topological order and relax outgoing arcs after their predecessors have been processed. This takes O(n+m) operations and permits negative costs because no directed cycle can occur.
  • With nonnegative costs in a general digraph, Dijkstra's algorithm applies. A basic implementation takes O(n2), while the stated Fibonacci-heap bound is O(m+nlogn); the prerequisite notes do not develop the advanced data structure.
  • With negative costs, Bellman–Ford gives the stated O(nm) bound when no relevant negative cycle occurs, and its extension detects a negative cycle. The notes impose the stronger global absence of negative cycles for the shortest-path assertion.

A negative cycle that can be reached from s and can reach t makes costs of unrestricted s-to-t traversals unbounded below; it must not be confused with minimizing over simple paths or with a negative cycle in an irrelevant component. Dijkstra's nonnegativity condition cannot be dropped merely because a particular graph happens to have a finite answer.

Exercise 3 supplies a directed weighted graph including an arc of cost −3; the official answer states minimum path weight 11. In its diagram a route attaining 11 goes from s to the middle-left vertex (4), the center (3), the top vertex immediately right of s (−3), the next top vertex (3), the lower vertex beneath it (1), then t (3). This is a weighted example distinct from the unit-edge maze task.

The continuation states Bellman–Ford's dynamic-programming viewpoint: track minimum costs of source-to-vertex traversals of a prescribed number of edges. Such traversals may repeat vertices and edges, so they use a broader convention than the course's edge-nonrepeating “walk” definition. The notes' Theorem 1.17 states shortest path or negative-cycle output in O(nm).

Banach and Hilbert adjoints, annihilators and compactness · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Relates dual composition and Hilbert adjoints to annihilators, range closures, kernel identities and preservation of compactness.

Banach and Hilbert adjoints, annihilators and compactness

Dual composition

For bounded T:X→Y, define T*:Y*→X* by T*y*=y*∘T. Thus

⟨Tx,y*⟩Y,Y*=⟨x,T*y*⟩X,X*,‖T*‖=‖T‖,T**JX=JYT.

The norm equality follows by interchanging suprema over the two unit balls and using norming functionals. The evaluation pairing is continuous bilinear, with |x*(x)|≤‖x*‖‖x‖. It is not the complex Hilbert inner product: the Riesz identification is conjugate-linear under the convention linear in the first slot.

For the inclusion j:U↪X of a normed subspace, j*f=f|U: its adjoint is restriction of functionals.

If T is an isomorphism, (T*)−1=(T−1)*; if it is a surjective isometry, so is T*. The map T↦T* is an isometric linear embedding of operator spaces, not generally surjective onto all maps between the duals.

Hilbert identification and examples

Riesz representation gives the unique Hilbert adjoint characterized by ⟨Tx,y⟩=⟨x,T*y⟩. Then

kerT=(ranT*)⟂,kerT*=(ranT)⟂,T is isometric⟺T*T=I.

The right shift on ℓ2 has left-shift adjoint, T*T=I, but TT* is projection onto e1⟂; isometry does not imply surjectivity. In complex Hilbert space, T=T* iff ⟨Tx,x⟩ is real for every x: polarization with x+y and x+iy recovers the cross terms. This characterization depends on the complex field.

For multiplication Mϕ on Lp, 1≤p<∞, the Banach adjoint is multiplication by ϕ in the bilinear dual-density convention f↦∫fg. In complex Hilbert L2, the Hilbert adjoint instead multiplies by ϕ―. It is self-adjoint iff ϕ is real a.e. Likewise a real integral kernel is transposed by the adjoint; the complex Hilbert kernel is conjugate-transposed.

Annihilators and compactness

For normed spaces,

T(X)―=(kerT*)∘={y∈Y:y*(y)=0 for all y*∈kerT*}.

One inclusion follows from composition; Hahn–Banach separates any point outside the closed range closure to prove the reverse. The closure cannot be omitted without an additional closed-range hypothesis.

For Banach spaces, T is compact iff T* is compact. Restrict a bounded sequence of Y* functionals to the compact closure of T(BX): the restrictions are uniformly bounded and Lipschitz, hence have a uniformly convergent subsequence by Arzelà–Ascoli. Uniform convergence there is precisely the needed Cauchy control of T*yn*. Conversely compactness of T* gives compactness of T**JX=JYT; the closed isometric image JY(Y) converts its limits back into Y.

Arzelà–Ascoli compactness and continuous-kernel operators · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Characterizes compact closure of bounded equicontinuous families on compact domains and applies it to continuous-kernel operators.

Arzelà–Ascoli compactness and continuous-kernel operators

Criterion

Let K⊂Rn be compact. A family F⊂C(K;K) is relatively compact in the sup norm—its closure is compact—iff it is bounded and equicontinuous. Equicontinuity means: for each x∈K and ε>0, a single δ>0 controls |f(x)−f(y)|<ε for every f∈F when y∈K, ‖x−y‖<δ.

A uniform Lipschitz constant suffices. On a convex domain, uniformly bounded first derivatives imply a uniform Lipschitz estimate by integrating along line segments. Domain geometry matters for that derivative argument; bounded derivatives on an arbitrary disconnected domain do not by themselves give a global Lipschitz bound.

The criterion concerns compactness of the closure of the family, not automatic closedness of the family itself.

Continuous-kernel integral operator

For continuous k:[0,1]2→R, define

(Tf)(x)=∫01k(x,t)f(t)dt

on C([0,1]). Continuity under the integral makes Tf continuous, and ‖Tf‖∞≤‖k‖∞‖f‖∞. The image of the unit ball is bounded. Uniform continuity of k also gives

|Tf(x)−Tf(y)|≤∫01|k(x,t)−k(y,t)|dt

uniformly for ‖f‖∞≤1. Thus its closure is compact by Arzelà–Ascoli. This establishes compact-operator behavior through a function-family criterion, beyond a boundedness estimate alone.

Baire category and the obstruction to countable-dimensional Banach spaces · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Uses dense-open intersections in complete metric spaces to rule out countably infinite algebraic bases for Banach spaces.

Baire category and the obstruction to countable-dimensional Banach spaces

Dense-open intersection theorem

Let (X,d) be a complete metric space and Un⊂X countably many open dense sets. Then ⋂n=1∞Un is dense in X. Density means intersection with every nonempty open V, not equality with X.

Nested-ball proof: choose a closed ball K(x1,r1)⊂U1∩V. Inductively choose positive rn<1/n with

K(xn,rn)⊂Un∩B(xn−1,rn−1).

Openness and density allow each choice. All later centers lie in an arbitrarily small earlier ball, so they are Cauchy. Completeness gives a limit x; closedness of each nested ball places x in every Un and in V.

Application to finite sequences and polynomials

A set is nowhere dense when the interior of its closure is empty, and meagre (first category) when it is a countable union of nowhere dense sets. In a nonempty complete metric space, the complement of a countable union of closed nowhere dense sets is dense. Equivalently, any countable closed cover has a member with nonempty interior. The notes mention continuous nowhere-differentiable functions as a dense-set application, without providing that proof.

Suppose an infinite-dimensional normed space is the union of an increasing sequence of finite-dimensional subspaces An. Each An is closed and proper, hence has empty interior. Its complement Un is open dense, but

⋂nUn=X⧵⋃nAn=∅.

Baire therefore rules out completeness.

In particular, no norm can turn the space ce of finitely supported sequences into a Banach space: take An=span{e1,…,en}. The same obstruction applies to the algebraic polynomial space R[t]. This is stronger than failure of completeness for one particular norm, and does not apply to uncountable-dimensional Banach spaces merely because they are separable.

Category and measure describe different notions of size

Enumerate Q={am:m≥1}. For each n≥1, surround am by an open interval Imn of length 2−(m+n). Then Bn=⋃mImn is open dense and has Lebesgue measure at most 2−n. Therefore

B=⋂nBn,A=R⧵B

partition R, with B null and A=⋃n(R⧵Bn) of first category: each complement is closed with empty interior. A meagre set can thus have full Lebesgue measure, while a dense countable intersection of open sets can be null.

Normed spaces, completeness and function-space examples · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Develops norm completeness through sequence and function spaces, with examples distinguishing completeness from other topological properties.

Normed spaces, completeness and function-space examples

Framework

Over K=R or C, a norm is positive definite, absolutely homogeneous and subadditive. It defines d(x,y)=‖x−y‖, open/closed balls and sequential convergence. A Banach space is a normed space in which every Cauchy sequence converges in the space. The closure, interior and boundary are taken in this norm topology.

A complete linear subspace is closed in its ambient normed space; a closed subspace of a Banach space is complete. For the latter, take the ambient limit of a Cauchy sequence and use closedness. Finite-dimensional subspaces are closed: equivalence of finite-dimensional norms makes them complete. Every proper linear subspace has empty interior, since scaling a vector outside it gives arbitrarily small perturbations outside it.

Principal examples and proof mechanisms

  • Kn with any norm is complete. On a finite product X1×⋯×Xm, the component p-norms and maximum norm are equivalent; convergence is componentwise and completeness holds exactly when every factor is complete. Addition and scalar multiplication are continuous.
  • Bounded functions B(D;K) are complete in the supremum norm. For compact metric D, continuous functions C(D;K) form a closed subspace: a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
  • Lp(D;K), 1≤p<∞, uses (∫D|f|p)1/p and identifies functions equal almost everywhere. Without that identification the expression is not positive definite on individual functions.
  • ℓ∞ consists of bounded sequences; c and c0 are its closed subspaces of convergent and null sequences. A uniform approximation argument transfers the scalar Cauchy or null property to the limit.
  • ℓp, 1≤p<∞, uses (∑k|xk|p)1/p. Minkowski on finite sums proves the triangle inequality. For completeness, a norm-Cauchy sequence has coordinatewise limits; bounds on every finite partial sum pass to these limits, then to the infinite sum, establishing membership and norm convergence.

What completeness does not imply

In C([0,1]) with the sup norm, V={f:f(0)=f(1)=0} is closed with empty interior. It need not give convergent subsequences: triangular functions of height n in V are unbounded.

The same vector space C([0,1]), equipped instead with ‖·‖2, is an incomplete pre-Hilbert space. Let fn be zero up to 1/2, increase linearly to one on [1/2,1/2+1/n], then remain one. For m≥n,

‖fn−fm‖22≤1/n.

An L2 limit would equal the step function almost everywhere; no continuous function can be zero on the left half and one on the right half. Completeness therefore depends on both the space and its norm; taking an inner product alone does not make a Hilbert space.

Bounded linear operators and operator norms · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Connects linear continuity to uniform norm bounds and proves completeness of operator spaces when the codomain is Banach.

Bounded linear operators and operator norms

Continuity and the operator space

For linear T:X→Y between normed spaces, continuity everywhere, continuity at zero, a bound ‖Tx‖≤C‖x‖, and Lipschitz continuity are equivalent. To prove the nontrivial implication, failure of a bound yields xn with ‖Txn‖>n‖xn‖; normalization produces zn→0 but ‖Tzn‖>1.

On L(X;Y),

‖T‖=supx≠0‖Tx‖‖x‖=sup‖x‖≤1‖Tx‖,‖ST‖≤‖S‖‖T‖.

For nonzero X one may also take the supremum over the unit sphere. If Y is Banach, L(X;Y) is Banach even when X is not: an operator-norm Cauchy sequence defines Tx=limTnx; its uniform Cauchy bound proves boundedness and norm convergence. In particular, X*=L(X;K) is complete.

The initial ODE example becomes an operator equation:

y′=f(t,y),y(t0)=y0⟺y(t)=y0+∫t0tf(s,y(s))ds.

This motivates a map on continuous functions; the opening example alone supplies no contraction or existence theorem.

Norm-sensitive examples

  • Mf(t)=tf(t) is bounded on C([0,1]) with the sup norm.
  • Tf(t)=tf(1) is bounded in the sup norm, but not when both spaces use the L1 norm: fn(t)=tn has norm 1/(n+1), while Tfn(t)=t has fixed norm 1/2.
  • On finitely supported sequences with the sup norm, Tek=k defines an unbounded functional.
  • Polynomials with coefficient norm ‖∑aktk‖coef=∑|ak| are isometric to finite sequences with the ℓ1 norm. Translation f(t)↦f(t+1) is unbounded: tm has norm 1 but its translate has coefficient norm 2m. Integration f(t)↦∫0tf(s)ds is bounded by 1. The worksheet's subscript p here names this coefficient norm, not a variable exponent.

Closed graph theorem and differentiation on an incomplete domain · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Derives boundedness from a closed graph on Banach domains and contrasts it with differentiation on an incomplete domain.

Closed graph theorem and differentiation on an incomplete domain

Theorem and proof mechanism

Let X,Y be Banach and T:X→Y an everywhere-defined linear map. Then T is bounded exactly when graphT={(x,Tx):x∈X} is closed in the product norm.

Boundedness implies that xn→x, Txn→y forces y=Tx. Conversely a closed linear graph is a Banach subspace of X×Y. Its coordinate projection onto X is a bounded linear bijection; the bounded inverse theorem gives a bounded inverse Q:x↦(x,Tx). Composition with the Y-projection proves T bounded.

This replaces a direct estimate with a uniqueness-of-limit test: it is enough to identify y whenever both xn and Txn already converge. It does not assert boundedness for operators defined only on arbitrary noncomplete domains.

Why the hypotheses matter

Let D:C1([−1,1])→C([−1,1]), Df=f′, with both spaces using the sup norm. Its graph is closed: uniform limits fn→f, fn′→g satisfy f(t)−f(0)=∫0tg(s)ds, so f′=g. But fn(t)=tn has norm 1 and ‖Dfn‖∞=n; D is unbounded.

There is no contradiction: C1([−1,1]) with only the sup norm is incomplete. The functions t2+1/n converge uniformly to |t|, which is not C1.

Everywhere-defined formal adjoints: Hellinger–Toeplitz

If linear maps A,B:H→H on an entire Hilbert space satisfy ⟨Ax,z⟩=⟨x,Bz⟩ for all x,z, both are bounded. Indeed, xn→x, Axn→y gives

⟨y,z⟩=limn⟨xn,Bz⟩=⟨x,Bz⟩=⟨Ax,z⟩.

Therefore y=Ax, its graph is closed, and the closed graph theorem applies. The argument for B is symmetric. The full-domain hypothesis is crucial; this is not a boundedness result for arbitrary densely defined operators.

The same graph argument proves that an everywhere-defined linear map T:X→Y between Banach spaces is bounded if it preserves weakly null sequences. For xn→x and Txn→y, the hypothesis gives T(xn−x)⇀0, while strong convergence gives T(xn−x)⇀y−Tx. Uniqueness of weak limits implies y=Tx.

Compact operators, weak-to-strong continuity and norm approximation · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Establishes sequential compactness criteria, weak-to-strong mapping and norm-closedness, with finite-rank and sequence-space examples.

Compact operators, weak-to-strong continuity and norm approximation

Equivalent criteria and weak inputs

A linear map T:X→Y between Banach spaces is compact if the image of the closed unit ball has compact closure. Equivalently, every bounded set has relatively compact image, or every bounded sequence has an image subsequence converging in norm. In the sequential criterion, points in the closure of the image can be approximated by actual image points with errors 1/n. Compact operators are bounded because relatively compact sets are bounded.

If xn⇀x, then Txn→Tx in norm. The inputs are bounded. Every image subsequence has a norm-convergent further subsequence; testing any such limit with y*∈Y* gives y*(Tx), because y*T∈X*. Dual separation identifies every cluster limit as Tx; a subsequence staying away from Tx would contradict compactness. No weakly convergent subsequence of every bounded input sequence is presumed.

Stability and finite-rank approximation

Compact operators form a linear, operator-norm closed subspace K(X;Y). For Tm→T and bounded xn, diagonal extraction makes each Tmxnk converge. Then

‖Txnk−Txnj‖≤2C‖T−Tm‖+‖Tmxnk−Tmxnj‖

makes the selected image Cauchy; completeness of Y supplies its limit. Composing a compact map on either side with a compatible bounded map preserves compactness. Finite-rank bounded maps are compact, so their operator-norm limits are compact. The reverse approximation assertion is false for arbitrary Banach spaces; the notes cite Enflo's counterexample, without constructing it.

A surjective compact map between Banach spaces must have finite-dimensional target. Open mapping puts a target ball inside its relatively compact unit-ball image; an infinite-dimensional normed space cannot have a compact closed ball.

Explicit tests

  • On ℓp, 1≤p<∞, (Dax)n=anxn for a∈ℓ∞ is compact iff a∈c0. Truncation has error ‖Da−Da(N)‖=supn>N|an|. If coefficients stay away from zero on a subsequence, its images of coordinate vectors stay separated.
  • The inclusion ℓg1↪ℓ1, ‖x‖g=∑n|xn|, is compact: factor through the isometry x↦(nxn) and compact diagonal multiplication by 1/n.
  • The unilateral right shift on ℓp is not compact: coordinate-vector images have no norm-convergent subsequence.
  • More generally, an isometry on a Banach space is compact iff the space is finite-dimensional: it preserves the unit-ball distances, so relative compactness of its image would make the original closed unit ball compact.
  • C1([0,1])↪C([0,1]), with the derivative-inclusive domain norm, is compact by uniform boundedness and equicontinuity of the image ball. Rellich similarly gives compact Sobolev-to-Lp inclusions under its domain hypotheses.

Spectral decomposition and finite-rank approximation of compact normal maps · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Expands compact normal maps in orthogonal eigenvectors and bounds finite-rank truncation errors by omitted eigenvalue magnitudes.

Spectral decomposition and finite-rank approximation of compact normal maps

Let T be compact and normal on a complex separable Hilbert space H. For Uλ=ker(λI−T), choose an orthonormal basis Eλ; for nonzero eigenvalues each Uλ is finite-dimensional, and their union is at most countable. Let {ej} enumerate those nonzero-eigenvalue basis vectors, with repeated λj according to multiplicity, and let E0 be a basis of kerT.

Orthogonal representation

Then E0∪{ej} is an orthonormal basis, and

H=kerT⊕span―{ej},ranT―=span―{ej},
Tx=∑λ≠0λPλx=∑jλj⟨x,ej⟩ej,

where Pλ is orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace and the sums converge in norm. The range closure is necessary; compact infinite-rank maps need not have closed range.

For completeness, the orthogonal complement V of all the eigenvectors is invariant under T and T*. If the compact normal restriction T|V were nonzero, its spectral radius equals its positive norm, giving a nonzero eigenvector in V, a contradiction. Thus T|V=0; then V⊂kerT and orthogonality forces V=0.

For nonzero T, ‖T‖=maxj|λj|; the zero operator has norm zero without requiring a nonzero-eigenvalue maximum. Separability can be removed: the nonzero-eigenvalue part remains at most countable, while the kernel may have an uncountable orthonormal basis.

Operator-norm approximation

Define Tnx=∑j=1nλj⟨x,ej⟩ej. Then

‖T−Tn‖=supj>n|λj|⟶0,

with error zero after the last term for finite rank. The upper bound uses orthogonality; testing omitted unit eigenvectors gives the lower bound. Compactness leaves only finitely many eigenvalues above any fixed magnitude, including their finite multiplicities, so the tail tends to zero. The enumeration is a mathematical representation, not the chronology of source material.

Compact-operator spectra and spectral effects of compact perturbations · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Derives finite-multiplicity nonzero eigenvalues, accumulation only at zero and spectral agreement outside eigenvalues under compact perturbations.

Compact-operator spectra and spectral effects of compact perturbations

Nonzero spectral points

For compact S on a Banach space, every nonzero spectral value λ is an eigenvalue with finite-dimensional eigenspace. Indeed, λI−S=λ(I−λ−1S) is Fredholm of index zero. If injective it is surjective, hence invertible. Its kernel is finite-dimensional by the Fredholm property.

For every ε>0, there are only finitely many spectral values with |λ|≥ε; consequently there are at most countably many nonzero spectral values, with zero the only possible accumulation point. If infinitely many distinct eigenvalues stayed away from zero, their eigenvectors would generate strictly increasing finite-dimensional invariant spaces Xn. Riesz's lemma selects unit yn∈Xn at distance at least 1/2 from Xn−1. The relation λnyn−Syn∈Xn−1 then makes the Syn separated by at least ε/2, contradicting compactness.

On infinite-dimensional X, zero is always spectral: otherwise I=S−1S would be compact. It need not be an eigenvalue, as Volterra integration illustrates.

For a square-integrable-kernel integral map S, the second-kind equation

λx(t)−∫01k(s,t)x(s)ds=y(t),λ≠0,

is uniquely solvable for every y∈L2 exactly when λ is not an eigenvalue. Otherwise homogeneous solutions form a finite-dimensional space and adjoint compatibility conditions control inhomogeneous solvability.

Comparing compactly perturbed operators

If S−T is compact, then

σ(S)⧵M=σ(T)⧵M,M=σp(S)∪σp(T).

For the key step, if T were invertible, then S=T[I+T−1(S−T)]. The bracket is identity plus compact, so is either invertible or has a nonzero kernel. Thus a spectral non-eigenvalue of S must also be spectral for T. Apply this argument to λI−S,λI−T, then interchange them.

This permits changes at eigenvalues; it does not assert equality of complete spectra or invariance of individual eigenvalues.

Complemented Banach subspaces and bounded projections · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Distinguishes algebraic complements from closed Banach decompositions and constructs bounded projections in finite-dimensional cases.

Complemented Banach subspaces and bounded projections

Algebraic versus topological decomposition

An algebraic complement V of U⊂X satisfies U∩V=0 and U+V=X. Such complements exist by extending a vector-space basis. In a Banach space a complemented decomposition X=U⊕V additionally requires both subspaces closed. Algebraic complement existence alone does not provide continuous coordinate projections.

For closed U, a closed complement exists iff a bounded projection P:X→X satisfies P2=P, P(X)=U. Given such P, V=kerP is closed and x=Px+(I−P)x. Conversely, for closed U,V, the addition map from Banach U×V to X is a bounded bijection; bounded inverse makes the coordinate projection continuous.

Finite dimension and codimension

For finite-dimensional U=span{ui}i=1n, extend its coordinate functionals to fi∈X* by Hahn–Banach. Then

Px=∑i=1nfi(x)ui

is a bounded projection onto U. If U is closed and dim(X/U)<∞, any algebraic complement is finite-dimensional, hence closed. Codimension equals the dimension of any complement.

Every closed Hilbert subspace has its orthogonal complement. General Banach spaces need not: the notes state that C([0,1]) is not complemented in L∞(0,1). They also state, without proofs, the Lindenstrauss–Tzafriri characterization of spaces whose every closed subspace is complemented as spaces isomorphic to Hilbert space, and the contrasting Gowers–Maurey example.

Explicit decompositions

  • In C([0,1]), functions vanishing at 0 have complement the constants and codimension 1.
  • Functions vanishing at both endpoints have complement span{1,x} and codimension 2.
  • In C([−1,1]), even and odd continuous functions are complementary via f(x)=[f(x)+f(−x)]/2+[f(x)−f(−x)]/2. Both dimensions are infinite.
  • In convergent sequences c, the null sequences c0 have complement the constant sequences; x=(x−limx)+(limx)1, so the codimension is 1.

Continuous extension of bounded operators from dense subspaces · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Extends bounded linear maps uniquely from dense subspaces into Banach codomains while preserving the operator norm.

Continuous extension of bounded operators from dense subspaces

Extension from a dense subspace

Let X be normed, Y Banach, U⊂X a dense linear subspace, and S:U→Y bounded linear. There is a unique bounded linear extension T:X→Y, with ‖T‖=‖S‖.

For un→x, set Tx=limSun. Boundedness makes Sun Cauchy; completeness of Y supplies its limit, and the same bound proves independence from the approximating sequence. Density proves uniqueness and equality of norms. Completeness of the codomain, not necessarily X, is required. This is not Hahn–Banach extension from an arbitrary subspace.

For scalar-valued maps this shows that restriction from X* to U* is an isometric isomorphism whenever U is dense in normed X. Injectivity follows from density and continuity; extension gives surjectivity and equality of norms. No completeness of U or X is needed because the scalar field is complete.

Projection onto closed convex sets in Hilbert spaces · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Proves nearest-point existence and uniqueness in Hilbert spaces and characterizes projections by a variational inequality.

Projection onto closed convex sets in Hilbert spaces

Existence and uniqueness

Let H be Hilbert and K⊂H nonempty, closed and convex. For every x∈H there is a unique PKx∈K satisfying

‖x−PKx‖=infz∈K‖x−z‖=:d.

For a minimizing sequence yn∈K, the parallelogram identity and convexity give

‖yn−ym‖2≤2‖x−yn‖2+2‖x−ym‖2−4d2→0.

Completeness supplies a limit, closedness keeps it in K, and continuity of the norm proves attainment. Applying the same estimate to two minimizers proves uniqueness.

Variational characterization and stability

For y∈K,

y=PKx⟺Re⟨x−y,z−y⟩≤0for every z∈K.

The forward implication follows by testing the segment y+t(z−y) and letting t↓0; the reverse follows by expanding ‖x−z‖2. Applying this inequality to PKx and PKx~, then adding and using Cauchy–Schwarz, yields

‖PKx−PKx~‖≤‖x−x~‖.

Thus the best approximation is nonexpansive. It is not generally a linear map; linearity holds for closed subspaces.

Closedness is substantive

The finite sequences ce are dense but not closed in ℓ2. For x∈ℓ2⧵ce, the distance to ce is zero but no finite sequence attains it. Completeness of the ambient space does not compensate for a nonclosed feasible set.

Minkowski functionals and separation of convex sets · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Builds sublinear gauges from convex sets and uses them to separate points and convex sets under precise openness or closedness assumptions.

Minkowski functionals and separation of convex sets

From geometry to a sublinear functional

For A⊂X, define MA(x)=inf{t>0:x/t∈A}, with value +∞ if no such t exists. The set is absorbing if this value is finite for every vector. For convex absorbing A, MA is sublinear: if x/t,y/s∈A, convexity places (x+y)/(t+s)∈A, giving subadditivity by approximation to the infima. Positive homogeneity follows by scaling.

In a normed space, 0∈intA implies absorption. The unit ball's gauge is the norm. For open convex A containing zero, MA(x)<1 on A; a ball of radius ε contained in A yields MA(x)≤‖x‖/ε.

Separation statements over the real field

For nonempty open convex K⊂X and x0∉K, there is a nonzero f∈X* with

f(x)<f(x0)(x∈K).

After translating K to contain zero, extend the functional tx0↦tMK(x0) dominated by MK. Gauge bounds give continuity, and f(x)<1≤f(x0) gives separation.

If K1,K2 are disjoint nonempty convex sets with K1 open, apply this result to K1−K2 and zero. There are f≠0 and α∈R such that

f(x1)<α≤f(x2)(xi∈Ki).

Openness makes the K1 inequality strict; it is not a uniform positive gap.

For nonempty closed convex K and x0∉K, the stronger point–set form holds:

f(x)≤α<f(x0)(x∈K).

Separate K from an open ball around x0 disjoint from K, reversing the functional's sign as needed. Closedness alone does not assert strict separation of every pair of closed convex sets.

A nonzero real continuous functional defines a hyperplane f(x)=α and its two half-spaces. For complex spaces, separation inequalities concern real parts of complex-linear functionals, not an order on C.

Density, separability and coordinate expansions · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Uses finite-coordinate approximation to distinguish separable sequence spaces from the nonseparable space of bounded sequences.

Density, separability and coordinate expansions

Density and countable approximation

A subset A is dense in X when A―=X, equivalently every nonempty open set meets A. A metric space is separable when it has a finite or countably infinite dense subset. Density is transitive through a dense intermediate subspace.

If span{xn:n∈N}―=X, rational finite linear combinations of xn form a countable dense set (use Q+iQ over C). Approximate a vector by a finite linear combination, then approximate its finitely many coefficients; the triangle inequality bounds the error. The worksheet supplies this proof of Proposition 1.17.

By Weierstrass approximation and coefficient approximation, polynomials with rational real/imaginary coefficients are dense in C([a,b];K) with the sup norm.

Finite sequences and the norm-dependent closure

Write ce for finitely supported sequences and ek for coordinate vectors. For x∈ℓp, 1≤p<∞, truncations PNx=∑k=1Nxkek satisfy

‖x−PNx‖pp=∑k>N|xk|p→0.

Thus ce―ℓp=ℓp and these spaces are separable. In the sup norm,

ce―ℓ∞=c0,‖x−PNx‖∞=supk>N|xk|.

Since c0 is closed, both inclusions follow. Consequently ∑kxkek converges in ℓ∞ exactly for x∈c0, not for every bounded sequence. Outside c0, arbitrarily distant partial sums differ by at least a fixed positive amount.

The characteristic sequences of all subsets of N form an uncountable family at pairwise distance 1. Their disjoint open balls of radius 1/2 exclude any countable dense set in ℓ∞. This is stronger than failure of density of ce.

The notes also state separability of Lp(D), 1≤p<∞, for open D⊂Rn, and nonseparability of L∞(D) for nonempty such D. For bounded domains they invoke density of continuous functions and polynomial approximation. For unbounded domains they use the closure of the union of bounded-domain spaces, interpreted by zero extension to D: bounded-support approximations, not a claim that every function has bounded support. The unbounded-domain density argument is sketched rather than proved in detail.

Diagonal multiplication, eigenvalues and spectral limit points · tum-functional-analysis · Type: method

Computes diagonal spectra from coefficient closures and relates eigenvalue multiplicity and truncation convergence to coefficient behavior.

Diagonal multiplication, eigenvalues and spectral limit points

For bounded coefficients a, (Dax)n=anxn defines a bounded map on ℓ2 or ℓ∞, with norm supn|an|. Its eigenvalues are exactly the attained coefficients {an}. At λ, eigenvectors are the nonzero sequences supported on {n:an=λ}, belonging to the ambient sequence space. In ℓ2, this is the closed span of the corresponding coordinate vectors; multiplicity is the size of that index set, possibly infinite. Self-adjointness in complex ℓ2 is equivalent to all coefficients being real.

The full spectrum is

σ(Da)={an:n≥1}―.

Outside this closure, infn|λ−an|>0, and

((λI−Da)−1y)n=ynλ−an

is bounded. If λ lies in the closure but is not attained, λI−Da is injective, yet its inverse on its range is unbounded: choose coordinate vectors with |λ−ank|→0. It cannot be surjective by bounded inverse. Spectral points therefore need not be eigenvalues.

For truncation a(N)=(a1,…,aN,0,…),

‖Da−Da(N)‖=supn>N|an|.

Thus finite-rank truncations converge in operator norm exactly when a∈c0. On ℓ2, this is also exactly the compactness condition; a merely bounded sequence of coefficients does not ensure convergence of this approximation.

Smooth regularization of distributions · tum-functional-analysis · Type: method

Approximates arbitrary distributions by smooth convolutions and tracks the limits of their derivatives, including Dirac examples.

Smooth regularization of distributions

Convolution through test functions

Choose a nonnegative, even, smooth compactly supported kernel ω, supported in the closed unit ball, with integral 1, and put ωn(z)=ndω(nz). For f∈D′, define

fn(x)=(f*ωn)(x)=f(ωn(·−x)).

The test-function dependence on x is smooth. Derivatives act on that dependence:

∂xαfn(x)=(−1)|α|f((∂αωn)(·−x)).

This sign matches τxφ(y)=φ(y−x). For a regular distribution Tu, evenness of the kernel identifies this construction with ordinary u*ωn.

Recovery of the distribution

For every φ∈D,

Tfn(φ)=f(φ*ωn)⟶f(φ).

Indeed φ*ωn→φ in D: supports stay in one enlarged compact set and each derivative converges uniformly. The supplement justifies interchanging the functional and integration by finite Riemann sums converging in the test-function space. Hence every distribution is a distributional limit of smooth regular distributions.

For regular f=Tu, convergence strengthens to u*ωn→u in Lloc1. Differentiation is continuous in D′, so

T∂αfn⟶∂αf.

If u has weak derivative v=∂αu∈Lloc1, then ∂α(u*ωn)=v*ωn→v locally in L1. Singular limits require distributional rather than integrable-density convergence.

Examples

  • δ0*ωn=ωn: concentrating smooth unit-mass bumps converge to a point mass.
  • In one dimension, δ0′*ωn=ωn′=n2ω′(nx), with positive derivative sign despite the minus sign in δ0′(φ)=−φ′(0).
  • The average on [−1,1] regularizes to 121[−1,1]*ωn, smoothing the two edges.

These distinguish approximation of an ordinary density, a singular mass and a derivative of a singular mass; a narrow smooth peak need not converge to a finite pointwise density.

Distributional derivatives and integrable weak derivatives · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Defines derivatives through test-function duality and distinguishes regular weak derivatives from singular derivatives such as point masses.

Distributional derivatives and integrable weak derivatives

Differentiation by duality

For f∈D′(Rd) and multi-index α, define

(∂αf)(φ)=(−1)|α|f(∂αφ).

It is again a distribution because differentiation of tests is continuous. Every distribution has derivatives of every order, and fn→f implies ∂αfn→∂αf, by evaluating the same derivative of each test.

For smooth u, integration by parts with compactly supported φ gives ∂αTu=T∂αu. Thus the definition extends classical differentiation without requiring pointwise values for general distributions.

Weak derivatives are regular distributional derivatives

If u,v∈Lloc1, then v is the weak α-derivative of u iff

∂αTu=Tv⟺∫vφ=(−1)|α|∫u∂αφ(φ∈Cc∞).

Uniqueness follows from uniqueness of regular densities. On an open domain the same definition uses tests supported inside that domain; no boundary term remains. Requiring both u and its weak derivatives in Lp leads to Sobolev spaces.

In one dimension, split integration at zero:

−∫R|x|φ′(x)dx=−∫−∞0φ+∫0∞φ=∫Rsign(x)φ(x)dx.

Consequently |x| has weak derivative sign(x). A second differentiation gives

∂xTsign(φ)=−∫sign(x)φ′(x)dx=2φ(0)=2δ0(φ).

This derivative exists as a distribution but has no locally integrable density. Distributional differentiability therefore does not imply weak differentiability by a function, even though the first derivative of |x| is bounded.

Test functions and distributions as generalized functions · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Defines test-function convergence and continuous linear distributions, distinguishing integrable densities from singular point evaluations.

Test functions and distributions as generalized functions

Test-function convergence

For real-valued functions on Rd, let D=Cc∞(Rd). Convergence φn→φ in D means all derivatives converge uniformly and all supports lie in one compact set. In C∞, only locally uniform convergence of each derivative is required. For nonzero φ∈D, n−1φ(x/n)→0 in C∞, but its expanding supports prevent convergence in D.

Differentiation is sequentially continuous on D: derivatives keep the common compact support and convergence of each further derivative is already required. Translations τξφ(x)=φ(x−ξ) are continuous, including dependence on ξ. With this sign convention,

τhejφ−φh⟶−∂jφin D.

The minus sign follows from the translated argument; the supplement's Example 3 prints the opposite sign.

Generalized functions

A distribution f∈D′ is a linear, sequentially continuous functional on D. Distributional convergence is convergence of fn(φ) for every test function, rather than pointwise convergence of ordinary functions. On each fixed compact support K, continuity is characterized by a finite-order bound

|f(φ)|≤MK∑|α|≤mK‖∂αφ‖∞,suppφ⊂K.

The restriction to tests supported in K is essential. The supplement uses sequential convergence and does not develop the full test-function topology.

A locally integrable u gives the regular distribution

Tu(φ)=∫Rduφ.

Its density is unique almost everywhere: zero pairings with every smooth compactly supported test imply u=0 a.e. Thus equivalence classes, rather than pointwise values, embed injectively in D′.

The average over a measurable finite-positive-volume set A has density 1A/|A|. By contrast, δξ(φ)=φ(ξ) is singular: no locally integrable density represents point evaluation. Further examples integrate directional derivatives of tests along compact smooth submanifolds against finite measures. This viewpoint models spatially weighted measurements and admits objects more singular than integrable densities.

Representations of dual spaces · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Constructs coefficient and integral representations of duals and explains their limits for bounded and convergent sequence spaces.

Representations of dual spaces

Sequence-space duals

For 1<p<∞, 1/p+1/q=1,

a∈ℓq↦Fa,Fa(x)=∑kakxk

is a linear isometric isomorphism ℓq≅(ℓp)*. Hölder gives absolute convergence and ‖Fa‖≤‖a‖q. Given F, set ak=F(ek). Testing on finite vectors with coordinates ak―|ak|q−2 (zero at ak=0) proves

(∑k=1N|ak|q)1/q≤‖F‖.

Pass to the limit, then use density of ce and continuous extension to get F=Fa and norm equality.

The same pairing gives

(c0)*≅ℓ1,(ℓ1)*≅ℓ∞.

Sheet 2 develops the first in full: the endpoint Hölder bound proves continuity; finite vectors with coordinates ak―/|ak|, set to 1 when ak=0, prove the lower norm bound. For arbitrary F∈(c0)*, those tests bound ∑k=1N|F(ek)|; coordinate truncation then reconstructs F. The notes state the second endpoint identification without proving it here. They do not identify (ℓ∞)* with ℓ1.

Scalar convention: these are linear functionals with the bilinear pairing ∑akxk, not a sesquilinear inner product. The conjugated phase in the complex test vector matters. Sheet 2 explicitly prints it; the notes' sign notation on pp. 16–17 must be interpreted consistently with this pairing.

Function-space representations and scope

Functionals on bounded sequences beyond summable coefficients

Each a∈ℓ1 defines Fa(x)=∑nanxn on ℓ∞, with norm ‖a‖1. But these do not exhaust (ℓ∞)*. The limit functional on c has norm 1; extend it to ℓ∞ by Hahn–Banach. Any coefficient representation would vanish on every coordinate vector, forcing all coefficients zero, yet its value at the constant sequence 1 is 1.

On real ℓ∞, a dominated extension gives a functional L with

lim infnxn≤L(x)≤lim supnxn.

Use the sublinear functional p(x)=lim supxn to dominate the limit on c, and apply domination also to −x. The inequalities imply boundedness and norm 1. No shift invariance is asserted by this construction.

For open D⊂Rn, the notes state

(Lp(D))*≅Lq(D)(1<p<∞),(L1(D))*≅L∞(D),

through Fh(f)=∫Dhf. Hölder establishes boundedness; the 1<p<∞ surjectivity sketch invokes Radon–Nikodym, rather than proving it in this chapter. These are Lebesgue spaces of almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

For compact D⊂Rn, the real dual C(D;R)* is represented by signed regular Borel measures via F(f)=∫Dfdμ, isometrically. This measure-representation result is stated, not proved here; it is distinct from the Hilbert-space Riesz theorem of Chapter 2.

Transporting a dual representation through an isomorphism

Using zero-based indexing, let a(x)=limnxn and Tx=(a(x),x0−a(x),x1−a(x),…), the bounded isomorphism c→c0. Its inverse is (Sy)n=y0+yn+1. If fz(y)=∑n≥0znyn, z∈ℓ1, then

(T*fz)(x)=a(x)(z0−∑n≥0zn+1)+∑n≥0zn+1xn.

All of c* is represented this way because T* is a bounded isomorphism, with inverse S*. This construction retains both the limit functional and the summable coordinate part; coordinate coefficients alone do not exhaust the dual of the convergent-sequence space in this form.

Fredholm operators, index stability and compatibility conditions · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Relates finite-dimensional defects and index stability to solvability and adjoint compatibility for identity-minus-compact equations.

Fredholm operators, index stability and compatibility conditions

Kernel, cokernel and index

For Banach spaces X,Y, bounded T:X→Y is Fredholm if dimkerT<∞ and dim(Y/T(X))<∞. Its range is then closed, and

indT=dimkerT−codimT(X).

Finite algebraic codimension of a bounded Banach-space operator's range already forces closedness: first divide by the closed kernel, then adjoin finitely many missing range directions to obtain a bounded bijection from a Banach product onto Y. Its bounded inverse identifies the original range as a closed subspace. In finite dimensions the index is simply dimX−dimY, independent of the particular map.

Differentiation D:C1([0,1])→C([0,1]), with ‖f‖∞+‖f′‖∞ on the domain, has constant kernel, surjective range and index 1. Restricting the domain to f(0)=f(1) keeps the one-dimensional kernel but restricts the range to {g:∫01g=0}; its cokernel has dimension 1 and the index is 0.

Powers of shifts provide explicit indices on ℓ2: the left shift by two has two-dimensional kernel and is onto, so its index is 2; the right shift by five has zero kernel and range of codimension 5, so its index is −5.

Identity minus a compact map

For compact S:X→X, I−S is Fredholm. On its kernel, the identity agrees with compact S, forcing finite dimension. Choose a closed complement V of the kernel. If the inverse of (I−S)|V were unbounded, there would be unit vn∈V with (I−S)vn→0. A convergent subsequence of Svn then forces vn to converge to a unit vector in V∩ker(I−S), a contradiction. The inverse is bounded, so the range is complete and closed. Compactness of S*, together with

(X/ran(I−S))*≅ker(I−S*),

gives finite codimension.

Stability of the index

Fredholm operators form an open set in operator norm; their index is locally constant. Split X=kerT⊕V, Y=T(X)⊕W, with the defect spaces finite-dimensional. The map (v,w)↦Tv+w is invertible. Small perturbations (v,w)↦Av+w remain invertible by the Neumann perturbation argument. Comparing the remaining finite-dimensional kernel and range directions shows indA=indT.

Consequently the index is constant along continuous Fredholm paths. The path I−tS, 0≤t≤1, consists of Fredholm operators and starts at index 0. Therefore ind(I−S)=0.

Solvability alternative

For a Fredholm map T:X→X of index 0, injectivity is equivalent to surjectivity. Either every Tx=y has a unique solution, or the homogeneous problem has a nonzero finite-dimensional solution space and

Tx=y is solvable⟺y*(y)=0∀y*∈kerT*.

In the second case dimkerT=dimkerT*, and all solutions, when they exist, differ by kerT. These compatibility conditions use closedness of the range; annihilating the adjoint kernel would otherwise characterize only the range closure.

Hahn–Banach extension and norming functionals · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Extends dominated linear functionals without increasing their norm and derives norming functionals and minimal-extension properties.

Hahn–Banach extension and norming functionals

Dominated extension

On a real vector space X, let p:X→R be sublinear: positively homogeneous for nonnegative scalars and subadditive. If a linear f:U→R on a subspace satisfies f≤p, it extends linearly to F:X→R with F≤p.

For a one-dimensional enlargement U+Ry, define F(u+ty)=f(u)+tr. A permissible r exists because

supu∈U[f(u)−p(u−y)]≤infu∈U[p(u+y)−f(u)].

The inequality follows by applying domination and subadditivity to two vectors in U. Partially order dominated extensions by restriction; a chain has the union extension as upper bound. Zorn's lemma gives a maximal extension, and the one-step construction forces its domain to be all of X.

Norm-preserving form

For any real or complex normed space X, any linear subspace U and f∈U*, there exists F∈X* with

F|U=f,‖F‖=‖f‖.

Neither completeness nor density nor closedness of U is required. Over R, take p(x)=‖f‖‖x‖, and apply domination to x,−x. Over C, extend g=Ref as a real functional, then set F(x)=g(x)−ig(ix). Rotation by a unit scalar turns F(x) into its absolute value and proves the norm bound.

Every nonzero x∈X admits a norm-one functional F with F(x)=‖x‖, by extending from its span. Hence

‖x‖=max‖F‖≤1|F(x)|.

For a closed subspace U and x∉U, apply a norming functional on X/U to obtain F|U=0, F(x)≠0. In particular U is dense exactly when the only continuous functional vanishing on U is zero.

Minimal extensions and uniqueness

Restriction gives ‖F‖≥‖f‖; Hahn–Banach attains this lower bound: ‖f‖=minF|U=f‖F‖. The norm-preserving extensions form a convex set, because convex combinations still restrict to f, have norm at most ‖f‖, and cannot have smaller norm. If X* is strictly convex, this extension is unique: two different normalized extensions would have midpoint norm strictly less than 1, contradicting the lower bound. Strict convexity is a substantive extra condition; Hahn–Banach alone gives no uniqueness.

Hardy-space coefficient geometry and bounded point evaluation · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Builds a Hilbert space from square-summable power-series coefficients and represents interior evaluation by an explicit kernel.

Hardy-space coefficient geometry and bounded point evaluation

On the unit disk D⊂C, form

H={fa(z)=∑n=0∞anzn:a∈ℓ2}.

Square-summable coefficients are bounded, so the power series converges absolutely for |z|<1 and defines a holomorphic function. Uniqueness of power-series coefficients makes a↦fa bijective. Transporting the ℓ2 inner product gives

⟨fa,fb⟩H=∑n=0∞anbn―.

This makes H a Hilbert space isometrically isomorphic to ℓ2; the construction is by coefficient norm, not a sup norm on the disk.

For λ∈D, the vector (λ―n)n≥0∈ℓ2 corresponds to

gλ(z)=∑n=0∞λ―nzn=11−λ―z,f(λ)=⟨f,gλ⟩H.

Thus evaluation is a bounded functional represented by an explicit kernel. Cauchy–Schwarz gives

|f(λ)|≤‖f‖H‖gλ‖H,‖gλ‖H=(1−|λ|2)−1/2.

The displayed norm follows from the geometric coefficient series. Interior evaluation is controlled, but the bound grows near the unit circle; no boundary-evaluation theorem is asserted.

Riesz representation of Hilbert-space functionals · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Represents each continuous Hilbert-space functional by a unique vector, preserving norms and the complex conjugate-linear convention.

Riesz representation of Hilbert-space functionals

Representation and scalar convention

Let H be a real or complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in the first argument. For each F∈H*, there is a unique h∈H with

F(z)=⟨z,h⟩,‖F‖=‖h‖.

Thus J:h↦⟨·,h⟩ is bijective and isometric; over C it is conjugate linear, J(αh+βk)=α―Jh+β―Jk.

Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the functional by ‖h‖, and testing h/‖h‖ gives equality when h≠0. For surjectivity, take nonzero F, let U=kerF, and choose u∈U⟂ with F(u)=1. Since z−F(z)u∈U,

⟨z,u⟩=F(z)‖u‖2,h=u/‖u‖2.

Orthogonal decomposition ensures such u exists. Uniqueness follows by testing the difference of two representing vectors.

For H=L2(D;K), this gives F(z)=∫Dz(t)h(t)―dt. The conjugate in this Hilbert representation differs from the coefficient convention Fa(z)=∫az in the linear Lp-dual identification; both describe continuous linear functionals with consistent conventions. The Hilbert theorem is also distinct from representation of C(D;R)* by signed measures.
