Inner-product geometry and Hilbert norms · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Derives Cauchy–Schwarz, polarization and parallelogram identities and distinguishes Hilbert norms from general sequence-space norms.

Inner-product geometry and Hilbert norms

Scalar convention and completeness

An inner product on a real or complex vector space is positive definite, conjugate symmetric and linear in the first argument. Thus

⟨x,αy+βz⟩=α―⟨x,y⟩+β―⟨x,z⟩,‖x‖=⟨x,x⟩.

An inner-product space is pre-Hilbert; it is Hilbert when complete for this norm. Examples are Kn, ℓ2, and Lebesgue L2(D), with products ∑xky―k or ∫xy―. Hölder ensures the infinite products are well-defined. Incompleteness of continuous functions under the L2 norm is a separate completeness example in Normed spaces.

Cauchy–Schwarz and recovery of the product

For y≠0, nonnegativity of ‖x−⟨x,y⟩y/‖y‖2‖2 proves

|⟨x,y⟩|≤‖x‖‖y‖.

The triangle inequality follows by expanding ‖x+y‖2. Cauchy–Schwarz also gives continuity of the product in both arguments. Orthogonality implies Pythagoras.

Every inner-product norm satisfies

‖x+y‖2+‖x−y‖2=2‖x‖2+2‖y‖2.

Conversely the parallelogram identity characterizes norms induced by an inner product. The product is recovered by polarization:

⟨x,y⟩=14(‖x+y‖2−‖x−y‖2)

over R, with the additional term i(‖x+iy‖2−‖x−iy‖2)/4 over C.

For a linear T on a Hilbert space, preservation of norms is equivalent to preservation of inner products, by polarization. Surjectivity is not part of this equivalence.

Why exponent two is special

For distinct coordinate vectors in ℓp, 1≤p<∞, the left side of the parallelogram identity is 21+2/p, while its right side is 4. Equality holds only for p=2; for p=∞, the left side is 2. Hence these given norms are not inner-product norms for p≠2. Normalized functions supported on two disjoint sets of finite positive measure give the same obstruction in Lebesgue Lp(Ω) for a Borel Ω⊂Rn of positive measure.

Evaluation functionals and bounded integral operators · tum-functional-analysis · Type: method

Bounds evaluation and integration functionals and proves compactness of square-integrable-kernel maps using translation estimates.

Evaluation functionals and bounded integral operators

Functionals and integral operators

For C(D) with the sup norm, evaluation f↦f(a) has norm 1. Integration over [a,b] has norm b−a in the sup norm, but norm 1 on L1([a,b]), assuming a<b. A weighted functional on L1, f↦∫hf with continuous h, has norm ‖h‖∞: concentrated normalized indicator functions near a maximizer give the lower bound.

For k∈L2((0,1)2),

(Tf)(s)=∫01k(s,t)f(t)dt,‖T‖≤‖k‖L2.

Fubini/Tonelli and Cauchy–Schwarz justify the definition almost everywhere and the bound. This estimate establishes boundedness; it does not establish compactness.

Compactness from kernel translations

For the same square-integrable kernel, zero-extend in the output variable. Cauchy–Schwarz gives

‖Tf(·+h)−Tf‖L2(0,1)2≤‖f‖22∫01∫01|k(s+h,t)−k(s,t)|2dtds.

Translation continuity of the fixed L2 kernel makes the right side tend to zero uniformly over the input unit ball. The image is bounded by the kernel norm, so Fréchet–Riesz–Kolmogorov makes its closure compact. Thus these integral operators are compact, including when their kernels are not continuous. Every bounded input sequence has an output subsequence convergent in L2.

Fréchet–Riesz–Kolmogorov compactness in finite-exponent spaces · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Characterizes relative compactness on bounded domains through boundedness and uniform translation control at finite integrability exponents.

Fréchet–Riesz–Kolmogorov compactness in finite-exponent spaces

Family-level translation criterion

Let Ω⊂Rn be open and bounded and 1≤p<∞. A family F⊂Lp(Ω) is relatively compact iff it is bounded and, after zero extension,

limh→0supf∈F∫Ω|f(x+h)−f(x)|pdx=0.

The theorem controls small translations uniformly over the family. For each fixed f, translation continuity is automatic, but that pointwise fact alone is insufficient for compactness of F. The bounded-domain and finite-p hypotheses delimit the source's statement; no criterion for unbounded domains without additional tail control is asserted.

This is an Lp analogue of equicontinuity-based compactness, replacing pointwise function oscillations by translation differences in norm. Relative compactness means compact closure; closedness must be added to conclude that F itself is compact.

Metric compactness, finite nets and tail control · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Uses finite nets and uniform tail bounds to prove compactness and constructs bounded function sequences without norm-convergent subsequences.

Metric compactness, finite nets and tail control

Compactness through finite approximations

In metric spaces, open-cover compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness. A compact subset of a normed space is closed and bounded, but that converse holds for all closed bounded sets only in finite dimension.

For a closed subset F of a complete metric space, compactness is equivalent to total boundedness: for every ε>0, finitely many balls of radius ε, centered in F, cover it. Failure of a finite net permits recursive selection of points at pairwise distances at least ε, contradicting sequential compactness. Conversely, successive finite covers of radii 2−n let one select a nested subsequence with arbitrarily small diameter; a diagonal choice is Cauchy. Completeness and closedness supply a limit in F.

Total boundedness, unlike mere boundedness, controls the number of approximating points at every accuracy.

A compact infinite-dimensional box

The subset

C={x∈ℓ2(R):|xk|≤1/k}

is compact. Coordinate continuity makes it closed. Uniform tail control gives supx∈C∑k>N|xk|2≤∑k>Nk−2→0. For a fixed accuracy, truncate far enough, cover the resulting finite-dimensional box by a finite net, and combine head and tail errors. This produces a finite net for C. It illustrates compactness of particular subsets without compactness of the ambient unit ball.

Bounded but noncompact sequences

The triangular functions fn(t)=max(0,1−nt) have norm 1 in C([0,1]) with the sup norm and in L∞, but tend to zero almost everywhere. A norm-convergent subsequence would have zero as its almost-everywhere limit, contradicting the norms. In Lp, 1≤p<∞, normalize these functions by their Lp norms: they again have norm 1 and tend to zero almost everywhere, precluding any norm-convergent subsequence.

Convolution, mollification and translation continuity · tum-functional-analysis · Type: method

Constructs smooth approximate identities, establishes finite-exponent approximation and translation continuity, and qualifies convolution differentiation.

Convolution, mollification and translation continuity

Smooth approximation

For f,g∈L1(Rn),

(f*g)(y)=∫Rnf(x)g(y−x)dx,f*g=g*f,‖f*g‖1≤‖f‖1‖g‖1.

Choose a nonnegative radial C∞ kernel η, supported in the closed unit ball, with integral 1; the notes construct it by normalizing exp[−1/(1−‖x‖2)] inside that ball and zero outside. Set ηε(x)=ε−nη(x/ε).

For bounded open Ω⊂Rn and f∈Lp(Ω), 1≤p<∞, extend f by zero to f~ and set fε=f~*ηε. Differentiating the smooth kernel under the integral gives smoothness and

∂αfε=f~*(∂αηε).

The support stays within distance ε of Ω―; the smoothed function is not in general supported inside Ω. Nonnegativity, unit mass, Hölder/Jensen and Fubini give ‖fε‖Lp(Ω)≤‖f‖Lp(Ω).

Approximation and translations

For compactly supported continuous functions on Rn, uniform continuity bounds

|fε(y)−f(y)|≤sup‖x−y‖≤ε|f(x)−f(y)|→0

uniformly. For Lp functions, dense continuous approximants and the convolution norm bound yield fε→f in Lp. The finite-exponent restriction is substantive; uniform approximation of discontinuities is not implied.

For the zero extension and τhf(x)=f(x+h), translation is continuous in Lp, p<∞: insert a smooth approximation between τhf and f, control the two approximation errors, then use uniform continuity of the smooth function. Continuity for one f does not imply uniform continuity across every bounded family of functions.

Differentiating convolution

In one dimension, for f∈L1(R) and differentiable g with bounded derivative, wherever the convolution is well-defined,

(f*g)′=f*g′.

The difference quotient of g is bounded by ‖g′‖∞, so dominated convergence applies with majorant |f|‖g′‖∞. Existence of f*g remains an assumption: bounded g′ alone permits an unbounded g; bounded g, for example, supplies existence for every L1 input.

Normal, self-adjoint and positive Hilbert-space operators · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Derives adjoint norm identities, orthogonality of normal eigenspaces and spectral consequences of normality and self-adjointness.

Normal, self-adjoint and positive Hilbert-space operators

Algebra and norm identities

With inner product linear in the first argument, the Hilbert adjoint satisfies

T**=T,‖T*‖=‖T‖,(ST)*=T*S*,(αT)*=α―T*.

An operator is normal if T*T=TT*, self-adjoint (also called Hermitian over C) if T=T*, and positive if ⟨Tx,x⟩≥0. Both T*T and TT* are positive self-adjoint, and

‖T*T‖=‖T‖2.

Indeed ⟨T*Tx,x⟩=‖Tx‖2 gives one norm inequality, and submultiplicativity plus ‖T*‖=‖T‖ gives the other.

Powers of normal T are normal and ‖Tn‖=‖T‖n. Normality permits rearrangement of T,T*, yielding the identity first for squares and then the successive-power argument. In complex Hilbert space, the spectral-radius formula therefore gives r(T)=‖T‖. This equality does not hold for all nonnormal operators.

Kernels, eigenvectors and spectrum

For normal T, ‖Tx‖=‖T*x‖, so their kernels agree. The same applies to normal λI−T, hence

Tx=λx⟺T*x=λ―x.

If Tx=λx, Ty=μy and λ≠μ, then λ⟨x,y⟩=⟨Tx,y⟩=⟨x,T*y⟩=μ⟨x,y⟩; different eigenspaces are orthogonal.

Normal operators have no residual spectrum: injectivity of λI−T implies a zero adjoint kernel, hence dense range. It need not imply surjectivity. For self-adjoint T and λ=a+ib, b≠0,

‖(λI−T)x‖2=‖(T−aI)x‖2+b2‖x‖2.

The lower bound gives closed range and injectivity; normality gives dense range. Thus the map is onto and σ(T)⊂R. The exercise assumes compactness, but its estimate does not use it.

Norm equivalence and isomorphisms of normed spaces · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Distinguishes equivalent norms and bounded isomorphisms from merely algebraic bijections using weighted sequence-space counterexamples.

Norm equivalence and isomorphisms of normed spaces

An isomorphism is linear, bijective, bounded and has bounded inverse. Two norms on the same vector space are equivalent when each bounds the other up to a constant. Equal-dimensional finite-dimensional normed spaces are isomorphic; their linear maps into any normed space are continuous. Matrix operator norms depend on the chosen domain/range norms. Infinite-dimensional spaces can be isomorphic to proper subspaces: for x∈c, set

(Tx)1=limjxj,(Tx)k=xk−1−limjxj(k≥2).

This maps c onto c0, with inverse (Sy)k=yk+1+y1; both norms are bounded by 2.

A bounded bijection need not have bounded inverse

On ce with the supremum norm, Tx=(xn/n)n is bounded and bijective; its inverse Sx=(nxn)n still maps finite sequences to finite sequences but is unbounded since ‖Sen‖∞=n. The image of the open unit ball under T contains zero but not T(en)=en/n, which tends to zero; thus that image is not open. Completeness cannot be omitted from the bounded-inverse/open-mapping conclusions.

Pulling back a norm

If linear T:X→X is injective and ‖·‖a is a norm, then ‖x‖b=‖Tx‖a is a norm. Injectivity supplies definiteness; linearity transfers homogeneity and the triangle inequality. This does not imply equivalence to the old norm.

On zero-indexed finite sequences, ‖x‖a=maxk(k+1)|xk| makes Tx=((k+1)xk)k an isometric isomorphism to the same vector space with sup norm. But the identity from the sup-norm space to the weighted-norm space is unbounded: ‖en‖∞=1, ‖en‖a=n+1. An isometry between differently represented spaces and equivalence of norms under the identity are distinct assertions.

Open mapping and the bounded inverse theorem · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Proves openness of bounded Banach-space surjections and obtains bounded inverses and consequences for complete norms.

Open mapping and the bounded inverse theorem

Quantitative openness

For Banach spaces X,Y and bounded linear T:X→Y, these are equivalent:

  • T maps every open subset of X to an open subset of Y;
  • some δ>0 satisfies BY(0,δ)⊂T(BX(0,1));
  • T is surjective.

The ball inclusion scales by linearity and transfers to balls around every preimage. Conversely, surjectivity gives Y=⋃n≥1T(BX(0,n))―. Baire supplies a closure with nonempty interior; symmetry and convexity then give a ball around zero in that closure.

To remove the closure, choose approximate preimages successively, halving residuals. In the notes' normalization, take xj∈BX(0,k) and yj+1=2(yj−Txj)∈BY(0,ε). Then

T∑j=0m2−jxj=y0−2−(m+1)ym+1→y0.

The preimage series converges in X, with norm at most 2k<3k. Thus BY(0,ε)⊂T(BX(0,3k)). Completeness is used both in Baire on Y and in summing preimage corrections in X.

Consequences and limitations

A bounded linear bijection between Banach spaces has bounded inverse, since images of open sets become inverse preimages of open sets. Consequently two complete norms on one vector space are equivalent if one globally bounds the other. The non-equivalent sup and L1 norms on C([a,b]), a<b, therefore cannot both be complete.

Openness concerns images of open sets, not images of closed sets. The diagonal bounded bijection on incomplete ce in normed isomorphisms shows why completeness matters.

The notes also state a stability consequence: if T(X) is dense in Y but not all of Y, some y∈Y has the property that every sequence Txn→y satisfies ‖xn‖→∞. This is an asserted corollary, with proof assigned as an exercise, rather than a derived error bound for arbitrary inverse problems.

Pointwise versus operator-norm convergence · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Separates pointwise from operator-norm convergence and uses uniform boundedness to control pointwise limits on Banach domains.

Pointwise versus operator-norm convergence

Two different limits

For bounded linear maps Tn:X→Y, operator-norm convergence to T implies Tnx→Tx for every fixed x, because

‖(Tn−T)x‖≤‖Tn−T‖‖x‖.

The converse fails: pointwise convergence tests each vector separately, whereas the operator norm takes a supremum over the unit ball.

Diagonal and tail operators on ℓ2

Using the worksheet's zero-based coordinates, define

(Anx)k=xkn(k+1),(Bnx)k={0k<n,xkk≥n.

Then ‖Anx‖2≤‖x‖2/n, hence ‖An‖≤1/n and convergence is in operator norm. For Bn,

‖Bnx‖22=∑k=n∞|xk|2⟶0

for each x∈ℓ2, but a unit coordinate vector in the retained tail gives ‖Bn‖=1. For n<m, choosing a coordinate in n≤k<m gives ‖Bn−Bm‖=1: the sequence is not even norm-Cauchy.

These examples separate convergence of outputs on fixed inputs from a uniform error bound on all unit inputs.

When the pointwise limit is bounded

Let X,Y be Banach spaces and suppose Tnx converges in Y for each x∈X. Its limit Tx is linear. Convergence gives supn‖Tnx‖<∞ for each x; the uniform boundedness principle then yields C=supn‖Tn‖<∞. Passing to the limit gives ‖Tx‖≤C‖x‖. This does not give operator-norm convergence, as the tail projections above show.

Completeness of the domain matters: on ce with the sup norm, Fnx=nxn is continuous with norm n, but for each finite sequence x, Fnx=0 eventually and supn|Fnx|<∞. Pointwise boundedness on this incomplete domain gives no uniform operator bound.

Orthogonal complements, subspace projections and total sets · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Connects closed-subspace projections and double orthogonal complements to totality and dense linear spans.

Orthogonal complements, subspace projections and total sets

Orthogonal decomposition

For Y⊂H, set Y⟂={x:⟨x,y⟩=0 ∀y∈Y}. It is a closed linear subspace. Inclusion reverses under orthogonal complements, and

Y⟂=(spanY)⟂=(spanY―)⟂,Y⟂⟂=spanY―.

The last equality uses Hilbert-space completeness; the first properties follow from linearity and continuity of the product.

For a closed subspace U⊂H, y=PUx is characterized by y∈U and x−y⟂U. The convex-projection variational inequality becomes equality by testing both signs and, over C, imaginary multiples. Uniqueness gives linearity of PU and

H=U⊕U⟂,kerPU=U⟂,PU⟂=I−PU,‖x‖2=‖PUx‖2+‖x−PUx‖2.

Consequently x↦(PUx,x−PUx) is an isometric isomorphism onto the product with its Euclidean product norm, and ‖PU‖=1 for U≠{0}.

A bounded P:H→H is such an orthogonal projection exactly when

P2=P,⟨x,Py⟩=⟨Px,y⟩.

Indeed kerP=ran(I−P); symmetry makes ranP orthogonal to that kernel, yielding the decomposition. Conversely the orthogonal decomposition gives idempotence and symmetry.

Totality does not mean a basis

A set is total when Y⟂={0}, equivalently its linear span is dense in a Hilbert space. In ℓ2, let d=(1,1/2,1/3,…) and Y={en:n≥1}∪{d}. Removing any one member leaves a total set: if ej is removed, orthogonality to all remaining coordinates leaves only the j-coordinate, then orthogonality to d kills it. Removing two members destroys totality: two omitted coordinate directions admit a nonzero combination orthogonal to d, or removing d,ej leaves ej orthogonal.

The ambient space matters. Let Y={y∈ce:∑nyn/n=0}. Its orthogonal complement inside the incomplete pre-Hilbert space ce is zero: finite-support test vectors force every coordinate of a finite-support orthogonal vector to vanish. In ℓ2, however, the nonzero vector d lies in Y⟂. One cannot apply Hilbert double-complement conclusions indiscriminately in an incomplete space.

Orthonormal bases, Fourier expansions and Hilbert coordinates · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Develops Bessel and Parseval identities, Hilbert coefficient isomorphisms and Fourier examples while distinguishing orthonormality from completeness.

Orthonormal bases, Fourier expansions and Hilbert coordinates

Systems, bases and finite projection

An orthonormal system S consists of unit vectors orthogonal in pairs. An orthonormal basis is a maximal such system, not an algebraic basis of finite expansions. Every orthonormal system in a Hilbert space extends to a basis: partially order its orthonormal extensions by inclusion; unions of chains are upper bounds, so Zorn's lemma gives a maximal extension.

In a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, every orthonormal basis is countably infinite. Distinct orthonormal vectors are at distance 2, excluding an uncountable system in a separable space; a finite system can be extended using the orthogonal component of a vector outside its span.

For U=span{e1,…,en},

PUx=∑k=1n⟨x,ek⟩ek,∑k=1n|⟨x,ek⟩|2≤‖x‖2.

Orthogonality characterizes the projection; Pythagoras gives Bessel's inequality. Even for an uncountable system, each vector has at most countably many nonzero coefficients: for each positive threshold only finitely many can exceed it, by Bessel.

Completeness and coordinates

For a countable orthonormal system in a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, the following are equivalent:

  • maximal orthonormality;
  • S⟂={0};
  • spanS―=H;
  • x=∑k=1∞⟨x,ek⟩ek in norm for every x;
  • Parseval: ‖x‖2=∑k=1∞|⟨x,ek⟩|2.

Double orthogonal complements connect totality and density. Projections onto the growing finite spans approximate any vector in the dense span's closure; Pythagoras then yields Parseval. If maximality fails, a unit vector orthogonal to all of S contradicts Parseval.

The coefficient map x↦(⟨x,ek⟩)k is a linear isometric isomorphism H≅ℓ2. Surjectivity follows by extending the isometric finite-series synthesis map from ce to ℓ2. Such series are order-independent but need not converge absolutely: xk=1/k in ℓ2 gives summable squared coefficients but divergent ∑k‖xkek‖2.

Fourier application and non-complete systems

In L2((−π,π);C), the established orthonormal basis ek(t)=(2π)−1/2eikt, k∈Z, gives

f=∑k∈Zckek,ck=(2π)−1/2∫−ππf(t)e−iktdt.

Convergence here is in L2, not a claim of pointwise or uniform convergence. Bessel for the normalized sine and cosine systems also proves the L2 Riemann–Lebesgue conclusion: both integrals against sin(nt) and cos(nt) tend to zero.

On the unit disk with area measure, Pn(z)=(n+1)/πzn is an orthonormal system by polar-coordinate integration, but not a basis of all L2(D): the nonzero function z― is orthogonal to every Pn. Orthonormality alone does not establish completeness.

Quotient norms and factorization through kernels · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Constructs complete quotient spaces and relates kernel factorization, closed-range isomorphisms and duals of subspaces and cokernels.

Quotient norms and factorization through kernels

Seminorm and quotient construction

A seminorm is absolutely homogeneous and subadditive but may vanish on nonzero vectors. If q is a seminorm on Y and T:X→Y is linear, then q(Tx) is a seminorm on X. Examples include |x1|, |f(a)|, |∫f|, and ‖f′‖∞ on their respective source spaces.

For a linear subspace U⊂X, identify x~y when x−y∈U. Set

[x]=x+U,Qx=[x],‖[x]‖X/U=infu∈U‖x−u‖≤‖x‖.

This is well-defined and is always a seminorm. When U is closed it is a norm: distance zero implies x∈U―=U. If X is Banach and U closed, the quotient is Banach.

Completeness argument: pass from a quotient-Cauchy sequence to a subsequence with successive quotient distances bounded by 2−n. Choose representatives whose increments are at most twice those distances. The summable bound makes representatives Cauchy in X; their ambient limit yields the quotient limit, and the original Cauchy sequence has the same limit. A zero quotient increment permits identical representatives.

For X=C([0,1]) with sup norm and U={f:f(0)=0}, the quotient norm is |f(0)|; evaluation identifies X/U isometrically with K.

Kernel factorization and functionals

For bounded linear T:X→Y, the kernel is closed as T−1({0}), and

T0:X/kerT→Y,T0[x]=Tx

is well-defined, injective, bounded, with ‖T0‖=‖T‖. Taking an infimum over representatives proves ‖T0‖≤‖T‖; T=T0Q and ‖Q‖≤1 give the reverse inequality. This does not assert that its inverse on the range is bounded.

For nonzero f∈X*, choose y with f(y)=1. Every x has the unique decomposition

x=(x−f(x)y)+f(x)y∈kerf⊕span{y}.

If two continuous linear functionals have the same kernel, they are proportional; if both vanish the assertion is trivial. Thus the kernel determines a nonzero functional up to a scalar, not its normalization.

Dual of a subspace as a quotient

For a closed subspace U⊂X, write U⟂={f∈X*:f|U=0} for its annihilator in the dual (not an inner-product orthogonal complement). Restriction R:X*→U* has this kernel and is surjective by Hahn–Banach. It induces a linear isometric isomorphism

X*/U⟂≅U*.

Indeed, all extensions of u* form one coset, and its quotient norm is the infimum of their norms, equal to ‖u*‖ with attainment by Hahn–Banach. This sharpens generic kernel factorization: equality of operator norms alone would not prove this induced map is an isometry.

Closed-range isomorphisms and the cokernel dual

More generally, if bounded T:X→Y vanishes on closed U, it factors uniquely through X/U with equal operator norm. For Banach X,Y and closed T(X), bounded inverse applied to the kernel quotient gives

X/kerT≃T(X).

Surjectivity gives X/kerT≃Y. These are topological isomorphisms, not generally isometries. Closedness is what upgrades the earlier injective factorization to a boundedly invertible map onto the range.

For closed range, quotient composition g↦gQ is an isometric isomorphism

(Y/T(X))*≅kerT*.

The functionals in the adjoint kernel are exactly those vanishing on the range, hence precisely those that descend to its quotient. This identifies the dual of the cokernel with the homogeneous adjoint solutions.

Best approximation via reflexivity and strict convexity · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Uses bounded minimizing sequences, weak closedness and lower semicontinuity for existence, with strict convexity separately ensuring uniqueness.

Best approximation via reflexivity and strict convexity

Existence by weak limits

Let X be a reflexive Banach space, K⊂X nonempty, norm-closed and convex, and x∈X. Then the distance from x to K is attained.

Take a minimizing sequence yn∈K. Since ‖yn‖≤‖x−yn‖+‖x‖, it is bounded and has a weakly convergent subsequence ynk⇀y. Weak sequential closedness gives y∈K. Weak lower semicontinuity gives

‖x−y‖≤lim infk‖x−ynk‖=infz∈K‖x−z‖.

This is a direct-method argument: boundedness supplies weak subsequences, convex closedness preserves feasibility, and lower semicontinuity preserves the infimum. It establishes existence, not a numerical procedure or an orthogonal projection formula in a general Banach space.

Uniqueness is a separate hypothesis

A norm is strictly convex if distinct unit vectors have midpoint norm less than 1. In a strictly convex normed space, approximation to a convex set has at most one minimizer. If y,y~ were distinct minimizers at distance d>0, apply strict convexity to (x−y)/d and (x−y~)/d: their midpoint corresponds to a feasible point strictly closer to x.

Thus reflexivity/completeness and closedness guarantee existence here, while strict convexity guarantees uniqueness. They should not be collapsed into one hypothesis. For ℓp and Lebesgue Lp, 1<p<∞, both conditions hold; each nonempty closed convex set has a unique best approximation. The notes state the converse characterization by unique solvability for all such sets without proof.

Canonical bidual embedding, reflexivity and norm attainment · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Studies the canonical bidual embedding, stability of reflexivity and norm attainment, with explicit nonreflexive sequence and function spaces.

Canonical bidual embedding, reflexivity and norm attainment

Canonical embedding

The map JX:X→X**, (JXx)(f)=f(x), is linear and isometric by the dual norm formula. Since X** is Banach, JX(X) is closed exactly when X is complete; its closure supplies a completion otherwise. A Banach space is reflexive when this canonical map is surjective. An arbitrary isometric isomorphism X≅X** is not sufficient to establish canonical surjectivity.

Finite-dimensional spaces are reflexive by equality of dimensions. Hilbert spaces are reflexive by Riesz representation. With the first-argument-linear convention, for Φ∈H** and the conjugate-linear Riesz map R, the functional y↦Φ(Ry)― is linear; represent it by a vector x to obtain Φ(Ry)=(Ry)(x). Surjectivity of R proves Φ=JHx.

The coefficient duality (ℓp)*≅ℓq proves reflexivity for 1<p<∞: composition of a bidual element with the coefficient map is a functional on ℓq, hence is evaluation by some x∈ℓp. The same reasoning applies to Lebesgue Lp(D) in this exponent range.

Stability properties

Closed subspaces of reflexive Banach spaces are reflexive. Given ϕ∈U**, define Φ(f)=ϕ(f|U) on X* and write Φ=JXx. All functionals annihilating U vanish on x, so Hahn–Banach separation implies x∈U. Extending each u*∈U* to X then proves ϕ=JUx.

For Banach X, X is reflexive iff X* is reflexive. Forward, for Ψ∈X***, take f=Ψ∘JX; surjectivity of JX gives Ψ=JX*f. Reverse, X** is reflexive and its closed subspace JX(X) is reflexive.

Explicit failures and norm attainment

Under (c0)*≅ℓ1, the bidual functional F(fa)=∑nan is bounded but cannot equal evaluation at any x∈c0: testing a=en forces xn=1 for every n. Thus c0 is not reflexive, and dual reflexivity also excludes ℓ1 and ℓ∞.

For a nonzero reflexive X, every f∈X* attains its norm on a unit vector. Apply the norming-functional corollary to f in X*, then use canonical surjectivity to represent that bidual functional by a unit x. On c0, choose strictly positive summable coefficients an=2−n, n≥1. Then fa(x)=∑anxn has norm 1 but no unit x∈c0 attains it: some positive-weight coordinate satisfies |xn|<1, so |fa(x)|<1. Positivity on all coordinates is important; not every functional on c0 fails to attain its norm.

The notes also show L1(0,1) is not reflexive. In L∞(0,1), let U be the norm closure of functions vanishing on some (0,1/k). The constant 1 stays at distance 1 from U. Hahn–Banach gives F∈(L∞)* vanishing on U but not at 1. An integral representation F(g)=∫hg, h∈L1, would force F(1)=0 by dominated convergence along 1(1/k,1), a contradiction.

A second obstruction for ℓ1 uses weak compactness: its unit vectors are bounded but no subsequence is weakly convergent. For any selected indices nk, a bounded dual coefficient sequence with values (−1)k at those indices prevents convergence of that one dual pairing. A reflexive Banach space would supply a weakly convergent subsequence, so ℓ1 is not reflexive.

Countable norming families and separable-space embeddings · tum-functional-analysis · Type: method

Constructs countable norming families and closed embeddings into bounded sequences, and proves that dual separability implies separability.

Countable norming families and separable-space embeddings

Embedding into bounded sequences

For a nonzero separable Banach space X, choose a countable dense set {xn} and Hahn–Banach norming functionals fn∈X* with ‖fn‖=1, fn(xn)=‖xn‖. Then

Tx=(fn(x))n∈ℓ∞,‖Tx‖∞=‖x‖.

The upper bound follows from the norms of fn. Choosing xn within ε of x gives

|fn(x)|≥‖xn‖−‖x−xn‖≥‖x‖−2ε.

Thus T is a linear isometry. Completeness of X makes T(X) closed in ℓ∞. This realizes arbitrary separable Banach geometry inside bounded sequences without asserting that ℓ∞ is separable.

Separability of the dual implies separability of the space

If X* is norm-separable, its unit sphere has a countable dense family {fn}. Choose unit xn with |fn(xn)|≥1/2. A norm-one functional vanishing on U=span{xn} could be approximated within 1/4 by some fj, contradicting |fj(xj)|≥1/2. The Hahn–Banach annihilator criterion therefore gives U―=X; rational finite combinations make X separable. Complex spaces use rational real and imaginary coefficients. The zero space is immediate.

The auxiliary metric fact is that every subset of a separable metric space is separable: choose representatives from a countable family of balls meeting that subset. The converse implication X separable ⇒X* separable does not follow; X=ℓ1, X*=ℓ∞ is a counterexample.

Banach-space series and Neumann inversion · tum-functional-analysis · Type: method

Uses absolutely convergent Banach-space series to invert small operator perturbations and solve a concrete integral equation.

Banach-space series and Neumann inversion

Series and the role of completeness

A series ∑k=1∞xk converges when its partial sums converge in norm. Absolute convergence means ∑k‖xk‖<∞. In a Banach space, absolute convergence implies convergence and

‖∑kxk‖≤∑k‖xk‖.

Indeed ‖∑k=m+1nxk‖≤∑k=m+1n‖xk‖ makes the partial sums Cauchy. Every permutation has the same limit: retain all of a fixed finite initial block, then bound the remaining terms by the arbitrarily small absolute tail. Addition and scalar multiplication of convergent series follow from continuity.

Completeness is essential to this implication; the Cauchy estimate alone need not produce a limit inside an incomplete space.

Inverting a small bounded perturbation

Let X be Banach and A∈L(X;X) satisfy ‖A‖<1. Then

(I−A)−1=∑k=0∞Ak.

Submultiplicativity gives ‖Ak‖≤‖A‖k. Completeness of the operator space and the series result yield a bounded operator B. For partial sums BN=∑k=0NAk,

(I−A)BN=BN(I−A)=I−AN+1.

Pass to the operator-norm limit on both sides; ‖AN+1‖→0 proves both inverse identities. Thus one may solve (I−A)x=b by partial sums of ∑Akb. The strict norm bound is the stated sufficient condition, not a necessary criterion for invertibility.

Integral equation with a convergent power series despite norm one

On C([0,1]) with the sup norm, set

(Tx)(t)=2tλ(x),λ(x)=∫01sx(s)ds.

Here ‖T‖=1, so the strict-norm criterion above cannot be applied directly. Nevertheless

Tnx(t)=2(2/3)n−1tλ(x),‖Tn‖≤(2/3)n−1(n≥1).

Thus the operator series converges absolutely, and the same telescoping identities prove it is (I−T)−1. Since λ(sin(πt))=1/π, the solution of x(t)−∫012stx(s)ds=sin(πt) is

x(t)=sin(πt)+6t/π.

This example illustrates the sufficient nature of ‖T‖<1; summability of operator powers also suffices.

Stability of bounded invertibility

If T:X→Y is a bounded isomorphism between Banach spaces and ‖T~−T‖<1/‖T−1‖, then

T~=T(I−T−1(T−T~))

is again a bounded isomorphism. The operator inside the parentheses is invertible by the Neumann criterion. Thus boundedly invertible maps form an operator-norm open set; the admissible perturbation size depends on the inverse norm.

Shift operators and dependence of spectral type on the ambient space · tum-functional-analysis · Type: method

Computes shift spectra and shows how summability requirements change whether spectral points are eigenvalues or continuous-spectrum values.

Shift operators and dependence of spectral type on the ambient space

Right shift on complex square-summable sequences

Let S(x0,x1,…)=(0,x0,x1,…) on ℓ2(C). It is an isometry, with adjoint the left shift L. There are no eigenvalues: the eigen-equation and zero first output force zero for λ≠0, while λ=0 also has trivial kernel.

For |λ|<1, y=(1,λ―,λ―2,…)∈ℓ2 satisfies Ly=λ―y, so it annihilates the range of λI−S under the Hilbert pairing. That injective map has nondense range; the open unit disk belongs to the residual spectrum. Closedness of the spectrum and ‖S‖=1 then give

σ(S)={λ:|λ|≤1}.

Complex conjugation in the annihilating vector is essential under the inner-product convention linear in the first argument.

Left shift: the same rule on different spaces

For L(x0,x1,…)=(x1,x2,…), an eigenvector must be c(1,λ,λ2,…).

On ℓ2, it belongs to the space iff |λ|<1. Every λI−L has dense range: solve the finite-support output equations backward to obtain a finite-support preimage (for λ=0, shift right with a minus sign). Since the full spectrum is the closed unit disk,

σp(L)={|λ|<1},σc(L)={|λ|=1},σr(L)=∅.

On ℓ∞, the same geometric vector is admissible for |λ|≤1. Hence the entire closed unit disk is point spectrum; continuous and residual spectra are empty. The algebraic formula of an operator does not determine its spectral classification independently of the domain's summability requirement.

Compact-operator SVD, optimal rank approximation and perturbation bounds · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Constructs compact-operator singular systems and derives optimal low-rank errors and perturbation bounds for singular values.

Compact-operator SVD, optimal rank approximation and perturbation bounds

Construction without normality

For compact T on Hilbert space, T*T is compact, positive and self-adjoint. Let T*Tek=νkek, νk>0, on the orthonormal basis of the kernel's orthogonal complement. Define

sk=νk,fk=sk−1Tek.

Since ker(T*T)=kerT by ⟨T*Tx,x⟩=‖Tx‖2, expanding x in the ek and kernel basis gives

Tx=∑ksk⟨x,ek⟩fk.

The output vectors are orthonormal: ⟨fk,fm⟩=(sksm)−1⟨T*Tek,em⟩=δkm. Unlike a normal spectral expansion, the input and output systems need not coincide. The construction extends to compact maps between distinct Hilbert spaces. For a normal compact map, its singular values are the magnitudes of its eigenvalues, with multiplicity.

Truncation and optimality

Order singular values decreasingly with multiplicity, padding by zeros when appropriate. For nonzero T, ‖T‖=s1. The truncation

Tnx=∑k=1nsk⟨x,ek⟩fk

has rank at most n, exactly n if sn>0, and

‖T−Tn‖=sn+1⟶0.

Thus every compact Hilbert-space operator is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank maps; this does not extend to all Banach spaces.

The stronger best-approximation statement is

sn(T)=infrankQ<n‖T−Q‖.

The notes state this optimality theorem without proof; it identifies the truncation error with the best achievable operator-norm error at the corresponding rank.

Stable singular values

For compact T,S, rank subadditivity and best approximation give

sn+m−1(T+S)≤sn(T)+sm(S).

Indeed rank-<n and rank-<m approximants sum to rank <n+m−1, and their approximation errors add. Taking m=1 for S=T~−T, then interchanging T,T~, gives

|sn(T)−sn(T~)|≤‖T−T~‖.

Singular values therefore provide stable operator-norm-sensitive descriptors and controlled low-rank approximations even without normality. The source contrasts this with the lack of such a general eigenvalue perturbation bound; it does not report a numerical implementation.

Translation estimates and Rellich compact embedding · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Uses gradient-controlled translations and extension operators to obtain strong subsequences from bounded Sobolev families on suitable bounded domains.

Translation estimates and Rellich compact embedding

Gradient control of translations

For u∈Cc∞(Ω), extend by zero. With 1≤p<∞ and conjugate q, the fundamental theorem along the segment x+th, followed by Hölder, gives

u(x+h)−u(x)=∫01∇u(x+th)·hdt,‖u(·+h)−u‖Lp(Rd)p≤‖∇u‖Lp(Rd;ℓp)p‖h‖ℓqp.

Integration over the whole space and translation invariance control the shifted gradient; the same bound holds when restricting the left side to Ω.

Zero-boundary compactness

For bounded open Ω, a bounded F⊂W01,p(Ω) is relatively compact in Lp(Ω). Given a sequence un∈F, choose vn∈Cc∞(Ω) with ‖un−vn‖W1,p≤1/n. The vn have uniformly bounded gradients, so the translation estimate gives the uniform continuity criterion of Fréchet–Riesz–Kolmogorov. A strongly Lp-convergent subsequence of vn gives the same limit for un.

The bounded-domain condition is needed for this use of the preceding compactness theorem. Proposition 7.11 omits it in its printed statement; no unrestricted compact embedding on an unbounded domain follows from the translation estimate alone.

Removing the zero-boundary restriction

If Ω is bounded with sufficiently smooth boundary, the notes use a bounded linear extension

E:W1,p(Ω)⟶W01,p(V),(Eu)|Ω=u,

where Ω⋐V and V is bounded and open. Extension maps bounded sets to bounded sets; apply the zero-boundary result on V, then restrict the strongly convergent subsequence to Ω. Thus bounded subsets of W1,p(Ω) are relatively compact in Lp(Ω), 1≤p<∞ (Rellich).

The extension's existence is cited, not constructed, and the notes do not specify a sharp boundary-regularity class. Compactness here gains strong convergence in a weaker norm; it does not assert compactness in the original Sobolev norm.

Smooth approximation in Sobolev norms · tum-functional-analysis · Type: method

Uses interior mollification and partitions of unity to approximate Sobolev functions smoothly while preserving distinctions about boundary conditions.

Smooth approximation in Sobolev norms

Interior smoothing

Let u∈Wk,p(Ω), 1≤p<∞, and U⋐Ω. For a standard mollifier with ε<dist(U,∂Ω),

∂α(u*ηε)=(∂αu)*ηεon U,u*ηε→u in Wk,p(U).

The kernel is then a valid interior test; transferring its derivative to the weak derivative introduces no boundary term. Convergence follows from Lp approximation of each derivative. Arbitrary zero extension need not preserve Sobolev derivatives across the boundary, so this interior argument cannot simply set U=Ω.

On all of Rd there is no boundary obstruction, giving global approximation in Wk,p(Rd). The finite-exponent hypothesis is important: approximate identities do not converge in general L∞ norm for discontinuous derivative densities. The supplement's Lemma 11 must be read with this restriction for its Sobolev-norm convergence conclusion.

Arbitrary open domains

For every open Ω, C∞(Ω)∩Wk,p(Ω) is dense in Wk,p(Ω), p<∞. The construction handles different distances to the boundary:

  1. Exhaust Ω by Uj={x:dist(x,∂Ω)>1/j, |x|<j}.
  2. Choose a locally finite smooth partition of unity βj on overlapping shells Vj=Uj+3⧵U―j+1, together with the interior set V0=U3.
  3. Smooth each localized βju at an individual radius εj, small enough to retain shell-local support and ensure
‖wj−βju‖Wk,p≤2−(j+1)δ.
  1. Sum the locally finite family w=∑jwj. It is smooth and ‖w−u‖Wk,p≤δ.

The result gives smooth approximants, not necessarily compactly supported approximants. The latter closure defines the generally smaller W0k,p. Distinguishing these two density claims preserves the boundary condition.

One-dimensional Sobolev regularity and Hölder representatives · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Derives a Hölder-continuous representative from one-dimensional weak-derivative control for integrability exponents strictly between one and infinity.

One-dimensional Sobolev regularity and Hölder representatives

For 1<p<∞, every u∈W1,p(R) has a representative u~ satisfying

|u~(x)−u~(y)|≤‖u‖W1,p|x−y|1−1/p.

The representative agrees with u almost everywhere; the assertion does not assign pointwise meaning to every arbitrary representative of its equivalence class.

For smooth mollifications un=u*ωn, the fundamental theorem and Hölder give

|un(y)−un(x)|≤(∫xy|un′(t)|pdt)1/p|y−x|1−1/p≤‖un′‖p|y−x|1−1/p.

Convergence un→u in W1,p bounds these Hölder constants. Together with bounded Lp norms this bounds function values on compact intervals. Arzelà–Ascoli, followed by a diagonal choice over expanding intervals, gives a locally uniformly convergent subsequence. Its continuous limit inherits the estimate; convergence in Lp identifies that limit with u almost everywhere.

This connects integral control of one weak derivative to regularity of a representative, with dimension and exponent explicitly fixed. The supplement presents this one-dimensional result as an example, not a general-dimensional Sobolev-embedding classification.

Sobolev spaces as closed derivative graphs in product spaces · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Constructs complete weak-derivative spaces as closed product-space subspaces and derives reflexivity, separability and Hilbert special cases.

Sobolev spaces as closed derivative graphs in product spaces

Definition and norms

On an open Ω⊂Rd,

Wk,p(Ω)={u∈Lp(Ω):∂αu∈Lp(Ω), |α|≤k},

where derivatives are weak derivatives tested against Cc∞(Ω), not pointwise derivatives. For p<∞,

‖u‖Wk,p=(∑|α|≤k‖∂αu‖pp)1/p.

For p=∞, the main notes use the sum of derivative sup norms, whereas the supplement uses their maximum. These are equivalent norms because only finitely many multi-indices occur. In particular W0,p=Lp.

Completeness and inherited structure

For a Sobolev-Cauchy sequence, each ∂αun is Cauchy in Lp, with limit uα; let u=u0. Passing to the limit against a fixed compactly supported smooth test gives

∫uαφ=(−1)|α|∫u∂αφ.

Thus the limiting components remain derivatives of the same function: uα=∂αu. This proves completeness, including p=∞ using the corresponding L1 bounds on tests.

The derivative map

T:u↦(∂αu)|α|≤kinto∏|α|≤kLp(Ω)

is an isometry for the matching product norm and has closed image. Consequently Wk,p is reflexive for 1<p<∞, and separable for 1≤p<∞, by the corresponding product-space and closed-subspace results. Reflexivity at p=1 or ∞ is not asserted.

Hilbert and zero-boundary subspaces

For finite p, define

W0k,p(Ω)=Cc∞(Ω)―Wk,p.

It is a closed Banach subspace. Its zero-boundary interpretation is through this closure; pointwise boundary values of arbitrary a.e. equivalence classes are not part of the definition.

Write Hk=Wk,2 and H0k=W0k,2. They are Hilbert spaces for

⟨u,v⟩Hk=∑|α|≤k∫Ω∂αu∂αv―.

The norm records regularity of the function and its derivatives simultaneously; it is stronger than merely measuring u in Lp.

Polynomial spectral mapping and commuting factorizations · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Transfers complex polynomial factorization to commuting operator factors to identify the spectrum of a polynomial in an operator.

Polynomial spectral mapping and commuting factorizations

For bounded T on a nonzero complex Banach space and polynomial p(z)=∑j=0ncjzj, define p(T)=∑j=0ncjTj. Then

σ(p(T))=p(σ(T)).

The proof transfers scalar polynomial factorization to commuting operator factors. If AB=BA and AB is boundedly invertible, both A,B are boundedly invertible. The product inverse gives a right and a left inverse for each factor; a left inverse and a right inverse must coincide. Commutation is necessary to that argument.

For λ∈σ(T), factor p(z)−p(λ)=(z−λ)q(z). If p(T)−p(λ)I were invertible, the commuting-factor result would make T−λI invertible, a contradiction. This gives one inclusion.

Conversely, for μ∈σ(p(T)), the fundamental theorem of algebra gives

p(z)−μ=c∏j=1n(z−λj),p(T)−μI=c∏j=1n(T−λjI).

Some factor must fail to be invertible, so λj∈σ(T) and μ=p(λj). Constant polynomials are handled separately: p(T)=cI has spectrum {c}.

In particular σ(Tn)={λn:λ∈σ(T)}. The source proves polynomial mapping, not a general holomorphic functional calculus.

Spectral radius and asymptotic operator-power growth · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Identifies spectral radius with asymptotic operator-power growth using spectral mapping and scalar resolvent expansions.

Spectral radius and asymptotic operator-power growth

For bounded T on a nonzero complex Banach space,

r(T)=maxλ∈σ(T)|λ|=limn→∞‖Tn‖1/n=infn≥1‖Tn‖1/n.

Polynomial spectral mapping gives λn∈σ(Tn), hence |λ|n≤‖Tn‖. Taking a maximum and then an infimum proves the lower bound for the power-growth expression.

For the reverse bound, apply ℓ∈L(X)* to the resolvent. Its Laurent series for |λ|>‖T‖ is

ℓ(Rλ)=∑k=0∞λ−k−1ℓ(Tk).

Holomorphy and uniqueness of the Laurent expansion continue this scalar series to |λ|>r(T). Its terms tend to zero, so λ−kTk is weakly null in L(X). Weak convergence implies norm-boundedness, yielding ‖Tk‖1/k≤|λ|M1/k. Thus lim supk‖Tk‖1/k≤|λ|, and letting |λ|↓r(T) proves equality.

The radius measures asymptotic growth, while ‖T‖ controls one application. They need not be equal for an arbitrary bounded operator. For a normal Hilbert-space operator, the separate identity ‖Tn‖=‖T‖n makes them equal.

Resolvent expansions and the different kinds of spectrum · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Classifies spectral points, constructs local inverse expansions and uses approximate eigenvectors to diagnose failure of bounded invertibility.

Resolvent expansions and the different kinds of spectrum

Invertibility and spectral classification

For bounded T on a nonzero Banach space X over K,

ρ(T)={λ:λI−T bijective},Rλ=(λI−T)−1,σ(T)=K⧵ρ(T).

Bounded inverse makes Rλ bounded. The spectrum partitions into:

  • Point spectrum: ker(λI−T)≠0.
  • Continuous spectrum: λI−T injective with dense, proper range.
  • Residual spectrum: λI−T injective with nondense range.

Finite-dimensional injectivity implies surjectivity, so only point spectrum occurs there. In infinite dimensions, diagonal multiplication by 1/n on ℓ2 is injective with dense, proper range: zero is continuous spectrum. Right shift has closed range {y:y1=0}, making zero residual spectrum.

Local resolvent series and the spectral bound

For λ0∈ρ(T), factor λI−T=(λ0I−T)[I−(λ0−λ)Rλ0]. Neumann inversion yields

Rλ=∑k=0∞(λ0−λ)kRλ0k+1,|λ−λ0|<‖Rλ0‖−1.

Thus the resolvent set is open. If |λ|>‖T‖,

Rλ=λ−1∑k=0∞(T/λ)k,‖Rλ‖≤1|λ|−‖T‖.

Consequently σ(T) is compact and contained in {|λ|≤‖T‖}. Over C it is nonempty. If it were empty, every scalar function ℓ(Rλ), ℓ∈L(X)*, would be entire by the local power series, bounded and tending to zero at infinity. Liouville and Hahn–Banach would force Rλ=0, contradicting invertibility. Nonemptiness is not asserted over R.

Approximate eigenvectors and lower bounds

If ‖xn‖=1 and (λI−T)xn→0, then λ∈σ(T): a bounded inverse would imply 1≤‖Rλ‖‖(λI−T)xn‖→0. These are approximate eigenvectors, not necessarily exact eigenvectors.

Conversely a bound ‖(λI−T)x‖≥c‖x‖, c>0, implies injectivity and closed range: a Cauchy sequence of outputs has Cauchy preimages. It excludes point and continuous spectrum, but may leave residual spectrum.

For the Cesàro map on ℓ∞, (Ax)n=n−1∑k=1nxk, ‖A‖=1 and ‖Aen‖∞=1/n. It is injective (successive partial sums recover the coordinates), but cannot be bijective: the inverse would violate bounded inverse on these unit-vector tests. Hence zero is spectral without being an eigenvalue.

Uniform boundedness of operator families · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Uses Baire category to turn pointwise bounds on bounded-operator families over a Banach domain into a common operator-norm bound.

Uniform boundedness of operator families

Statement and proof

Let X be Banach, Y normed, and T⊂L(X;Y). If supT∈T‖Tx‖<∞ for each x∈X, then supT∈T‖T‖<∞. Completeness of Y is not required.

The sets An={x:supT‖Tx‖≤n} are closed and cover X. Baire gives one Ak containing a ball K(x0,ε). For x≠0, put z=x0+εx/‖x‖. Since both z,x0∈Ak,

‖Tx‖=‖x‖ε‖Tz−Tx0‖≤2kε‖x‖.

This single bound applies to the whole family. Pointwise boundedness does not mean that the bound initially given for each vector is already uniform on the unit ball.

Dual boundedness criterion

A subset M of any normed space X is norm-bounded exactly when f(M) is bounded for every f∈X*. Apply uniform boundedness on the Banach space X* to the evaluation operators JXx:f↦f(x), x∈M. Hahn–Banach gives ‖JXx‖=‖x‖. Thus completeness of X itself is not required for this criterion.

The consequences and incomplete-domain counterexample for pointwise operator limits are in operator convergence.

Distance from subspaces and noncompact unit balls · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Constructs unit vectors separated from proper closed subspaces and proves that compact unit balls characterize finite dimension.

Distance from subspaces and noncompact unit balls

Approximate separation without Hilbert geometry

Let X be normed and U⊊X a closed linear subspace. There are unit vectors xn with dist(xn,U)→1.

Choose a∉U, set d=dist(a,U)>0, and choose un∈U with ‖a−un‖→d. For xn=(a−un)/‖a−un‖,

1≥dist(xn,U)≥d/‖a−un‖→1.

The lower bound follows by scaling a competitor in U. In a Hilbert space an exactly orthogonal unit vector attains distance 1, but that exact conclusion need not hold in a general normed space.

Compactness characterizes finite dimension

In infinite dimension, construct unit vectors recursively, choosing xn+1 at distance at least 1/2 from Un=span{x1,…,xn}. These finite-dimensional subspaces are closed and proper, so the preceding result applies. The resulting sequence has pairwise distances at least 1/2, hence no convergent subsequence. The closed unit ball is therefore not compact, even if X is Banach.

Conversely finite-dimensional norm equivalence and finite-dimensional compactness make the closed unit ball compact. Thus a normed space has compact closed unit ball exactly when it is finite-dimensional.

Volterra integration and a spectral point without eigenvectors · tum-functional-analysis · Type: method

Shows that Volterra integration has no eigenvalues despite a spectral point at zero and proves compactness on continuous functions.

Volterra integration and a spectral point without eigenvectors

On L2(0,1), define

(Vf)(x)=∫0xf(t)dt.

Since ‖f‖1≤‖f‖2, ‖Vf‖2≤‖f‖2; this defines a bounded linear map on a.e. equivalence classes with a specific continuous representative for each output. Moreover

|Vf(y)−Vf(x)|≤|y−x|1/2‖f‖2.

If Vf=λf, λ≠0, that representative makes f continuous, then differentiable, with λf′=f. Thus f(x)=cex/λ, but Vf(0)=0 forces f(0)=0 and hence c=0. For λ=0, vanishing indefinite integral also forces f=0 a.e. There are therefore no eigenvalues.

Nevertheless 0∈σ(V): a nonzero constant a.e. class cannot be an output, since the continuous representative of every Vf vanishes at zero. The full spectrum and the point spectrum are different objects; lack of eigenvectors does not imply invertibility.

Continuous-function domain

On C([0,1]) with sup norm, the same integration formula is compact. The image unit ball is bounded by 1 and satisfies |Vf(y)−Vf(x)|≤|y−x|, so its closure is compact by Arzelà–Ascoli. This proof uses a uniformly Lipschitz family, distinct from the L2 half-Hölder estimate above.

Weak and weak-star compactness and subsequence extraction · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Separates weak-star topological compactness from sequential results and derives subsequence extraction using separability or reflexivity.

Weak and weak-star compactness and subsequence extraction

Separable preduals: a diagonal argument

If X is a separable normed space, the closed unit ball of X* is weak-star sequentially compact. For a sequence ‖fn‖≤1, choose successive subsequences whose evaluations converge at the first, second and subsequent members of a countable dense set {xm}. A diagonal subsequence converges on their span. Its limit is linear with |f(x)|≤‖x‖; extend it continuously to X. The bound

|f(x)−fnk(x)|≤2‖x−z‖+|f(z)−fnk(z)|

for dense-span z proves convergence at every x. Thus every bounded sequence in X* has a weak-star convergent subsequence.

For Lebesgue Lp(D), 1<p≤∞, use the separable predual Lq(D), q=p/(p−1)<∞. Bounded sequences admit subsequences whose pairings converge against all Lq tests; the p=∞ conclusion is weak-star, not an unrestricted weak-convergence statement.

On C([a,b])*, moving point evaluations have weak-star limits along convergent point subsequences. More generally, probability measures on the compact interval have a subsequence converging on all continuous test functions to a probability measure; positivity and unit mass pass to the limit.

Reflexive spaces

In a reflexive Banach space, the closed unit ball is weakly sequentially compact; every bounded sequence therefore has a weakly convergent subsequence. For a proof without global separability, restrict to the closed span Y of the given sequence. It is separable and reflexive. Since Y**≅Y is separable, dual separability implies Y* separable. Apply the preceding diagonal result to JYxn∈(Y*)*, then use reflexivity to identify its limit with a vector in Y. Restriction of X* tests yields weak convergence in X.

The converse—that weak sequential compactness of the unit ball implies reflexivity—is stated in the notes without proof.

Topological compactness is different

Banach–Alaoglu gives weak-star compactness of the dual unit ball for every normed X, without separability. This is open-cover compactness in the weak-star topology. It need not imply sequential compactness; a general weak-star compact dual ball is not necessarily metrizable.

For X=L∞(0,1), define

fn(g)=εn−1∫0εng(t)dt,εn↓0,εn+1/εn→0.

These norm-one functionals have no weak-star convergent subsequence in X*: for any subsequence, choose bounded g alternating on successive selected annuli. Its selected averages approach alternating signs, since the inner interval's relative contribution tends to zero. On the smaller test space C([0,1]), however, the same averages converge to g(0), hence weak-star to δ0. The predual/test space is essential to the meaning of the limit.

Weak and weak-star convergence through dual tests · tum-functional-analysis · Type: concept

Characterizes weak limits by dual tests and boundedness, with mixed-pairing conditions and examples separating weak, weak-star and norm convergence.

Weak and weak-star convergence through dual tests

Functional tests and topology

In a normed space X, xn⇀x means f(xn)→f(x) for every f∈X*. In X*, weak-star convergence fn⇀*f tests only evaluations at vectors of X; weak convergence in X* instead tests every member of X**. Norm convergence implies weak convergence, but not conversely.

A weakly convergent sequence is norm-bounded: apply uniform boundedness to JXxn acting on the Banach space X*. For a bounded sequence, it suffices to test a norm-dense set D⊂X*. Indeed, with M=supn‖xn‖,

|g(xn−x)|≤‖g−f‖(M+‖x‖)+|f(xn−x)|,f∈D.

Approximate g by f, then pass to large n. Without boundedness, dense testing is not justified by this estimate.

In Hilbert space, Riesz representation makes weak convergence equivalent to convergence of all inner products against fixed vectors. Weak convergence together with ‖xn‖→‖x‖ implies norm convergence by expanding ‖xn−x‖2=‖xn‖2+‖x‖2−2Re⟨xn,x⟩. An orthonormal sequence is weakly null by Bessel but has constant norm 1. Testing coordinates in an orthonormal basis suffices for weak-null convergence if the sequence is bounded.

Products, subspaces and changes of variables

Weak and weak-star limits are unique: weak-star equality follows from evaluation on every vector, and weak equality from separation by the dual. In a reflexive space X, weak and weak-star convergence in X* coincide; in finite dimension these also coincide with norm convergence. Weak-star convergent sequences are norm-bounded when their predual X is Banach, by uniform boundedness.

For mixed limits, if xn→x in norm and fn⇀*f with supn‖fn‖<∞, then

|fn(xn)−f(x)|≤‖fn‖‖xn−x‖+|(fn−f)(x)|→0.

The bound is automatic for a Banach predual, but cannot be dropped for a general incomplete predual: on ce with sup norm, fn(x)=nxn is weak-star null and x(n)=en/n→0, yet fn(x(n))=1. This qualifies the unbounded-predual form of the notes' Lemma 6.5. If instead xn⇀x and fn→f in norm, boundedness of xn gives pairing convergence. Two weak limits alone do not suffice: in ℓ2, a coordinate vector paired with its own coordinate functional always gives 1 although both sequences are weakly null.

For the sum-norm product X×Y, each continuous functional decomposes uniquely as f(x)+g(y). Hence weak convergence is componentwise. For un,u∈U⊂X, weak convergence in U agrees with weak convergence in X: use restriction one way and Hahn–Banach extension the other. A bounded linear bijection between Banach spaces preserves weak convergence in both directions, since both it and its inverse are bounded.

Examples distinguishing the limits

  • In c0, the finite truncations of (1,1/2,1/3,…) converge in norm. The vectors (n,n−1,…,1,0,…) do not even converge weakly because they are unbounded.
  • Right shifts of (1,1/2,1/3,…) by n coordinates are weakly null in c0: each ℓ1 coefficient functional is bounded by its own tail sum. Distinct shifts have distance 1, so norm convergence fails.
  • The unit vectors of ℓ1 have no weakly convergent subsequence. For any chosen subsequence enj, choose one bounded coefficient sequence taking values (−1)j on those indices; its functional prevents convergence. Boundedness alone does not supply weak subsequences.
  • 1[n−1,n] is weak-star null in L∞(R)=(L1(R))*, since its pairing with g∈L1 is bounded by ∫n−1n|g|→0. The same functions form an orthonormal sequence in L2(R), hence are weakly null there.
  • For 1<p<∞, n1/p1(0,1/n) is weakly null in Lp(0,1) but has norm 1. Bounded continuous test functions give an integral bound ‖g‖∞n1/p−1→0; density in Lq and boundedness extend it to all dual tests.
  • sin(2πnt) is also weakly null in Lp(0,1), 1<p<∞. First test continuous functions through the L2 orthonormal-system argument, then use density in Lq. Its p-th norm power is the positive constant ∫01|sin(2πt)|pdt; it is not norm-null. Weak and strong limits, when both exist, agree.

Weak lower semicontinuity and convex closedness · tum-functional-analysis · Type: theorem

Proves weak lower semicontinuity of norms and support functionals and weak sequential closedness of norm-closed convex sets.

Weak lower semicontinuity and convex closedness

Norms and support functionals

If xn⇀x in a normed space, then

‖x‖≤lim infn‖xn‖.

Choose a norming functional for x; its values converge and are bounded by ‖xn‖. Similarly weak-star convergence fn→f gives ‖f‖≤lim infn‖fn‖ by testing each unit vector and taking the supremum. Equality need not hold: orthonormal vectors converge weakly to zero with norm 1.

For a nonempty family F⊂X* on a real normed space with ‖f‖≤1, the support functional ϕ(x)=supf∈Ff(x) is finite, convex and 1-Lipschitz:

|ϕ(x)−ϕ(y)|≤‖x−y‖.

It is weakly sequentially lower semicontinuous. Indeed a subsequence with ϕ(xnk)≤α<ϕ(x) is contradicted by one f∈F with f(x)>α. Taking the dual unit ball gives ϕ(x)=‖x‖.

Closed convex feasible sets

A norm-closed convex K⊂X is weakly sequentially closed. If xn∈K and xn⇀x∉K, strict point–set separation gives a functional with f(x)>supKf≥f(xn), contradicting convergence. Over C, use real parts. Convexity is material; arbitrary norm-closed sets need not contain weak limits.

These two properties keep feasibility and prevent an objective jump upward when taking weak limits of minimizing sequences.

Alternating projections onto intersecting closed convex sets · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: algorithm

Proves finite-dimensional convergence using projection inequalities and relates the line case to the angle between directions.

Alternating projections onto intersecting closed convex sets

Let C,D⊂Rd be nonempty closed convex sets with nonempty intersection. Starting at x0∈C, iterate

yk=PDxk,xk+1=PCyk.

Both sequences converge to a common point of C∩D.

The projection variational inequality gives, for c∈C,

‖x−PCx‖22≤‖x−c‖22−‖PCx−c‖22.

Apply it to both half steps with any z∈C∩D:

‖yk−z‖2≤‖xk−z‖2−‖yk−xk‖2,‖xk+1−z‖2≤‖yk−z‖2−‖xk+1−yk‖2.

Distances to z decrease, hence the iterates are bounded. Telescoping the inequalities shows that the sum of squared half-step gaps is finite, so both gaps tend to zero. This argument does not require those gaps themselves to decrease monotonically.

Finite-dimensional boundedness gives a convergent subsequence xkj→x*∈C. Since ykj−xkj→0 and D is closed, x*∈D. Applying the decreasing-distance property to this intersection point, and using the subsequence limit, gives convergence of the entire sequence to x*; the vanishing gap gives the same limit for yk. These arguments do not establish arbitrary infinite-dimensional norm convergence or behavior for disjoint sets, nor do they identify the limit as the nearest intersection point to x0.

For two lines Vi=spanvi with unit directions and c=⟨v1,v2⟩,

(PV2PV1)nx=c2n−1⟨x,v1⟩v2(n≥1).

For distinct lines |c|<1, so this tends to their intersection zero, with a factor c2 per full cycle after the first. If |c|=1, the lines coincide and the iterates equal the common projection after the first cycle. In the example v1=(3/2,1/2)T, v2=(1/2,3/2)T, the cycle factor is 3/4.

The compactness step uses Bolzano–Weierstrass specifically in finite-dimensional Euclidean space: every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence, and a norm bound passes to its limit. It applies to a fixed-size matrix sequence by viewing its entries as a finite vector. Merely knowing boundedness in an arbitrary infinite-dimensional space does not supply the same norm-convergent subsequence.

Dimension-dependent ball volumes and sphere areas · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: result

Expresses unit-ball geometry through the Gamma function and identifies its nonmonotone dependence on dimension.

Dimension-dependent ball volumes and sphere areas

For integer n≥1, the unit ball volume and unit sphere boundary area are

V(n)=2πn/2nΓ(n/2),A(n)=2πn/2Γ(n/2)=nV(n),Γ(x)=∫0∞tx−1e−tdt(x>0).

Scaling the radius to r multiplies volume by rn. The booklet's dimension plot and solution identify the integer maxima at n=5 for volume and n=7 for area; both tend to zero as n→∞. Increasing dimension therefore does not monotonically increase the volume of a fixed-radius ball. This statement holds with radius fixed at one, not under an arbitrary dimension-dependent rescaling.

Lagrange dual of basis pursuit · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Derives the l-infinity dual feasibility constraint for l1 minimization with equality data constraints.

Lagrange dual of basis pursuit

Basis pursuit solves

minx‖x‖1subject to Ax=y,A∈Rm×n.

Using the source's multiplier sign convention,

L(x,ξ)=‖x‖1+ξT(Ax−y),H(ξ)=infxL(x,ξ).

Set z=ATξ. If ‖z‖∞≤1, then xTz≥−‖x‖1‖z‖∞, hence L(x,ξ)≥−ξTy; equality holds at x=0. If some |zi|>1, take x=−tsign(zi)ei. Its variable-dependent objective is t(1−|zi|)→−∞. Thus

H(ξ)={−ξTy‖ATξ‖∞≤1,−∞otherwise,

and the dual problem is

max‖ATξ‖∞≤1−ξTy.

The ℓ∞ condition arises from its dual pairing with the ℓ1 norm, not from a componentwise primal constraint. Changing the multiplier sign would change the displayed dual objective consistently. The derivation supplies a dual lower bound on any feasible primal value; it does not by itself prove feasibility, attainment, equality of optimal values, or a sparse-recovery guarantee for an arbitrary A,y.

Bernstein concentration from a local quadratic MGF bound · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Derives the quadratic and linear tail regimes for independent centered subexponential weighted sums.

Bernstein concentration from a local quadratic MGF bound

Let independent centered variables Xi obey the common local MGF bound EeθXi≤ec2θ2 for |θ|≤c1, with positive constants. For nonzero a, independence and exponential Markov yield

P(S>t)≤exp(−θt+c2θ2‖a‖22),S=∑iaiXi,0<θ≤c1/‖a‖∞.

Choose θ~=min{t/(2c2‖a‖22),c1/‖a‖∞}. Then c2θ~2‖a‖22≤θ~t/2. Applying the same calculation to −S gives

P(|S|>t)≤2exp(−θ~t/2)=2exp[−min{t24c2‖a‖22,c1t2‖a‖∞}].

The coefficient Euclidean norm controls the small-deviation quadratic regime, and the largest coefficient controls the large-deviation linear regime and the admissible exponential tilt. If a=0, the tail probability is zero and the quotients are unnecessary. The sample exam assumes identically distributed subexponential variables and supplies the local MGF statement without proof; the calculation needs only independence and common MGF constants.

The printed target and final handwritten conclusion omit the factor one half in the exponent for the stated θ~. The handwritten blue annotation correctly asks for exponent at most −θt/2; the bound above is what the displayed MGF derivation establishes. Constants must be adjusted before writing a stronger-looking exponent.

Exponential-moment tail bounds and tilt selection · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Applies Markov to an exponential transform and optimizes the positive tilt within the MGF domain.

Exponential-moment tail bounds and tilt selection

For θ>0 with finite MX(θ),

P(X>t)=P(eθX>eθt)≤e−θtMX(θ).

Minimize this expression over allowed positive θ, or equivalently minimize logMX(θ)−θt. The choice of tilt uses more distributional information than a first-moment bound; finiteness of the exponential moment matters.

For X~U[0,4],

MX(θ)=e4θ−14θ,P(X>3)≤e4θ−14θe3θ.

The booklet reports a numerical tilt near 0.89839, giving a bound around 66.5%, compared to the exact 25%. This example does not outperform its optimized power-moment estimate: exponential tilting is a family of bounds, not a universal claim of greater sharpness for every finite distribution.

For independent copies Ri, let CR(θ)=logEeθR on its finite domain. Factoring exponential moments gives, for any allowed θ>0,

P(1N∑iRi>μ+ε)≤exp{−N[θ(μ+ε)−CR(θ)]}.

Optimize by taking the supremum of the bracket over positive tilts. Lower tails use −R and C−R(θ)=CR(−θ). This derivation explains the review's Cramér-type exponential estimates; it supplies an upper bound rather than asserting an exact asymptotic equivalence without further hypotheses.

For the review's return law at price 10,

CR(θ)=log[0.05e−90θ+0.01e−290θ+0.94e10θ],μ=2.

This finite-support model has finite exponential moments for every real tilt. By contrast a density proportional to 1/(1+x4) has finite variance but lacks finite nonzero exponential moments on the full real line. One cannot infer exponential concentration merely from finite variance.

Conjugate transformation under an invertible affine change · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Tracks inverse-transpose coordinates, translations and linear terms in a transformed convex conjugate.

Conjugate transformation under an invertible affine change

Let ρ:Rn→(−∞,+∞] be convex, A∈Rn×n invertible, a,c∈Rn, and b∈R. For

f(x)=ρ(A(x−c))+aTx+b,

its conjugate is

f*(y)=ρ*(A−T(y−a))+cT(y−a)−b.

To derive it, substitute z=A(x−c), so x=A−1z+c. Then

yTx−f(x)=⟨A−T(y−a),z⟩−ρ(z)+cT(y−a)−b.

Invertibility makes this a supremum over all z∈Rn, giving the formula. The transpose comes from moving the inverse across the inner product. The translation pairs with y−a, not just y, and the scalar constant is subtracted. For a noninvertible A, this substitution does not range freely over every z, so the formula cannot be used without a different argument.

Unique fixed points of contractions on complete metric spaces · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

States the fixed-point guarantee for a contraction and identifies completeness and a uniform factor below one as essential assumptions.

Unique fixed points of contractions on complete metric spaces

Let (X,d) be a nonempty complete metric space and F:X→X satisfy

d(F(x),F(y))≤Ld(x,y)for all x,y∈X,0≤L<1.

Then F has exactly one fixed point x*∈X, with F(x*)=x*. The review states this theorem as an application of completeness.

The contraction condition uses one constant for every pair of points, and the map must preserve the underlying space. Uniqueness follows immediately: two fixed points would satisfy d(x*,y*)≤Ld(x*,y*), forcing their distance to be zero. Completeness supplies the existence part of the theorem; mere metric structure does not provide that guarantee.

Convex conjugates and a separable quartic example · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Maximizes affine-minus-function expressions and solves the quartic conjugate by coordinate stationarity.

Convex conjugates and a separable quartic example

The Legendre–Fenchel conjugate is

f*(y)=supx{⟨y,x⟩−f(x)},

allowing value +∞. Each fixed x gives an affine function of y, which motivates the convex character of the construction; finiteness is a separate issue.

The review introduces power objectives f(x)=1p∑i|xi|p, p>1, whose gradient has entries |xi|p−1sign(xi), and works out p=4. For

f(x)=14∑ixi4,

maximizing the conjugate expression is separable. Its stationarity equations are yi−xi3=0, hence xi=yi3, using real cube roots. The negative quartic makes the expression tend to −∞ as ‖x‖→∞, and each coordinate maximum is unique. Substitution gives

f*(y)=34∑i|yi|4/3.

For negative coordinates, the absolute-value expression makes the real interpretation of the handwritten yi4/3 explicit. Stationarity is sufficient in this example because of the concave maximization structure and attainment, not for arbitrary functions merely appearing inside a supremum.

For a differentiable strictly convex scalar function with injective derivative, and y∈rangef′, the equation f′(x)=y identifies the maximizer of yx−f(x). Thus

f*(y)=y(f′)−1(y)−f((f′)−1(y)).

The booklet assumes strong convexity for this step, but inverse-derivative evaluation on its range also applies to its strictly convex example f(x)=ex, which has no positive uniform strong-convexity constant on all of R. The inverse here is a function inverse, not the reciprocal of f′.

For that exponential, rangef′=(0,∞) and (f′)−1(y)=logy, so

f*(y)={ylogy−yy>0,0y=0,+∞y<0.

At zero the supremum is approached as x→−∞ without a finite maximizer; for negative y the same limit makes yx−ex unbounded above. One cannot apply the inverse-derivative formula outside its derivative range without checking the supremum separately.

The later review states the general conjugate pair 1p‖x‖pp↔1q‖y‖qq, for p>1, 1/p+1/q=1. Coordinate stationarity gives xi=sign(yi)|yi|1/(p−1); substituting yields |yi|q/q per coordinate. This includes the worked quartic case with q=4/3.

For the linear function f(x)=cTx, its conjugate is f*(y)=δ{c}(y): the supremum of (y−c)Tx is zero when y=c, and is unbounded above otherwise by taking x=t(y−c), t→∞. This turns an unconstrained linear supremum into an exact equality constraint in dual calculations.

Convex functions and convex epigraphs · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Interprets Jensen’s two-point inequality as epigraph convexity and explains the role of affine segments.

Convex functions and convex epigraphs

On a convex domain D, a function is convex if

f(λx+(1−λ)y)≤λf(x)+(1−λ)f(y)(x,y∈D, 0≤λ≤1).

Its graph lies below each chord. This is equivalent to convexity of epif: a convex combination of points above the graph remains above it, and conversely apply epigraph convexity to (x,f(x)) and (y,f(y)).

Affine behavior on a segment produces equality along that segment and can allow several minimizers. Convexity therefore does not assert strict curvature or uniqueness. A flat minimum region remains compatible with the definition. The epigraph description distinguishes convexity of a function from the earlier convexity of its input domain, and from closedness of the epigraph.

The same definition extends to functions with values in (−∞,+∞], using the effective domain of finite values. The epigraph equivalence still holds: pairs with finite height only involve finite function values; endpoints with infinite objective make the corresponding interior-weight convex inequality automatic. This avoids trying to place (x,+∞) inside the finite-coordinate epigraph.

Convex combinations and feasible-set geometry · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Extends segment convexity to finite combinations and contrasts affine feasible geometry with nonlinearity of rank-constrained matrix sets.

Convex combinations and feasible-set geometry

A set C is convex if every segment λx+(1−λ)y, x,y∈C, 0≤λ≤1, stays in C. This two-point condition implies closure under every finite convex combination:

x1,…,xk∈C,θi≥0,∑iθi=1⟹∑iθixi∈C.

Induct on the number of points. If θ1≠1, normalize the remaining coefficients by 1−θ1, combine them using the induction hypothesis, and then apply two-point convexity. If θ1=1, the combination is just x1. Nonnegativity is required for every coefficient, not just the last one.

An affine hyperplane {x:aTx=b}, a≠0, is convex because the affine equation is preserved under combinations with weights summing to one. Convexity is not the same as being a linear subspace: when b≠0, the hyperplane does not contain zero.

Nor do rank bounds generally define a linear space. For example two matrices diag(1,0) and diag(0,1) both have rank one, while their sum has rank two. Linear combinations therefore cannot in general be used as feasible operations for rank-constrained matrix problems in the same way as for a subspace. Convex feasible geometry is the hypothesis later used in the projection theorem.

The same argument applies to a finite system of affine equalities and inequalities: if two points satisfy each constraint, every convex combination satisfies each equality and preserves each inequality by nonnegative weighting. Thus intersections described by these affine constraints are convex, even when they are not linear subspaces.

Intersections of convex sets remain convex, since a segment between common points belongs to each set. Unions need not be convex. A norm ball {x:‖x‖≤r}, r≥0, is convex by the triangle inequality and homogeneity. Closed halfspaces {x:⟨a,x⟩≤b} provide basic examples. An intersection of closed halfspaces is closed, so a representation by such halfspaces cannot describe a nonclosed convex set; the review's unqualified “every convex set” phrasing needs this restriction.

The Minkowski sum A+B={a+b:a∈A,b∈B} of two convex sets is convex: a convex combination of two such sums groups into a convex combination in A plus one in B. This operation preserves convexity without requiring the sets to be linear subspaces.

Hilbert projection onto closed convex sets · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Uses minimizing Cauchy sequences to obtain unique Hilbert projections and derives the Euclidean ball formula and its sphere limitation.

Hilbert projection onto closed convex sets

For a nonempty, closed convex K in a real Hilbert space and any v, there is a unique nearest point PKv. Nonemptiness is necessary in addition to the printed closedness/convexity conditions.

Existence through a minimizing Cauchy sequence

Translate v to zero and set d=infw∈K‖w‖, without assuming attainment. The parallelogram identity and feasibility of the midpoint give

‖x−y‖2=2‖x‖2+2‖y‖2−4‖(x+y)/2‖2≤2‖x‖2+2‖y‖2−4d2.

A minimizing sequence is Cauchy, so completeness supplies a limit and closedness keeps it feasible. Its norm is d. For two minimizers the same bound forces distance zero, proving uniqueness.

Variational characterization

For p∈K,

p=PKv⟺⟨z−p,v−p⟩≤0∀z∈K.

If p is nearest, compare it to p+λ(z−p), expand the squared distances, divide by λ>0, then let λ↓0. Conversely expand ‖v−z‖2=‖v−p‖2+‖z−p‖2−2⟨v−p,z−p⟩; the sign condition makes p nearest.

For the Euclidean unit ball B2,

PB2(x)=xmax(1,‖x‖2).

An interior point projects to itself; an exterior point projects radially to the boundary. Replacing the ball by the sphere changes the problem: the sphere is not convex, at zero every sphere point is nearest, and the displayed ball formula would return an infeasible point for ‖x‖<1. The theorem is therefore not a generic nearest-point guarantee for all closed sets.

The assumptions also explain distinct failure modes. For an open ball and a point outside its closure, the infimum distance occurs only on the excluded boundary, so it is not attained in the set. A closed convex target can have several nearest points under a norm such as ℓ∞, whose unit ball has flat sides; the Hilbert-space uniqueness argument does not extend to arbitrary norms. Nonconvex sets can likewise admit ties even with the Euclidean norm. These are possible failures, not assertions that every non-Euclidean norm or nonconvex set always gives nonuniqueness.

Strict hyperplane separation via a closest convex pair · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Constructs a midpoint hyperplane separating a closed convex set from a disjoint compact convex set.

Strict hyperplane separation via a closest convex pair

Let A⊂Rn be nonempty, closed and convex, and B nonempty, compact and convex, with A∩B=∅. The distance function b↦dist(b,A) is continuous and strictly positive on B, hence attains a positive minimum at b*. Set a*=PAb*, q=b*−a*≠0, and m=(a*+b*)/2.

The separating hyperplane is

H={x:⟨x−m,q⟩=0}.

The closest-pair property and convex feasible segments give

⟨a−a*,q⟩≤0(a∈A),⟨b−b*,q⟩≥0(b∈B).

For instance, if the second inequality failed, expanding the squared distance of b*+t(b−b*) from a* would reduce it for small positive t, contradicting minimality. The first is the analogous projection inequality. Consequently,

⟨a−m,q⟩≤−12‖q‖2<0,⟨b−m,q⟩≥12‖q‖2>0.

The normal points from the closest point in A toward that in B. Compactness is what produces a positive attained gap against the closed set; disjointness alone does not justify this strict-margin construction for arbitrary unbounded closed sets.
