Pointwise suprema and convexity of the largest eigenvalue · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Preserves convexity under arbitrary pointwise suprema and applies the Rayleigh representation to symmetric matrices.

Pointwise suprema and convexity of the largest eigenvalue

If every fy is convex on the same convex domain, then g(x)=supyfy(x) is convex, allowing extended-real values. For interior weights,

g(λx+(1−λ)z)≤supy[λfy(x)+(1−λ)fy(z)]≤λg(x)+(1−λ)g(z).

Endpoint weights are immediate. No attainment of the supremum or convexity of its index set is needed for this pointwise argument; the booklet gives convex sets as sufficient setting, but does not use that additional index-set assumption in its proof.

For real symmetric matrices,

λmax(A)=sup‖u‖2=1uTAu.

Each fixed-unit-vector quadratic form is linear in the matrix entries. Thus the largest eigenvalue is a convex function on the vector space of symmetric matrices:

λmax(λA+(1−λ)B)≤λλmax(A)+(1−λ)λmax(B).

This concerns eigenvalues of symmetric matrices, where the real variational characterization applies; it does not define a comparable ordered-real maximum eigenvalue for arbitrary nonsymmetric matrices.

An alternative proof uses epig=⋂yepify. Each epigraph is convex and intersections preserve convexity. This also works for the unit-sphere index set in the Rayleigh representation, even though that sphere itself is not convex.

Covariance matrices and affine transformations of random vectors · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Propagates mean and covariance through deterministic affine maps and specializes linear functionals to Gaussian laws.

Covariance matrices and affine transformations of random vectors

For a real random vector X with finite second moments, define μ=EX and

Σ=Cov(X)=E[(X−μ)(X−μ)T].

Its diagonal entries are component variances and its off-diagonal entries are covariances. The matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite, since

vTΣv=Var(vTX)≥0.

Marginal variances alone omit the dependence information carried by the off-diagonal terms.

For deterministic A,b, linearity and centering give

E(AX+b)=Aμ+b,Cov(AX+b)=AΣAT.

In particular Var(aX+b)=a2Var(X) in one dimension, and Var(X+Y)=VarX+VarY+2Cov(X,Y). Translation does not affect dispersion; independence is unnecessary for mean propagation but removes covariance cross terms in sums.

If Σ is singular, every v∈kerΣ satisfies vT(X−μ)=0 almost surely. Thus the distribution is concentrated on the lower-dimensional affine space μ+rangeΣ, rather than necessarily a linear subspace through the origin.

For a jointly Gaussian vector, vTX~N(vTμ,vTΣv). Independent Gaussian components give diagonal covariance; general Gaussian marginals have variances Σii. The review's example has μ=(1,0,2)T and covariance rows (2,0,1), (0,3,1), (1,1,4), yielding X3~N(2,4) and 2X1−X3~N(0,8). The latter variance follows by evaluating (2,0,−1)Σ(2,0,−1)T; the handwritten value 5 is inconsistent with the displayed matrix.

Covariance, Pearson correlation and the limits of uncorrelatedness · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Measures linear association and separates zero correlation from independence except for jointly Gaussian variables.

Covariance, Pearson correlation and the limits of uncorrelatedness

For real variables with finite second moments,

Var(X)=E(X−EX)2=EX2−(EX)2,
Cov(X,Y)=E[(X−EX)(Y−EY)]=E(XY)−EXEY.

When both variances are positive, the Pearson coefficient is

ρX,Y=Cov(X,Y)Var(X)Var(Y).

It measures normalized linear association, not arbitrary dependence. The review's scatter examples contrast positive/negative line patterns with nonlinear shapes having zero correlation. Zero variance makes this normalized coefficient undefined.

Independence implies zero covariance whenever the needed moments exist, by factoring the product expectation. The converse fails in general: nonlinear dependence can survive a zero coefficient. In the special case of a jointly Gaussian pair, zero covariance does imply independence; Gaussian marginal distributions alone are not the same hypothesis as joint Gaussianity.

Convolution densities for sums of independent variables · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Integrates the independent joint density over a half-plane to recover the sum CDF and convolution density.

Convolution densities for sums of independent variables

For independent real variables X,Y with densities φX,φY, their joint density factors. Integrating over x+y≤t gives

FX+Y(t)=∫RφX(x)(∫−∞t−xφY(y)dy)dx=∫RφX(x)FY(t−x)dx.

Differentiation in the density sense yields, almost everywhere,

φX+Y(t)=∫RφX(x)φY(t−x)dx=(φX*φY)(t).

The half-plane limit t−x explains the shifted second factor. Independence and the density assumptions are necessary for this product-density derivation; one cannot obtain the sum density from marginal convolution for an arbitrary dependent pair. The CDF identity also avoids requiring pointwise differentiability of an arbitrary density everywhere.

First and second objective derivatives along curves · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Applies the chain rule to separate directional curvature from curve acceleration and derives objective decay along gradient flow.

First and second objective derivatives along curves

Let f:Rn→R and γ:R→Rn be twice continuously differentiable, and set g(t)=f(γ(t)). Then

g′(t)=∇f(γ(t))Tγ′(t),
g″(t)=γ′(t)T∇2f(γ(t))γ′(t)+∇f(γ(t))Tγ″(t).

The second derivative includes both the Hessian along the velocity and the effect of curve acceleration. For a line γ(t)=x+th, the acceleration vanishes, leaving g″(t)=hT∇2f(x+th)h, which connects line convexity to Hessian tests.

Along a differentiable gradient-flow trajectory γ′(t)=−∇f(γ(t)),

ddtf(γ(t))=−‖∇f(γ(t))‖22≤0.

This is continuous-time objective decay; it does not by itself establish global existence of the flow or convergence of a discrete gradient algorithm for arbitrary steps.

Lagrange multipliers for a smooth equality constraint · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Uses tangent and normal directions to derive constrained stationarity and compare extrema on an ellipse.

Lagrange multipliers for a smooth equality constraint

Consider a differentiable objective F:Rm→R constrained by g(x)=0, with g continuously differentiable. At a regular feasible point y, ∇g(y)≠0, the tangent space is orthogonal to ∇g(y). A constrained local extremum must have zero objective derivative in every tangent direction. Consequently,

∇F(y)=λ∇g(y),g(y)=0.

With L(x,λ)=F(x)−λg(x), these are the stationarity equations in x and λ. They identify candidates, not a sufficiency test; the nonzero constraint gradient is needed for the normal-space argument. Unconstrained differentiable local extrema instead satisfy ∇F(y)=0. For a nonzero gradient the unit direction of maximal first-order increase is its normalization, and its negative gives maximal decrease.

The review optimizes F(x1,x2)=3x1+x2 on 2x12+x22=1. The equations are

3=4λx1,1=2λx2,2x12+x22=1.

Thus x1=3x2/2, x2=±2/11. Comparing values gives the maximum at (322/11,2/11), and the minimum at its negative. The ellipse is compact and the gradient of its defining constraint is nonzero there, so the candidates exhaust the extrema. Coordinates here follow the equations in (x1,x2) order; the final handwritten ordered pairs swap their order.

Concentration of high-dimensional ball volume near an equator · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Bounds the volume outside a thin coordinate slab using cross-sectional integration and an inscribed-cylinder lower bound.

Concentration of high-dimensional ball volume near an equator

For the uniform volume distribution on the unit ball in Rn, n≥3, and c≥1,

P(|X1|>cn−1)≤2ce−c2/2.

Thus at least 1−2e−c2/2/c of the volume lies in a slab of width proportional to 1/n around a coordinate equator. If the slab already covers the ball, the event is empty. This is a volume result; the proof does not replace volume by boundary surface area.

For a=c/n−1≤1, the cap in the upper half ball H has volume

V(n−1)∫a1(1−t2)(n−1)/2dt.

Using 1−u≤e−u, extending the integral to infinity, and inserting tn−1/c≥1, bounds it by V(n−1)e−c2/2/(cn−1). Meanwhile H contains a cylinder of height 1/n−1 and base radius 1−1/(n−1). Its volume is at least V(n−1)/(2n−1), by the corresponding Bernoulli bound. Dividing gives the cap fraction 2e−c2/2/c within H. Reflection supplies the identical lower cap, hence the same relative bound for the full ball.

The shrinking transverse scale explains why a random point has a small coordinate along any fixed axis despite lying in a high-dimensional ball.

Expectations and squared distances of independent uniform variables · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Uses integration, linearity and independence to compute elementary moments and average squared distances.

Expectations and squared distances of independent uniform variables

For a variable with density φ, compute Eh(X)=∫h(x)φ(x)dx when the expectation exists. Linearity handles sums without independence; factoring E(XY)=EXEY requires independence (or another justified factorization).

For independent X,Y~U[0,1], the booklet's further tasks give

EX=1/2,EX2=1/3,E(X−Y)=0,E(XY)=1/4,

and expansion yields E(X−Y)2=2/3−1/2=1/6. Consequently two independent uniform points in the unit square have expected squared distance 1/6+1/6=1/3, summing the coordinate contributions. Squared distance is the quantity averaged here; taking a square root afterwards does not give the expected distance.

For the separate U[0,4] example, integrating gives EXr=4r/(r+1). These moments feed the probability-bound comparison, while direct density integration gives the exact probability P(X>3)=1/4.

For a finite discrete variable, the same expectation principle becomes Eh(X)=∑ih(xi)pi. The review's elementary three-year warranty model sets damage costs to 100 with probability 0.15, 300 with probability 0.05 and zero otherwise, yielding expected cost 100(0.15)+300(0.05)=30. Prices 25 and 35 differ from that expected cost by minus or plus 5 per contract. These are stipulated teaching probabilities and expectation arithmetic, not measured failure rates, a complete pricing model or financial advice; they do not eliminate variation in individual outcomes.

Conditional probabilities and exponential waiting-time memorylessness · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Normalizes event probabilities after conditioning and derives an unchanged exponential residual lifetime.

Conditional probabilities and exponential waiting-time memorylessness

For events A,B with P(B)>0,

P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)P(B).

Conditioning restricts attention to B and rescales it to probability one. If the two events are independent, P(A∣B)=P(A); the observed event then leaves that probability unchanged.

An exponential variable of rate α>0 has density αe−αx1x>0, normalized by integrating the exponential tail. Integration by parts gives EX=1/α. Its survival function is P(X>t)=e−αt for t≥0.

If a waiting time has already exceeded a≥0, then for b≥0,

P(X>a+b∣X>a)=P(X>a+b)P(X>a)=e−αb=P(X>b).

The intersection reduces to the smaller event because {X>a+b}⊂{X>a}. Thus the residual waiting time has the same exponential survival law; with mean waiting time T, the rate is 1/T. This memoryless property belongs to the assumed exponential model, not to arbitrary physical lifetimes.

Source references

Invariant-ball gradient descent for an exponential quadratic · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: algorithm

Bounds gradient smoothness and proves convergence from every point of the open unit ball by a radial contraction.

Invariant-ball gradient descent for an exponential quadratic

For f(x)=e‖x‖22 on the open unit ball B1⊂Rn,

∇f(x)=2e‖x‖2x,∇2f(x)=2e‖x‖2I+4e‖x‖2xxT.

Its Hessian operator norm is at most 6e on this convex domain, so the gradient is 6e-Lipschitz. The supplied solution obtains the same constant by adding and subtracting a mixed term, bounding the exponential derivative on [0,1], and using |‖x‖2−‖y‖2|≤2‖x−y‖.

Gradient descent with α=1/20 reads

xk+1=(1−110e‖xk‖2)xk.

For ‖xk‖<1, the multiplier lies between 1−e/10>0 and 9/10. Hence ‖xk+1‖≤(9/10)‖xk‖<1. Induction proves that every initial point in B1 stays there and satisfies ‖xk‖≤(9/10)k‖x0‖→0. The whole open ball is therefore a convergence set, and the limit is its unique minimizer because e‖x‖2≥1, with equality only at zero. Invariance is proved for the actual iterates; a local smoothness bound alone would not ensure they remain in its domain.

Extended-real indicators and constrained subgradient geometry · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Encodes constraints by zero/infinity indicators and derives the interval endpoint subdifferentials from supporting slopes.

Extended-real indicators and constrained subgradient geometry

Encode a constraint x∈C by the extended-real indicator

δC(x)={0x∈C,+∞x∉C.

Then minimizing f over C is equivalent to minimizing f+δC over the ambient space. This is a zero/infinity optimization indicator, distinct from the zero/one indicator used in probability.

The function is convex exactly when C is convex: combinations of feasible points have zero right-hand side, while a positive-weight infeasible endpoint makes the inequality automatic. It is lower semicontinuous exactly when C is closed. For a closed C, an exterior point has an open neighborhood outside C, so nearby indicator values are eventually infinite; at an interior or boundary feasible point all values are at least its value zero. Conversely, a missing limit point of C violates the liminf condition.

A convex subgradient g∈∂f(x), at a point of finite value, means f(z)≥f(x)+gT(z−x) for every z. For the indicator at a feasible point this becomes the normal condition gT(z−x)≤0 for every z∈C. For a nondegenerate closed interval C=[a,b],

∂δC(x)={{0}a<x<b,(−∞,0]x=a,[0,+∞)x=b,∅x∉[a,b].

At the left endpoint a nonpositive slope supports the epigraph; at the right endpoint a nonnegative slope does so. Exterior points are outside the finite domain and have no subgradients. This illustrates how extended-real constraints and supporting-plane geometry fit the same convex optimality framework.

Tail bounds for independent sums under finite factorial moment control · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Records the source exercise linking an even-moment bound to a Gaussian-type tail over a restricted deviation range.

Tail bounds for independent sums under finite factorial moment control

The further exercise considers X=∑i=1nXi with mutually independent, mean-zero summands, variance at most σ2>0, and an even positive integer s≤nσ2/2. It assumes

|EXir|≤σ2r!(r=3,…,s),0<a≤2nσ2.

Under these stated conditions its first requested bound is

P(|X|≥a)≤(2snσ2a2)s/2.

With the additional condition s≥a2/(4nσ2), it asks to show

P(|X|≥a)≤3exp(−a212nσ2).

These are source-stated exercise targets with no supplied solution, not an extracted proof of a general unlimited tail theorem. The finite moment order, parity, independence and restricted deviation range remain part of the statement. In particular finite variance alone does not justify the second exponential bound.

Subexponential Gaussian squares and concentration of Gaussian norms · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Uses centered Gaussian squares and Bernstein concentration to place isotropic Gaussian vectors in a thin radial shell.

Subexponential Gaussian squares and concentration of Gaussian norms

The booklet calls Z subexponential when P(|Z|>t)≤ce−Ct for positive absolute constants and all t>0. If G~N(0,1), translating its tail integral shows P(G>s)≤12e−s2/2. Reflection gives

P(G2>t)=P(|G|>t)≤e−t/2,

so a Gaussian square is subexponential, although its mean is one rather than zero. Centering it preserves the exponential tail class with suitable constants; equality of the original constants is not required.

For independent Gi~N(0,1), set Yi=Gi2−1. Then EYi=0, and a Bernstein inequality for independent centered subexponential variables gives the source's consequence

P(|∑iYi|>nε)≤2e−cε2n,0<ε<1,

for an absolute c>0. The squared-norm deviation is exactly this sum. Therefore, with probability at least 1−2e−cε2n,

n1−ε≤‖G‖2≤n1+ε.

The booklet invokes a lecture Bernstein result rather than supplying its general proof.

Its additional Gaussian Annulus Theorem states that for 0<β≤n,

P(n−β≤‖G‖2≤n+β)≥1−3e−cβ2.

This is radial concentration about n for mean zero and identity covariance, not concentration around the origin in a fixed-radius ball. The two shell formulations use different relative/absolute deviation parameters.

A further proof in the weekly solution uses EeθG2=(1−2θ)−1/2, valid for θ<1/2. For 0<θ<1/2, Markov gives P(G2>t)≤e−θt/1−2θ; even the fixed choice θ=1/4 already proves an exponential tail. The square-MGF domain differs from the all-real domain of a Gaussian variable's own MGF.

The later annulus proof uses the event implication

|‖G‖−n|>t ⟹\ |‖G‖2−n|>tn,

because ‖G‖+n≥n. The right-hand quantity is a sum of independent centered Gaussian squares, so Bernstein yields a bound Ce−ct2 for 0<t≤n. This proves an absolute-width shell estimate, rather than only asserting it as in the earlier booklet remark.

Gaussian random maps and fixed-vector norm concentration · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Computes the projected covariance and rescales the Gaussian annulus bound to obtain a near-isometry for a fixed vector.

Gaussian random maps and fixed-vector norm concentration

Let u1,…,uk be independent standard Gaussian vectors in Rd, 1≤k<d, and define f(v)=(⟨ui,v⟩)i=1k. For deterministic v, rotational invariance gives each component law N(0,‖v‖22). Different rows are independent, so

f(v)~N(0,‖v‖22Ik).

For nonzero v, divide by ‖v‖2 to obtain a standard k-dimensional Gaussian. Applying its annulus estimate at width εk yields, for 0<ε<1,

P(|‖f(v)‖2−k‖v‖2|≥εk‖v‖2)≤3e−ckε2

for an absolute c>0. The zero vector maps exactly to zero and should be treated separately from division or the degenerate “≥0” failure event.

For the normalized map Av=f(v)/k, entries are independent N(0,1/k), and the norm is within factors 1±ε of the input norm outside the failure event. The unnormalized map instead has typical amplification k; it is not already a near-isometry or an orthogonal projector.

The exercise asks for a plot of ‖f(v)‖−k‖v‖ for v=(1,…,1)/20∈R400, a unit vector, over k=1,…,400. The weekly solution supplies MATLAB screenshots and one realization of the absolute deviation, computed from successive row prefixes of a Gaussian matrix. Its blue comparison curve is 0.1k, although the task requests ε=10−2. The accompanying observation that the plotted threshold is not exceeded for k≥30 describes that realization at tolerance 0.1, not a uniform guarantee at tolerance 0.01. The theorem concerns a fixed vector independent of the random matrix, not a vector chosen after seeing its rows.

Independence of the tested vector is essential. Let G∈Rm×n have independent standard Gaussian entries and let g1 be its own first row, viewed as a column input. The self-inner-product contributes E⟨g1,g1⟩2=n2+2n, using Eg1j4=3. Each other independent row contributes E⟨gi,g1⟩2=n. Thus

E‖Gg1/m‖22=n2+2n+(m−1)nm=n+n2+nm.

This exceeds E‖g1‖2=n, potentially by a large factor. It does not contradict fixed-vector or finite-set embedding guarantees: the input was selected from the very matrix used to embed it, violating independence.

Bounding gradient Lipschitz constants by Hessians · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Distinguishes function Lipschitz continuity from gradient smoothness and bounds the latter by Hessian operator norms.

Bounding gradient Lipschitz constants by Hessians

For a twice continuously differentiable scalar function on a convex domain, a uniform Hessian bound ‖∇2f(x)‖2≤L implies

‖∇f(x)−∇f(y)‖2≤L‖x−y‖2.

Apply the Jacobian criterion to the vector map ∇f. For a symmetric Hessian the operator norm is the largest absolute eigenvalue, so negative eigenvalues also contribute; the largest signed eigenvalue alone is insufficient outside the positive-semidefinite case. The Frobenius norm is an accessible upper bound but can be less sharp.

This is a bound on the variation of the gradient. In contrast, a uniform bound on ‖∇f‖ controls the Lipschitz constant of f itself. These constants have different roles. The weekly gradient-descent review's rule η≤1/L uses a Lipschitz constant of the gradient; the bounded-gradient estimate for a function cannot be substituted for it. Convergence claims additionally require the relevant optimization assumptions; a Hessian norm bound by itself does not imply convexity or convergence to a global minimum.

Gram–Schmidt construction of orthonormal coordinates · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: algorithm

Subtracts previous projection components and normalizes the residual to build a basis for finite-dimensional projection.

Gram–Schmidt construction of orthonormal coordinates

Given linearly independent real vectors a1,…,ak, construct

rj=aj−∑i<j⟨aj,qi⟩qi,qj=rj/‖rj‖2.

At the first step the sum is empty. Removing the previous components makes rj orthogonal to all preceding qi; normalization makes its length one. Independence ensures the residual is nonzero. The resulting orthonormal vectors span the same subspace as the input and can be used in the Fourier projection formula. Normalizing the original vectors alone does not remove their mutual overlap.

The review works with a1=(1,1,0)T, a2=(0,1,1)T. They have dot product one. The first normalized vector is q1=(1,1,0)T/2. Subtracting ⟨a2,q1⟩q1 gives r2=(−1/2,1/2,1)T, with squared norm 3/2; hence

q2=(−1,1,2)T/6.

This is an exact-arithmetic construction; the review does not compare floating-point orthogonalization variants.

Hessian characterization of twice differentiable convex functions · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Equates convexity with positive semidefinite Hessians on open convex domains using supporting planes and Taylor formulas.

Hessian characterization of twice differentiable convex functions

Let C⊂Rn be open and convex and f∈C2(C). Then

f is convex⟺∇2f(x)⪰0for every x∈C.

For necessity, fix x and a direction z. Openness permits sufficiently small displacements x+tz in both signs. Convexity's differentiable supporting inequality and the second-order expansion give

0≤f(x+tz)−f(x)−t∇f(x)Tz=12t2zT∇2f(x)z+o(t2).

Divide by t2 and let t→0, obtaining a nonnegative quadratic form in every direction.

Conversely, along the segment from y to x, Taylor with an intermediate Hessian gives

f(x)=f(y)+∇f(y)T(x−y)+12(x−y)T∇2f(ζ)(x−y)≥f(y)+∇f(y)T(x−y).

This supporting-plane inequality characterizes differentiable convexity. To see it implies the chord inequality, apply it at z=λx+(1−λ)y to each endpoint, multiply by the corresponding weight, and add; the gradient terms cancel. Domain convexity keeps the segment feasible. The factor 1/2, absent in one printed solution display, is part of Taylor's formula and does not change the nonnegativity argument.

Finite-set distance preservation with Johnson–Lindenstrauss maps · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Relates pairwise squared-distance distortion to normalized linear images and uses a finite union bound rather than an ambient-space guarantee.

Finite-set distance preservation with Johnson–Lindenstrauss maps

For a linear map A and distinct points v,w, set x=v−w. The squared-distance inequalities

(1−ε)‖v−w‖22≤‖Av−Aw‖22≤(1+ε)‖v−w‖22

are equivalent to

|‖Ax‖22‖x‖22−1|≤ε.

Identical points satisfy distance preservation trivially and must be excluded from the quotient.

For a finite set of m points independent of a normalized Gaussian matrix, apply the fixed-vector concentration estimate to their at most m(m−1)/2 nonzero differences. A union bound controls simultaneous failure. Norm distortion δ gives squared-norm distortion at most 2δ+δ2; choosing δ proportional to ε retains an exponential e−ckε2 failure bound. Hence embedding dimension on the order of ε−2log(m/η) suffices to make this finite-set failure probability at most η, up to absolute constants. This is the standard finite-set consequence of the preceding original estimates, rather than a supplied proof of every version of the lecture lemma.

No dimension-reducing linear map can give that guarantee for all vectors in the ambient space: it has a nonzero kernel. The finite set and the order of randomness are essential.

The booklet proposes d=10000, 10000 random Gaussian test differences, tolerance 0.1, and k=200,300,…,3000, comparing independent Gaussian entries N(0,1/k) with independent signs ±1/k. This is a numerical comparison task; the Gaussian derivation alone does not prove the sign-matrix guarantee or provide successful measured dimensions. Testing 10000 chosen differences is not exhaustive testing of all pairs in a 10000-point dataset.

The weekly solution includes a source-reported fraction-of-tests plot, annotated at approximately 90% satisfaction for k=600 and 95% for k=800, with tolerance 0.1. The figure summarizes selected tests rather than proving that all differences satisfy the bound; its unsquared annotation also does not settle whether that plot tests exactly the squared-ratio criterion from part (a). It cannot establish a minimal universally sufficient dimension.

The review motivates embedding by storage: m points in dimension d require md coordinates, while an embedded dataset uses mk. Storing all pairwise distances instead costs order m2, which can be larger when there are many points. These are dataset-storage comparisons, excluding the separate cost of representing or applying the embedding itself. The normalized Gaussian scaling is still required even where the review abbreviates its matrix entries as standard Gaussians.

Euclidean projection onto an l1 ball by threshold selection · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: algorithm

Finds a shared nonnegative threshold for exterior points and preserves points already in the ball.

Euclidean projection onto an l1 ball by threshold selection

For the unit ℓ1 ball B1={x:‖x‖1≤1}, Euclidean projection minimizes 12‖y−x‖22 under the constraint. Its Lagrangian is

L(x,λ)=12‖y−x‖22+λ(‖x‖1−1),λ≥0.

For a fixed multiplier, minimization in x separates coordinatewise into xi=Sλ(yi).

If ‖y‖1≤1, take λ=0 and return y, already at zero distance. If ‖y‖1>1, choose the unique positive threshold satisfying

∑imax(|yi|−λ,0)=1.

The left side is continuous and strictly decreasing while positive, so the root lies between zero and maxi|yi|. Its piecewise-linear structure supports scalar root selection. Return the coordinatewise thresholded vector. It is feasible, minimizes its Lagrangian, and satisfies complementary slackness; comparing the Lagrangian values of feasible points proves projection optimality. Strict convexity of the squared-distance objective gives a unique projected point.

The booklet's unconditional boundary-equality prescription omits the feasible-input case. An interior input must remain itself, rather than being forced to norm one. The multiplier must also be nonnegative for the constraint ‖x‖1−1≤0; an arbitrary negative threshold is not the stated projection procedure.

Minimum-norm least-squares solutions through the pseudoinverse · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Projects inconsistent data onto the range and selects the least-norm input by removing kernel components.

Minimum-norm least-squares solutions through the pseudoinverse

For a real matrix A∈Rm×n, solving Ax=y raises two distinct issues. If y∉rangeA, no exact solution exists. If the data are in the range but kerA≠{0}, every x0+w, w∈kerA, is another solution. Rectangular shape suggests overdetermination or underdetermination but does not replace the actual rank tests.

The Moore–Penrose choice

x†=A†y=∑i=1r⟨y,ui⟩σivi

solves both problems geometrically:

Ax†=∑i=1r⟨y,ui⟩ui=PrangeAy,x†⟂kerA.

The output is the closest attainable output, so x† minimizes ‖Ax−y‖2. Every other least-squares solution differs from it by a kernel vector. Orthogonality then gives

‖x†+w‖22=‖x†‖22+‖w‖22,

so it is the unique minimum-norm solution among the least-squares minimizers. When y is attainable, this is the minimum-norm exact solution; otherwise it discards the unattainable output component. Not belonging to the range is different from being perpendicular to it.

The review uses a rank-two matrix with rows (0,1/2,1/2), (2,0,0), (0,0,0). Its kernel is spanned by (0,1,−1)T. For y=(1,2,0)T, the pseudoinverse returns (1,1/2,1/2)T, eliminating the kernel part from other exact inputs. Adding (0,0,1)T to the data leaves this input unchanged, because that component is perpendicular to the range. Purely perpendicular data give the minimum-norm input zero.

Matrix representations of linear maps and the transpose identity · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Relates bases to matrix columns, distinguishes inner and outer products, and moves linear maps across Euclidean scalar products.

Matrix representations of linear maps and the transpose identity

A linear map A:V→W preserves addition and scalar multiplication. Choose bases v1,…,vn of V and w1,…,wm of W. Writing

Avi=∑j=1majiwj

places the coordinates of each image in column i of an m×n matrix. The matrix depends on the chosen bases; its multiplication by a coordinate vector represents the abstract map.

Matrix multiplication represents composition when the intermediate dimensions agree. It is associative but generally not commutative; matrix addition is entrywise and requires equal shapes. Transposition swaps rows and columns, satisfies (AT)T=A, and reverses product order: (AB)T=BTAT.

For real column vectors, xTy is a scalar inner product, whereas xyT is an outer-product matrix. The latter has entries xiyj. A matrix cannot be pulled out of an inner product as if it were a scalar. Instead, for A∈Rm×n, x∈Rn, y∈Rm,

⟨Ax,y⟩=⟨x,ATy⟩.

The dimensions and transpose are essential. This identity is the Euclidean adjoint relation used in Gram-matrix and projection arguments.

Lagrange dual of an inequality-form linear program · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Resolves the dual function of a linear objective over componentwise inequalities by testing unbounded primal directions.

Lagrange dual of an inequality-form linear program

Consider inf{cTx:Ax≤b, x∈Rn}, where A∈Rm×n. For nonnegative multipliers λ∈Rm, the Lagrangian is

L(x,λ)=cTx+λT(Ax−b)=(c+ATλ)Tx−λTb.

Taking the infimum over unrestricted x resolves the dual function completely:

g(λ)={−bTλATλ+c=0,−∞otherwise.

When the linear coefficient is nonzero, choosing x=−t(c+ATλ) sends the value to minus infinity. The dual problem is therefore

supλ≥0, ATλ+c=0(−bTλ).

The sign of the equality and objective follows from using Ax−b≤0 in the primal Lagrangian. On a feasible primal point, L(x,λ)≤cTx, so each finite dual value is a lower bound on the primal minimum. The assessment derives this dual; it does not establish a numerical solver or a separate strong-duality argument. Its last handwritten rewrite minimizes bTλ, which selects equivalent optimizers when attained, but its optimum is the negative of the displayed dual maximum and must not be equated numerically to it.

Estimating Lipschitz constants by derivatives and algebra · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Combines Jacobian bounds, scalar sum and product rules, and conservative domain bounds to establish Lipschitz continuity.

Estimating Lipschitz constants by derivatives and algebra

A map F:D⊂Rn→Rm is L-Lipschitz when ‖F(x)−F(y)‖≤L‖x−y‖ for every pair in D. On a convex domain, a differentiable map with ‖DF(z)‖2≤L along every joining segment satisfies this inequality by integrating its derivative. Appropriate differentiability on a neighborhood handles boundary points. Conversely, on an open domain an L-Lipschitz differentiable map has derivative operator norm at most L, by taking directional difference quotients. The segment/domain condition matters; a bound on disconnected pieces alone does not control pairs in different pieces.

For scalar functions the derivative norm is ‖∇f‖2. For vector maps, ‖DF‖2≤‖DF‖F gives a convenient sufficient bound by summing squared Jacobian entries, although it may overestimate the needed constant. Any larger constant remains valid; to prove a specified bound, the established upper bound must be no larger than that target.

Sums of functions with constants L1,L2 have constant L1+L2. If scalar gi are also bounded by |gi|≤Bi, then adding and subtracting a mixed product gives

|g1(x)g2(x)−g1(y)g2(y)|≤(B1L2+B2L1)‖x−y‖.

For ex1+x2x22 on the unit disk, bounding on the containing square yields B1=e2,L1=2e2,B2=1,L2=2; hence (2+2)e2 is a valid product bound. Direct component bounds on the gradient also give e210. The review's displayed squared-gradient simplification is not used: the correct expression is e2(x1+x2)[x24+(x22+2x2)2].

A bound on separate coefficients does not justify factoring the same coefficient out of a difference: c1,c2≤b does not imply ‖c1v−c2w‖≤b‖v−w‖. The review's counterexample takes v=(1,0),w=(1,1),c1=1/2,c2=1,b=1.05, giving 1.25>1.05. Use an actual difference decomposition or derivative bound instead.

Lower semicontinuity through epigraphs and sequential limits · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Relates a closed epigraph to the prohibition of upward value jumps relative to nearby limiting values.

Lower semicontinuity through epigraphs and sequential limits

For a real-valued function on Rn, its epigraph is

epif={(x,r)∈Rn×R:r≥f(x)}.

Lower semicontinuity is equivalent to this set being closed, or to the sequential condition

f(x)≤lim infjf(xj)whenever xj→x.

Thus nearby values may approach a height above the value at the point, but cannot have a limiting inferior strictly below it. Continuous functions satisfy the condition; a downward spike can still be lower semicontinuous, while raising the function at a point above a lower nearby branch violates it.

The review's epigraph drawings explain the same distinction geometrically: missing lower boundary points prevent the epigraph from being closed. Convexity of the epigraph is a separate requirement defining a convex function; lower semicontinuity concerns closure rather than the segment condition. The examples concern values and topology, not an assumption that every convex function on an arbitrary domain is automatically lower semicontinuous at its boundary.

Arbitrary pointwise suprema preserve lower semicontinuity:

epi(supifi)=⋂iepi(fi).

Each epigraph is closed, and an arbitrary intersection of closed sets remains closed; the index set need not be countable. For a proper extended-real function f, its conjugate is lower semicontinuous because it is the supremum, over points where f is finite, of continuous affine functions y↦⟨y,x⟩−f(x). Terms with f(x)=+∞ do not contribute. This lower-semicontinuity argument does not require convexity of the original f.

The booklet proves epigraph closure directly as well: if r<f(x), choose r<β<f(x); lower semicontinuity supplies a neighborhood where f>β. Its product with (−∞,β) lies outside the epigraph, proving that the complement is open.

The sequential proof of epigraph closure must use lim inff(xj), since xj→x need not make f(xj) converge: from rj≥f(xj) and rj→r, obtain r≥lim inff(xj)≥f(x).

The review defines the lower limit as lim infjaj=supNinfj≥Naj, permitting infinite values; for a bounded real sequence it is its lowest subsequential limit. It preserves nonstrict inequalities, while strict inequalities may become equal at the limit. Whenever the extended sums are defined, lim inf(aj+bj)≥lim infaj+lim infbj; this proves that the sum of two real-valued lower semicontinuous functions is lower semicontinuous. The inequality need not be equality because the separate low subsequences may occur at different indices.

The supporting topology rules are asymmetric: arbitrary unions and finite intersections preserve openness, while arbitrary intersections and finite unions preserve closedness. A sequence converging to a point of an open set is eventually inside it; a convergent sequence entirely in a closed set retains its limit there.

Markov bounds and higher-moment tail control · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Bounds nonnegative tails by expectations and shows how moment choice changes the estimate and its sharpness.

Markov bounds and higher-moment tail control

For a nonnegative random variable Z and t>0,

P(Z≥t)≤EZt,

provided its expectation is finite. Apply this to |X|r to obtain P(|X|≥t)≤E|X|r/tr. More generally an increasing nonnegative transform can be used when its value at the threshold is positive. Higher moments do not guarantee monotonically improving bounds: the ratio must be compared.

For X~U[0,4] at threshold 3, the first moment gives 2/3, and the second gives 16/27. The integer r-moment bound is (4/3)r/(r+1). Allowing real r>0, differentiation gives the minimizing value r=1/log(4/3)−1≈2.48. The integer minimum must compare its two neighbors: r=2 and r=3 both give 16/27. The booklet's approximately 58.7% optimum uses a real exponent, although the exercise initially asks for an integer. The exact tail probability is only 25%.

The further two-point example P(X=a)=1/a, P(X=0)=1−1/a, a≥1, has mean one and attains Markov's bound at t=a: P(X≥a)=1/a. Thus the universal bound can be sharp even though it is loose for the uniform example.

Frobenius and spectral matrix norms · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Contrasts entrywise Euclidean size with maximum amplification and computes a diagonal spectral norm through constrained stationarity.

Frobenius and spectral matrix norms

For A∈Rm×n,

‖A‖F=(∑i,j|aij|2)1/2=‖vec(A)‖2,

where vectorization stacks the columns and is linear. Thus definiteness, homogeneity and the triangle inequality transfer directly from the Euclidean norm on Rmn. The norm measures all matrix entries collectively.

The spectral/operator norm measures maximum Euclidean amplification:

‖A‖2=max‖x‖2=1‖Ax‖2.

For A=diag(1,4), maximize its squared output x12+16x22 subject to x12+x22=1. The Lagrangian

L=x12+16x22−λ(x12+x22−1)

has stationarity equations (1−λ)x1=0, (16−λ)x2=0. Feasible stationary candidates are the two coordinate-axis pairs, with squared objective 1 or 16. Compactness of the sphere guarantees attainment; comparing the candidates yields ‖A‖2=4. Its Frobenius norm is 17, so the two norms are different even for a diagonal matrix.

The Lagrange multiplier corresponds here to the squared amplification, not directly to the unsquared matrix norm. This constrained-maximization formulation connects matrix geometry to optimality conditions without presuming an algorithm or numerical experiment.

More generally, the squared amplification is the quadratic form ‖Ax‖22=xTATAx. Thus its constrained stationarity equation on the Euclidean unit sphere is ATAx=λx; the diagonal example compares the corresponding squared objective values before taking the square root. A stationary candidate alone does not identify the maximum without that comparison.

In singular-value coordinates, orthogonal changes preserve Euclidean and Frobenius size, giving

‖A‖2=σ1,‖A‖F=(∑i=1rσi2)1/2,‖A‖*=∑i=1rσi.

The last quantity is the nuclear norm. For the symmetric matrix with diagonal 17 and off-diagonal 8, the singular values 25 and 9 give respectively 25,706,34. Nonnegative ordering matters even for diagonal matrices: diag(1,4) has leading singular value 4, not its first diagonal entry. Negative eigenvalues change singular-vector signs while singular values remain nonnegative.

Cauchy sequences, metric completeness and an integral-distance counterexample · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Contrasts convergence of a diagonal iteration with continuous functions whose integral-distance Cauchy limit lies outside the space.

Cauchy sequences, metric completeness and an integral-distance counterexample

A Cauchy sequence becomes arbitrarily close to itself in the chosen metric; completeness additionally requires its limit to belong to the space. Both the metric and the underlying set matter.

For ρ(x,y)=∑i|xi−yi| on R2 and A=diag(1/3,1/4),

xm=Amx0,ρ(xm,0)=3−m|(x0)1|+4−m|(x0)2|→0.

This explicitly verifies convergence of a contracting diagonal iteration in the specified metric.

In contrast C([0,1]) is not complete under ρ(f,g)=∫01|f(t)−g(t)|dt. For m≥2, let fm be zero on [0,1/2], rise linearly with slope m on (1/2,1/2+1/m), then equal one. If n≥m, the area between the ramps is

ρ(fm,fn)=12m−12n≤12m,

so the sequence is Cauchy. A continuous limit f in this metric would have to be zero on [0,1/2) and one on (1/2,1]: the nonnegative integrals of the respective differences tend to zero, and continuity upgrades a.e. equality on each open interval to equality everywhere there. Such an f cannot be continuous at 1/2.

The obstruction is not failure of the Cauchy property but exclusion of the discontinuous limit from the given space. Convergence in integral distance is weaker than uniform convergence; no claim of a complete function space follows merely from finite-dimensional intuition.

The integral distance is a genuine metric on continuous functions: symmetry and the triangle inequality follow pointwise and survive integration. If its integral is zero, continuity of the nonnegative integrand forces it to vanish everywhere; a positive value at one point would persist on a neighborhood of positive length. On arbitrary measurable functions the same integral instead identifies functions equal almost everywhere. The handwritten ramp argument also supplies the simpler Cauchy bound ρ(fm,fn)≤1/min(m,n), by bounding the height difference by one over its shrinking support.

More precisely, (xn) is Cauchy when for every ε>0 there is N such that d(xn,xm)<ε for all n,m≥N. A norm induces the distance d(x,y)=‖x−y‖; not every metric is induced by a norm. The review contrasts the incomplete integral-distance example with completeness of finite-dimensional real spaces under any norm and of continuous functions on a compact interval under the supremum norm. The topology induced by the chosen distance is part of the completeness assertion.

Moment-generating functions and independent Gaussian sums · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Factors independent exponential moments and derives Gaussian MGFs by completing the square.

Moment-generating functions and independent Gaussian sums

The moment-generating function is MX(θ)=EeθX, on the set of parameters where it is finite. Independence gives

MX+Y(θ)=E(eθXeθY)=MX(θ)MY(θ).

For X~N(0,1), completing the square gives θx−x2/2=−(x−θ)2/2+θ2/2. Translating the normalized Gaussian density yields MX(θ)=eθ2/2 for every real θ. More generally,

X~N(μ,σ2)⟹MX(θ)=exp(μθ+σ2θ2/2).

Consequently a sum of independent Gaussians has a Gaussian law with mean equal to the sum of means and variance equal to the sum of variances, as requested in the further exercise. Multiplication of MGFs records the full distributional structure here, rather than merely its first two moments; a sum of arbitrary independent variables with those moments need not be Gaussian.

When the MGF is finite on a neighborhood of zero, differentiating under its expectation recovers moments: MX′(0)=EX, MX′′(0)=EX2, and similarly higher derivatives. The review uses the standard Gaussian MGF eθ2/2 to express EX6 as its sixth derivative at zero, avoiding a separate sixth-moment integral. Finiteness near zero justifies this moment-generating use; existence of a finite variance by itself does not.

For a standard Gaussian vector g, a right singular vector vi of a fixed matrix A, and integer r≥1,

⟨(ATA)rg,vi⟩=σi2r⟨g,vi⟩~N(0,σi4r).

For σi>0, the Gaussian tail estimate therefore gives P(|⟨(ATA)rg,vi⟩|>t)≤exp[−t2/(2σi4r)]. A zero singular value instead gives the identically zero variable. The exponent tracks the variance after repeated Gram-matrix multiplication, not just the original Gaussian variance.

Infima, minimizers and minimizing sequences · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Separates convergence of objective values from attainment and convergence of the underlying feasible points.

Infima, minimizers and minimizing sequences

For an extended-real objective F on a nonempty set X, the infimum is the greatest lower bound of its values. A minimum requires a feasible point attaining that value; argminXF denotes all such points and may be empty or contain several points. A finite infimum need not be attained, while an objective unbounded below has infimum −∞, as for logx on x>0.

If c=infXF is finite, for each εn↓0 choose a feasible xn with

c≤F(xn)≤c+εn.

Then F(xn)→c. This defines a minimizing sequence; constructing its terms can still be difficult computationally.

Convergence of these scalar values does not ensure convergence of the points or attainment of a minimum. For F(x)=1/x on (0,∞), xn=n is minimizing, with values tending to zero, but the points diverge and zero is never attained. Existence arguments therefore need additional structure. In the Hilbert projection proof, the parallelogram identity makes the minimizing sequence Cauchy, completeness supplies its limit, and closedness keeps that limit feasible.

Moore–Penrose inverse from singular coordinates · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Inverts nonzero singular values and relates full-rank formulas to the four Penrose conditions.

Moore–Penrose inverse from singular coordinates

For a rank-r matrix with reduced SVD A=UrΣrVrH, form

A†=VrΣr−1UrH.

Only the nonzero singular values are reciprocated; zero directions are left at zero in a full representation. The resulting matrix satisfies

AA†A=A,A†AA†=A†,(AA†)H=AA†,(A†A)H=A†A.

These follow by multiplying the singular-coordinate factors and using orthonormality. In particular AA†=UrUrH and A†A=VrVrH are orthogonal projectors.

With independent columns, AHA is invertible and A†=(AHA)−1AH; then A†A=I. With independent rows, the corresponding expression is A†=AH(AAH)−1, with AA†=I. These ordinary inverse formulas need their rank assumptions. The booklet motivates the pseudoinverse by least-squares systems and asks for the conditions and SVD construction without supplying a separate worked solution.

For an invertible square B=UΣVT, the same formula is its ordinary inverse: B−1=VΣ−1UT=∑iσi−1viuiT. Multiplication collapses mixed terms by orthogonality and leaves the identity resolution I=∑iuiuiT. Inverting reverses the order of positive magnitudes: an ordered SVD of the inverse requires reordering the reciprocal values and their paired vectors.

For full column rank, the Penrose conditions can also be verified without an SVD. Let G=ATA, which is invertible and symmetric. Then A†A=G−1G=I, giving the first two conditions; AA†=AG−1AT is symmetric because (G−1)T=(GT)−1=G−1. The fourth condition follows from A†A=I.

Pairwise and mutual independence of events and variables · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Requires factorization over every finite subfamily and explains when density and transformed-expectation products are valid.

Pairwise and mutual independence of events and variables

Two events are independent when P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). A family A1,…,AN is mutually independent when the analogous product identity holds for every subfamily of distinct indices. Checking pairs alone is insufficient. The review's unit-square regions have individual probabilities 1/2, pair intersections 1/4, and triple intersection 1/4, whereas mutual independence would require 1/8.

Variables X,Y are independent when, for every pair of measurable value sets C,D,

P(X∈C,Y∈D)=P(X∈C)P(Y∈D).

The joint event is {(X,Y)∈C×D}. Marginal laws alone do not determine a general joint law. When both variables have densities, independence corresponds to φX,Y(x,y)=φX(x)φY(y) almost everywhere.

Measurable transforms of separate independent variables remain independent, so integrable transformed products factor as E[f(X)g(Y)]=Ef(X)Eg(Y). This does not justify factoring arbitrary functions that each depend on both variables, such as cos(X+Y) and Y. Nor may a nontrivial variable be treated as independent of itself: self-independence would require every one of its event probabilities p to satisfy p=p2. Degenerate almost-surely constant variables are the exception to the review's blanket warning.

Normalized gradient steps and competing stopping criteria · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: algorithm

Specifies a unit-direction gradient iteration with decaying travel lengths and three independent stopping tests.

Normalized gradient steps and competing stopping criteria

The numerical task minimizes

f(x1,x2)=(x1−3)4+(x1−3x2)2

using the normalized gradient direction:

xk+1=xk−λk∇f(xk)‖∇f(xk)‖,x0=(0,0),λk=0.9k+1.

Here ∇f=(4(x1−3)3+2(x1−3x2),−6(x1−3x2)). Normalization makes the displacement length exactly λk when the gradient is nonzero. Check for a zero gradient before dividing; it already satisfies the gradient stopping test. The nonnegative terms vanish together at the unique minimizer (3,1).

The task compares the first triggering of three tests: gradient norm at most 3.5; successive objective difference at most 0.4 in absolute value; and a cap of 10 iterations. The objective-difference test requires two available iterates, and an implementation must keep iteration indices consistent with the prescribed step sequence. These tests measure different things: stationarity, small observed progress, and computational budget. A small objective change alone does not prove proximity to the minimizer. The supplied booklet solution points to MATLAB code without providing a numerical trace or winner on these pages; no execution result is asserted here.

Spectral-gap convergence of normalized Gram-matrix powers · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Shows convergence to the averaged leading-eigenspace projector and quantifies decay through singular-value ratios.

Spectral-gap convergence of normalized Gram-matrix powers

Let A≠0 have positive singular values σ1≥⋯≥σr, B=ATA, and let the leading eigenvalue of B have multiplicity d. For E=span(v1,…,vd),

Mℓ=Bℓ∑i=1rσi2ℓ⟶PEd.

Indeed, divide numerator and denominator by σ12ℓ. The first d weights remain one; all other ratios vanish.

If r>d, define δ=maxi>dσi/σ1<1 and sℓ=∑i>d(σi/σ1)2ℓ. The signed coefficient on each leading projector in Mℓ−PE/d is

1d+sℓ−1d=−sℓd(d+sℓ).

Its absolute value is bounded by (r−d)δ2ℓ/d2; every remaining eigenvalue is bounded by δ2ℓ/d. In particular the decomposition and triangle inequality yield

‖Mℓ−PE/d‖2≤(r−dd2+1d)δ2ℓ.

The important rate is geometric in δ2ℓ, faster with a larger gap. If r=d, the normalized matrix already equals PE/d for every positive power, without defining a maximum over an empty set. If A=0, the normalization is undefined.

This is a matrix-power statement underlying the power method, not a promise that a repeated leading singular value selects one unique direction. The companion exercise requests computing dominant singular pairs by a power-method implementation, successive rank approximations, and comparison to MATLAB svd on countries_data.txt. Neither that dataset nor the requested implementation/output is supplied in the booklet.

Using the largest absolute eigenvalue, rather than summing the two coefficient bounds, gives the sharper estimate in the weekly solution:

‖Mℓ−PE/d‖2≤max{r−dd2,1d}δ2ℓ.

The erratum explicitly corrects the missing minus sign on the leading-eigenspace coefficient. The bound concerns its magnitude; a negative coefficient cannot simply be replaced by a positive one in the matrix identity.

Finite orthogonal coordinates and Pythagoras–Fourier projection identities · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Minimizes finite-basis approximation error by Fourier coefficients and derives projection-energy and residual identities.

Finite orthogonal coordinates and Pythagoras–Fourier projection identities

Let W be a finite-dimensional subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space, with orthonormal basis w1,…,wn. With inner product linear in its first argument,

PWv=∑i=1n⟨v,wi⟩wi.

To derive it, expand an arbitrary candidate w=∑iαiwi:

‖v−w‖2=‖v‖2−∑i|⟨v,wi⟩|2+∑i|αi−⟨v,wi⟩|2.

The last sum is minimized uniquely by the Fourier coefficients. Orthogonality gives

‖PWv‖2=∑i|⟨v,wi⟩|2,‖v−PWv‖2=‖v‖2−∑i|⟨v,wi⟩|2.

These identities describe exact finite-subspace approximation, not merely a coordinate convention. Finite-dimensional subspaces are closed, so the projection theorem applies; no completeness of an arbitrary infinite orthonormal system is asserted here.

The underlying inner-product norm also supplies Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality. The booklet's further exercises ask for their equivalence in a real pre-Hilbert space; these inequalities concern inner-product geometry and do not require completion. Completion is needed in the separate existence proof for projections onto arbitrary closed convex sets.

In real Euclidean space the normalized inner product of nonzero vectors is cosθ=⟨x,y⟩/(‖x‖2‖y‖2). It measures directional alignment: values near zero indicate near-orthogonality, while absolute values near one indicate alignment up to sign. This is geometric information, not by itself statistical independence. If Q has the orthonormal basis vectors as columns, the projection is QQTx. For example, projecting (3,2)T onto span(1,1)T gives (5/2,5/2)T.

The finite-subspace projection is linear and admits PW=∑iwiwiT, an SVD whose positive singular values are all one. Changing to another orthonormal basis of the same subspace leaves this operator unchanged. Its residual is perpendicular to every subspace vector: ⟨x−PWx,y⟩=0 for all y∈W; for a general closed convex set the corresponding condition is an inequality instead.

Recovering an SVD from orthogonal rank-one expansions · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Normalizes signed orthogonal dyads, handles common-direction differences and detects rank collapse from a repeated factor.

Recovering an SVD from orthogonal rank-one expansions

Suppose

A=∑iciaibiT,

where the nonzero ai are mutually orthogonal and the nonzero bi are mutually orthogonal. The coefficients need not be positive and the vectors need not be normalized. For each nonzero term, set

ui=sign(ci)ai/‖ai‖2,vi=bi/‖bi‖2,σi=|ci|‖ai‖2‖bi‖2.

Discard zero terms and sort the positive σi in decreasing order. The resulting expansion is an SVD. Sign changes preserve orthogonality; normalization transfers the missing lengths into the singular coefficients. A negative coefficient is not a negative singular value.

For two matrices sharing the same orthonormal left/right directions, subtract their coefficients first. Their difference has singular values equal to the absolute coefficient differences, after removing zeros and reordering. This shortcut requires shared directions: unrelated SVDs cannot generally be subtracted term by term. The review's common-direction example yields singular values 1 and 1/2, hence nuclear norm 3/2 and Frobenius norm 1+1/4 for either sign of the difference.

A repeated factor changes the situation. If

A=c1u1vT+c2u2vT=(c1u1+c2u2)vT,

with orthonormal u1,u2, unit v, and coefficients not both zero, then A has rank one, not two. Normalize the combined left vector to get its only positive singular value c12+c22. If both coefficients vanish the rank is zero. Counting dyads only determines rank when the required independence/orthogonality is present on both sides.

Principal-component coordinates for data visualization

The booklet's PCA exercise takes a high-dimensional data matrix and asks for its SVD and a plot in the first three principal components. Singular directions provide orthogonal coordinates; retaining the leading coordinates produces a low-dimensional representation associated with the leading rank approximation.

The prescribed example loads MATLAB's ovariancancer data, inspects the sample count and dimension, and plots diagnosed samples as red crosses and controls as blue circles. The supplied Code for Exercise 6.2 is MATLAB text: it calls load ovariancancer, whos, and [U,S,V]=svd(obs,'econ'), then plots diag(S) on a logarithmic scale. Each row obs(i,:) is an observation. Its first three coordinates are computed as V(:,j)Tobs(i,:)T, for j=1,2,3, and displayed in both 3D and the first two dimensions with class-dependent markers. Equivalently the scores are the first columns of obsV=UΣ.

The code applies SVD directly to obs: it contains no explicit mean subtraction or feature scaling. It therefore documents uncentered singular coordinates as supplied, rather than establishing an ordinary centered covariance-PCA pipeline. The group labels determine plot colors/markers; they are not used to train a classifier.

This is a concrete course-provided plotting script and a requested data-analysis exercise. The dataset is loaded from MATLAB rather than packaged in the archive, and no predictive metrics, medical findings or personally attributable implementation are established. The booklet's solution contains only a MATLAB-code pointer; the separate weekly asset supplies the script text.

Basis-independent principal angles and projection discrepancy · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Defines subspace angles from a cross-Gram SVD and expresses Frobenius projection discrepancy through their sines.

Basis-independent principal angles and projection discrepancy

Let V,W∈Rd×n have orthonormal columns spanning two n-dimensional subspaces. The principal angles θi∈[0,π/2] are defined by

cosθi=σi(WTV).

The singular values lie in [0,1], since taking inner products with orthonormal columns cannot increase Euclidean length.

For other orthonormal bases V′=VQ1, W′=WQ2, the cross-Gram matrix becomes Q2T(WTV)Q1. Orthogonal left/right factors preserve its singular values, so the angles depend on the subspaces, not their chosen bases.

With PV=VVT and PW⟂=I−WWT, cyclic trace and projector identities yield

‖PW⟂PV‖F2=tr((I−WWT)VVT)=n−‖WTV‖F2=∑isin2θi.

The discrepancy measures the part of one subspace left outside the other. The booklet's two planes in R3 give cross-Gram singular values 1 and 4/21: the first angle is zero and the other is approximately 29.2059∘. Its displayed projection matrices are computed as basis matrices times their transposes; rectangular orthonormal-column matrices are not square orthogonal matrices.

Geometrically, the first cosine maximizes ⟨v,w⟩ over unit vectors in the two subspaces. Subsequent cosines use vectors orthogonal to previously selected directions on each side. Maximizing cosine minimizes the corresponding acute angle. A common nonzero direction gives an angle zero. The review's coordinate planes span(e1,e2) and span(e2,e3) have cross-Gram singular values 1 and 0, hence angles 0 and π/2. The ordering is recovered from singular-value order, rather than the order of a displayed unsorted diagonal.

Mean-square convergence versus convergence in probability · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Proves the mean-square implication and uses rare growing values to disprove its converse.

Mean-square convergence versus convergence in probability

Mean-square convergence to X means E|Xn−X|2→0. Convergence in probability means P(|Xn−X|≥ε)→0 for every fixed ε>0. Markov applied to the squared difference gives

P(|Xn−X|≥ε)≤E|Xn−X|2ε2,

so mean-square convergence implies probability convergence.

The converse fails for P(Xn=n)=1/n, P(Xn=0)=1−1/n. For every fixed positive ε and sufficiently large n, the exceptional event has probability 1/n→0, but EXn2=n→∞. Rare events can vanish in probability while their squared magnitude dominates the expectation.

The accompanying diagram also records L2⇒L1⇒ convergence in probability and almost-sure convergence ⇒ convergence in probability ⇒ convergence in distribution. Here Lp convergence means E|Xn−X|p→0; almost-sure convergence means pathwise convergence outside a null event; convergence in distribution uses convergence of distribution functions at continuity points of the limit CDF. The continuity-point qualification is needed beyond the diagram's abbreviated CDF formula.

The same Markov argument works for any finite p≥1: P(|Xn−X|>ε)≤E|Xn−X|p/εp. On a probability space, Lp2 convergence implies Lp1 convergence for 1≤p1<p2, as noted in the handwritten solution. The implication does not by itself supply a sharp convergence rate; quantitative tail estimates require quantitative control of its numerator.

Events, random variables and probability laws · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Distinguishes events in the sample space from sets of variable values and computes probabilities through densities or discrete masses.

Events, random variables and probability laws

A probability space is (Ω,F,P): elementary outcomes lie in Ω, measurable events belong to F, and P assigns their probabilities. A real random variable is a measurable map X:Ω→R. For a measurable value set C, notation P(X∈C) means the probability of its inverse-image event {ω:X(ω)∈C}; C itself need not be an event in the original sample space.

For an absolutely continuous law, P(X∈C)=∫CφX(x)dx. For a finite discrete law with values xi and masses pi, it is ∑ipi1C(xi). For a fair die and C=[−3,3.2], this sums the masses of 1, 2 and 3, giving 1/2. Continuous and discrete probabilities require their respective representations; a finite discrete variable does not possess an ordinary Lebesgue density.

Monotonicity gives P(A∩B)≤min(P(A),P(B)). Inclusion–exclusion gives P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B), with simple additivity only for disjoint events. Likewise, when computing the probability of a union of value intervals, merge or disjointify overlapping intervals before summing their integrals.

Differentiating general quadratic forms and squared matrix norms · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Tracks matrix symmetry and dimensions when deriving gradients and constant Hessians of quadratic objectives.

Differentiating general quadratic forms and squared matrix norms

For A∈Rn×n, b∈Rn,

f(x)=xTAx+bTx+c,∇f(x)=(A+AT)x+b,∇2f=A+AT.

Differentiate ∑i,jxiAijxj: the terms in which the variable occurs as the first factor give Ax, and those in the second give ATx. Only for symmetric A does this simplify to 2Ax+b. With the conventional factor 1/2, a symmetric quadratic has gradient Ax+b and Hessian A. The antisymmetric part contributes zero to the scalar quadratic.

A rectangular matrix cannot be inserted into xTAx without matching dimensions. For A∈Rm×n, however,

‖Ax‖22=xTATAx,∇‖Ax‖22=2ATAx,∇2‖Ax‖22=2ATA.

The symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix ATA makes these formulas applicable to least-squares objectives and supplies their curvature and gradient Lipschitz bounds.

Gradient descent for a quadratic objective with a linear radial tail · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: algorithm

Proves finite entry into a quadratic region followed by geometric convergence for a fixed gradient step.

Gradient descent for a quadratic objective with a linear radial tail

Fix a∈R2, ‖a‖<1, and let

f(x)={‖x‖2−⟨a,x⟩‖x‖≤1,2‖x‖−⟨a,x⟩−1‖x‖>1.

Its gradient is 2x−a inside the unit ball and 2x/‖x‖−a outside; the formulas agree on the boundary. Consequently ‖∇f‖≤2+‖a‖<3, and integration along segments proves that f is 3-Lipschitz. A Lipschitz upper bound need not be the smallest possible constant. The unique minimizer is a/2: inside, complete the square; outside, the radial derivative along any ray is 2−⟨a,u⟩>0, so moving toward the unit ball decreases the value.

Apply xk+1=xk−η∇f(xk) with η=1/4. Inside the ball,

xk+1=12xk+14a,xk−12a=2−(k−k0)(xk0−12a).

The ball is invariant because ‖xk+1‖≤12+14‖a‖<1. Outside it,

xk+1=(‖xk‖−2η)xk‖xk‖+ηa,‖xk+1‖≤‖xk‖−2η+η‖a‖<‖xk‖−η.

The positive radial coefficient permits this estimate. The iterates therefore enter the ball after finitely many steps from every initial point and then converge geometrically to a/2.

More generally, the same invariant-ball and finite-entry proof works for 0<η≤1/2. The interior error recurrence is ek+1=(1−2η)ek; its formal stability condition 0<η<1 alone does not establish invariance or the outside-region argument. The booklet's specialized recurrence prints a minus sign before a/4; its general update, the weekly solution and the minimizer require the plus sign above.

Singular decompositions and the four fundamental subspaces · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Constructs singular pairs from Gram eigenvectors and reads range, kernel and orthogonal complements from the full decomposition.

Singular decompositions and the four fundamental subspaces

For a real rank-r matrix A∈Rm×n, a reduced singular value decomposition is

A=UrΣrVrT=∑i=1rσiuiviT,σ1≥⋯≥σr>0,UrTUr=VrTVr=Ir.

Right singular vectors satisfy ATAvi=σi2vi, and ui=Avi/σi. Consequently ⟨ui,uj⟩=(σj/σi)⟨vi,vj⟩, proving orthonormality. The successive-maximization formulation chooses a unit input orthogonal to previous right vectors; its feasible sets shrink, so the successive maximum amplifications cannot increase.

Extend these columns to orthogonal matrices U=[Ur,U^] and V=[Vr,V^]. A full SVD uses a rectangular m×n diagonal matrix with the positive singular values followed by zeros. It gives

rangeA=spanUr,kerA=spanV^,(rangeA)⟂=spanU^,(kerA)⟂=spanVr.

Here the kernel consists of inputs mapped to zero, and the range consists of all outputs. Their dimensions are n−r and r, respectively. The reduced form represents the same map but omits complement bases.

For A=(178817), the singular values are 25 and 9, with matching left/right vectors (1,1)T/2 and (1,−1)T/2. For the booklet's 3×4 matrix with rows (−1,0,1,1), (1,1,1,0), (−1,1,3,2), using the smaller matrix AAT gives eigenvalues 18, 3 and 0: the rank is two, the positive singular values are 18,3, and the left nullspace is spanned by (2,1,−1)T. Kernel basis vectors (1,−2,1,0)T, (1,0,−1,2)T are orthogonal but need normalization to be an ONB.

The further rotation task treats row vectors as points. Rotating every point by an orthogonal R produces C=ART, so if A=UΣVT, then C=UΣ(RV)T: the singular values are unchanged and the right directions rotate with the points. The named Bird_Data dataset is not supplied; this algebra does not constitute a performed numerical experiment.

Transposition exchanges the left and right singular vectors without changing the positive singular values. Thus one may diagonalize AAT instead of ATA when it is smaller, then recover the opposite singular vectors and swap their roles. A real singular pair can simultaneously change sign: replacing (ui,vi) by (−ui,−vi) leaves its rank-one term unchanged. For a repeated Gram eigenvalue, choose an orthonormal basis within its eigenspace, using Gram–Schmidt if needed; arbitrary unnormalized eigenvectors do not automatically form singular-vector matrices.

The complement identities also follow directly from the transpose relation: v∈kerA iff ⟨v,ATy⟩=0 for every y, so kerA=(rangeAT)⟂. Similarly kerAT=(rangeA)⟂. Finite-dimensional orthogonal decomposition and rank–nullity give Rn=kerA⊕rangeAT and n=dimkerA+rankA.

Ordered singular values are uniquely determined by the matrix; their vector bases need not be. For a repeated positive value σ, rotate its right basis by any orthogonal Q and its left basis by the same Q. The block product is unchanged because (UQ)σI(VQ)T=UσIVT. Distinct singular values leave simultaneous sign freedom over the reals, while repeated values permit arbitrary orthonormal bases of their singular subspaces.

Spectral-norm perturbation bound for singular values · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Bounds each ordered singular-value change by the perturbation size and separates scalar-value control from vector sensitivity.

Spectral-norm perturbation bound for singular values

For same-shaped real matrices A and A+E, ordered singular values satisfy

|σi(A+E)−σi(A)|≤‖E‖2.

The solution and review present this as a perturbation bound, calling it “Wedin's Bound”; they do not develop a general singular-subspace perturbation proof.

Each perturbed value therefore remains in [max(0,σi−η),σi+η] when ‖E‖2≤η. If adjacent uncertainty intervals are disjoint, their value clusters remain separated. For the source's values 10,8,5,4 and η=0.3, the intervals are respectively [9.7,10.3], [7.7,8.3], [4.7,5.3] and [3.7,4.3].

The scalar inequality does not itself bound the distance between individual singular vectors. The source contrasts separated values with a cluster such as 1.1,1.0, whose uncertainty intervals overlap at that perturbation size: directions within the cluster may change substantially. Choosing a truncation boundary outside such a cluster is conceptually different from selecting one of its individual directions. No numerical vector-angle estimate is supplied by this inequality alone.

Singular-vector sensitivity near repeated singular values · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: result

Exhibits an order-one leading-vector rotation under a perturbation tending to zero when the singular gap also closes.

Singular-vector sensitivity near repeated singular values

For 0<ε<1, consider

A=(1001+ε),E=(0εε−ε),A~=A+E=(1εε1).

The original leading right vector is e2, with singular value 1+ε. The perturbed matrix has leading right vector (1,1)T/2 with the same leading value, and second singular value 1−ε. Thus

‖E‖F=3ε→0,‖e2−(1,1)T2‖2=2−2.

Even choosing the closest sign of the perturbed vector leaves a nonvanishing distance. The small-ε restriction makes the stated perturbed diagonalization an SVD with nonnegative values; the exercise's “arbitrary positive” wording otherwise needs absolute values and possible reordering.

The example demonstrates sensitivity of individual directions as the spectral gap closes. It does not show that singular values have comparable instability, or that every well-separated singular vector behaves this way. Nonuniqueness of basis choices at a repeated value must likewise be separated from instability of the matrix represented by the SVD.

The weekly solution links this sensitivity to rank selection: when several adjacent values are close, truncating within that cluster may be more sensitive than retaining or discarding the whole cluster. Sign freedom alone is not the cause of the fixed angle in the displayed perturbation example; its gap shrinks with ε.

A contrasting sheet replaces the first diagonal entry by 2: B=diag(2,1+ε) and B+E=(2εε1). For small positive ε, the unperturbed leading direction is e1, and the separated limiting values are 2 and 1. The supplied numerical examples at ε=0.5,0.25,0.125 show the perturbed right directions approaching the coordinate directions as the perturbation decreases. This contrasts with the fixed angle in the closing-gap example; “separated” is relative to perturbation size, not an absolute label applicable at all positive ε.

Subgradient derivation of soft thresholding · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: algorithm

Solves quadratic-plus-absolute-value minimization and describes the piecewise-linear thresholded mass.

Subgradient derivation of soft thresholding

For λ≥0, minimize f(x)=12(y−x)2+λ|x| over real x. The absolute-value subdifferential is {1} at positive x, {−1} at negative x, and [−1,1] at zero. Convex subgradient optimality yields

0∈x−y+λ∂|x|⟺y∈x+λ∂|x|.

The three sign cases give the unique minimizer

Sλ(y)=sign(y)max(|y|−λ,0)={y−λy>λ,0|y|≤λ,y+λy<−λ.

The quadratic term makes the objective strongly convex, so satisfying the inclusion suffices and the minimizer is unique, including the equality thresholds. The vector problem with squared Euclidean discrepancy and ℓ1 penalty separates into these scalar problems.

For a fixed vector y,

h(λ)=‖Sλ(y)‖1=∑imax(|yi|−λ,0).

This is continuous, piecewise linear and nonincreasing, with h(0)=‖y‖1 and h(λ)=0 for λ≥maxi|yi|. Away from breakpoints its slope is minus the number of surviving coordinates. Equal-magnitude entries can disappear together, changing the slope by more than one; after all entries vanish it is constant. The booklet asks for a plot for a chosen vector but supplies the analytic shape rather than a measured run.

The weekly solution interprets subgradients as supporting affine functions: g∈∂f(x) means f(z)≥f(x)+gT(z−x) for every z. Thus 0∈∂f(x) is exactly global minimality for a convex function. For the absolute value, all supporting slopes at the kink lie between minus one and one, giving the interval used in the threshold inclusion; a subdifferential is a set, so optimality uses membership rather than equality to one arbitrary slope.

Gaussian normalization and high-dimensional sphere experiments · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method

Samples uniform sphere directions by Gaussian normalization and describes the source tasks on projected coordinates and pairwise distances.

Gaussian normalization and high-dimensional sphere experiments

If G=(G1,…,Gd) has independent standard Gaussian components, then G/‖G‖2 is uniform on Sd−1. The zero vector has probability zero. Rotational invariance of the Gaussian law and normalization make the direction rotationally invariant; this is surface sampling, distinct from sampling uniformly throughout the ball.

The booklet's numerical tasks explore several consequences and comparisons:

  • Generate 200 points on the unit sphere in 50-dimensional space, project them onto several uniform random lines, and plot the one-dimensional distributions to examine concentration near equators.
  • Compare histograms of all pairwise distances among 100 uniform points on S3 and S100.
  • Generate 20 points on a sphere of radius 30 in 900-dimensional space; project onto subspaces of dimensions 100, 50, 10, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1. Compare projected distances with k/d times the originals and report the maximal difference as a percentage of k.
  • Compare two ways to obtain 1000 nearly orthogonal vectors in R100: project 1000 orthonormal vectors from dimension 1000 into a random 100-dimensional subspace, or generate random Gaussian vectors. Orthogonality comparisons concern normalized directions rather than unnormalized magnitudes.

The final task's introductory statement about exactly d orthogonal unit vectors is an upper bound on the cardinality of a mutually orthogonal nonzero set, not a count of all unit vectors. These are proposed MATLAB experiments with no supplied programs or measurements; the tasks alone do not establish observed histograms or distortion results.

Strict convexity, uniqueness and quantitative strong convexity · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Separates strict segment inequalities from uniform quadratic curvature and states their consequences under appropriate smoothness.

Strict convexity, uniqueness and quantitative strong convexity

Strict convexity requires a strict chord inequality for distinct x,y and 0<λ<1. It permits at most one minimizer on a convex domain: two distinct minimizers would have a midpoint with smaller value. This is a uniqueness assertion conditional on existence, not an attainment theorem. For differentiable strictly convex functions on Rn, the gradient is injective, as stated in the review.

Strong convexity with parameter m>0 strengthens the chord bound to

f(λx+(1−λ)y)≤λf(x)+(1−λ)f(y)−m2λ(1−λ)‖x−y‖22.

It implies strict convexity by a uniform quadratic margin. If f is differentiable, the equivalent supporting inequality is

f(x)≥f(y)+∇f(y)T(x−y)+m2‖x−y‖22.

The factor m quantifies curvature; setting m=0 recovers ordinary convexity rather than strict convexity. A strictly convex function can have curvature weakening toward zero, so strictness alone is not the same as one positive uniform strong-convexity constant. The gradient statement requires differentiability even though strict convexity itself does not.

Subgaussian tails and independent weighted sums · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Optimizes an exponential quadratic MGF bound and tracks the coefficient norm in independent sums.

Subgaussian tails and independent weighted sums

A mean-zero variable is subgaussian in the booklet's convention if some K>0 satisfies

EeθX≤eK2θ2for all real θ.

For t>0, positive exponential tilting bounds each one-sided tail by eK2θ2−θt. Choosing θ=t/(2K2), and applying the same argument to −X, gives

P(|X|>t)≤2e−t2/(4K2).

The square on t and the event direction follow from this minimization; several displayed formulas in the booklet's solution omit or reverse them.

For independent mean-zero variables with the same bound and real coefficients ai, factor their MGFs:

Eexp(θ∑iaiXi)≤∏ieK2ai2θ2=eK2‖a‖22θ2.

Thus the sum is subgaussian with parameter K‖a‖2, and for a≠0,

P(|∑iaiXi|>t)≤2exp(−t24K2‖a‖22).

For zero coefficients the sum is identically zero. Independence enables the MGF product; identical distribution is sufficient but the uniform bound is the property actually used. For a standard Gaussian one may take K2=1/2.

The weekly solution allows distinct subgaussian parameters Ki: independence gives Eexp(θ∑iaiXi)≤exp(θ2∑iKi2ai2). Thus the tail denominator can be 4∑iKi2ai2; replacing every Ki by their maximum is a simpler, possibly looser bound. Neither symmetry of each variable's law nor identical distributions are needed when both signs of the MGF parameter are controlled.

Singular axes versus eigenvector directions · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: concept

Interprets singular values as ellipsoid semiaxes and explains why nonorthogonal eigenvectors do not determine Euclidean amplification.

Singular axes versus eigenvector directions

For A=UΣVT, a unit input is first expressed in right singular coordinates, stretched by the singular values, and mapped into the left singular directions. The image of a Euclidean unit ball is an ellipsoid in the range of A; its positive semiaxes have lengths σi along ui, with input directions vi satisfying Avi=σiui. In the invertible square case, the unit sphere maps to its boundary. The longest semiaxis is the spectral norm, while the Frobenius norm combines all squared semiaxis lengths.

Eigenvectors of a square diagonalizable matrix instead identify invariant lines: Av=λv. These lines need not be orthogonal, eigenvalues may be negative, and their magnitudes need not equal singular values. A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix is a special case where orthonormal eigenvectors also provide matching singular directions.

The review constructs

A=Qdiag(2,−4)Q−1=(−1−12−3/4−1),Q=(11−1/41/4).

Its eigenvectors are nearly aligned rather than orthogonal. The review gives approximate singular values 12.09 and 0.66, markedly different from the eigenvalue magnitudes 2 and 4. Plotting A(cost,sint)T reveals the ellipse axes directly. The example shows why a general eigenvalue decomposition cannot substitute for Euclidean singular geometry.

Grayscale image approximation with truncated singular factors · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: method
