Grayscale image approximation with truncated singular factors

Treat a grayscale image as a real matrix and retain the leading singular factors. The course solution shows MATLAB code that loads peppers.png with imread, converts with rgb2gray, casts to double, computes [U,S,V]=svd(image), and forms

Ik=U(:,1:k)S(1:k,1:k)V(:,1:k)T

for k=10,25,100. Display code converts the floored reconstructions to uint8; the matrix norms are computed on the floating-point residual before this display conversion.

The original RGB image is supplied as an asset. The solution's figure compares the original grayscale image with three reconstructions: rank 10 loses fine detail, rank 25 improves the shapes and shading, and rank 100 visually approaches the original. The screenshot reports:

Rank Frobenius residual norm Spectral residual norm
10 6.0144×103 1.8500×103
25 3.2952×103 779.4500
100 938.1950 150.5925

These are absolute errors in the demonstration's grayscale intensity scale, not relative percentages. Their decrease agrees with retaining more singular terms. The evidence consists of course-solution code/output screenshots, not a standalone executable solution file or a personally attributable implementation; the figures and values are source-reported rather than newly reproduced here.

Orthogonal diagonalization and positive semidefinite Gram matrices · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Characterizes symmetric positivity through eigenvalues and derives nonnegativity of Gram-matrix quadratic forms.

Orthogonal diagonalization and positive semidefinite Gram matrices

An eigenvector v≠0 satisfies Av=λv. If a square matrix has an eigenvector basis, collecting those vectors in Q gives Q−1AQ=diag(λi); such a basis need not exist for a general matrix.

A real symmetric matrix does admit an orthonormal eigenvector basis and real eigenvalues. Thus Q−1=QT and

A=Qdiag(λi)QT.

For symmetric A, positive semidefiniteness means xTAx≥0 for all x; positive definiteness requires strict positivity for every nonzero x. In orthogonal coordinates the quadratic form is ∑iλi(QTx)i2, so these properties correspond respectively to all eigenvalues being nonnegative or positive.

For a rectangular real matrix B, BBT is symmetric and positive semidefinite because

(BBT)T=BBT,xTBBTx=‖BTx‖22≥0.

Positive semidefiniteness alone does not imply invertibility: a nonzero vector killed by BT gives zero quadratic form. This construction connects a general linear map with the symmetric spectral structure needed for singular values.

In particular, ATA is positive definite exactly when A has independent columns, because xTATAx=‖Ax‖2 vanishes precisely on its kernel. A wide full-row-rank matrix still gives a singular ATA: full rank means rankA=min(m,n), not automatically n. Positive definiteness implies invertibility, but invertibility and symmetry alone do not imply positivity, as diag(1,−1) shows. For symmetric positive semidefinite A, its own singular values equal its nonnegative eigenvalues; the eigenvalues of ATA are their squares.

Taylor expansions with little-o and intermediate-point remainders · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Distinguishes local error order from exact intermediate-point formulas in scalar and multivariable Taylor expansions.

Taylor expansions with little-o and intermediate-point remainders

The notation r(t)=o(tp) as t→0 means r(t)/tp→0. For example t3=o(t2) and o(t), while t2=o(t). A first-order scalar expansion of a differentiable function is f(x+t)=f(x)+f′(x)t+o(t); for C2 functions it extends by f″(x)t2/2+o(t2).

For f∈C2 on an open neighborhood of x∈Rn, the vector form is

f(x+h)=f(x)+∇f(x)Th+12hT∇2f(x)h+o(‖h‖22).

The Hessian collects second partial derivatives and is symmetric under the stated continuous-second-derivative hypothesis. Its contribution is a scalar quadratic form, not a Hessian multiplied by the scalar ⟨h,h⟩.

On a segment in the domain, the first-order mean-value formula instead gives f(x+h)=f(x)+∇f(x+τh)Th for some 0<τ<1. The second-order version gives

f(x+h)=f(x)+∇f(x)Th+12hT∇2f(x+τh)h

for some such τ. These are exact equalities but the intermediate point is unspecified and may change with the displacement. They follow by applying scalar Taylor formulas to the line restriction t↦f(x+th). The local little-o formula evaluates derivatives at the base point and retains a remainder instead.

Cyclic trace and eigenvalue sums with multiplicity · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Derives cyclic trace identities and explains why eigenvalue sums require algebraic multiplicities and remain invariant under basis changes.

Cyclic trace and eigenvalue sums with multiplicity

For compatible rectangular matrices, tr(AB)=tr(BA). Indeed both traces sum the same products aijbji over all indices. This implies cyclic invariance for compatible triple products,

tr(ABC)=tr(BCA),

and invariance under similarity, in particular unitary change of basis. Cyclic permutation does not assert arbitrary permutation of matrix factors.

If a square matrix is diagonalizable, A=PDP−1, then cyclicity gives

tr(A)=tr(D)=∑jλj.

Distinct eigenvalues are sufficient for the diagonalization argument, but the trace formula also holds with repeated eigenvalues counted by algebraic multiplicity. The booklet identifies Jordan decomposition as the extension beyond the distinct-eigenvalue case without developing that theory. Summing only distinct numerical eigenvalues would generally lose the trace.

Thus trace gives a basis-independent aggregate spectral quantity, while not determining individual eigenvalues or eigenvectors.

For a real symmetric matrix, the diagonalizing matrix can be chosen orthogonal, so D=QTAQ and cyclicity gives tr(D)=tr(AQQT)=tr(A). This orthogonal form uses symmetry; a general diagonalizable matrix requires a general similarity transformation instead.

Optimal low-rank approximation by truncated SVD · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Retains leading singular terms to minimize spectral and Frobenius error and applies the formulation to image approximation tasks.

Optimal low-rank approximation by truncated SVD

For A=∑i=1rσiuiviT and 0≤k<r, retain

Ak=∑i=1kσiuiviT.

This is a best approximation among matrices of rank at most k in both spectral and Frobenius norms. The residual singular values are the discarded values, so

‖A−Ak‖2=σk+1,‖A−Ak‖F=(∑i>kσi2)1/2.

For k≥r, the residual is zero. Keeping a small discarded tail supports accurate compression; a rank choice alone gives no accuracy guarantee independent of that tail. The booklet uses the optimal-truncation theorem in worked examples rather than proving its full general form.

For (178817), the best rank-one truncation is 252(1111), with both errors 9. For diag(1,4), it is diag(0,4), with both errors 1. The leading singular direction, rather than matrix-entry order, determines the retained term.

For the sheet's extra diagonal example diag(1,−4), the leading singular value remains 4, while the matching left vector changes sign. Its best rank-one truncation is diag(0,−4), again with residual norms 1. A signed eigenvalue cannot be inserted as a negative singular value.

The image task applies this construction to grayscale peppers.png at ranks 10, 25 and 100. The separate weekly solution supplies code and numerical outputs for that application, beyond the booklet's brief code pointer.

If a repeated singular value straddles the truncation boundary, an optimal approximation need not be unique. For example, when σ1=σ2=σ3>σ4, keeping any two orthonormal singular pairs from the leading three-dimensional block gives the same optimal rank-two errors: spectral error σ1 and a Frobenius error determined by the identical discarded values. The rank approximation can differ while its optimal quality remains fixed. A drop in singular values is therefore useful when selecting a truncation rank.

A strict gap σk>σk+1 makes the truncation matrix independent of basis choices within either the retained or discarded blocks, even if values repeat inside those blocks. A tie across the boundary permits infinitely many choices, as rank-one projectors approximating the two-dimensional identity demonstrate. This basis-independence statement about SVD truncation should not be read as a uniqueness theorem for every minimizer under the spectral norm.

The assessment example takes A=(3−11−3), singular values 4,2, right vectors (1,−1)/2,(1,1)/2, and left vectors (1,1)/2,(1,−1)/2. The two singular dyads reconstruct A; retaining the first gives A1=(2−22−2). Its error is 2 in both spectral and Frobenius norms, because exactly one singular value of size 2 is discarded.

Simultaneous boundary concentration and near-orthogonality in a uniform ball · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Combines volume scaling and coordinate-slab bounds with finite union bounds for many independent points.

Simultaneous boundary concentration and near-orthogonality in a uniform ball

For a uniform point in the unit ball of Rd, scaling volume gives

P(‖X‖2≤α)=αd,0<α<1.

Let X1,…,Xn be independent such points, n≥2. If a=1−2logn/d lies in (0,1), then ad≤e−2logn=n−2. A union bound gives

P(‖Xi‖2≥a for every i)≥1−1/n.

If a≤0, the lower-norm condition is automatic. Thus many sampled points simultaneously lie near the boundary when d is large relative to logn.

For d≥3, condition on a nonzero Xi, rotate Xi/‖Xi‖ to a coordinate axis, and use independence and the uniform ball's rotational invariance. Since ‖Xi‖≤1,

|⟨Xi,Xj⟩|≤|⟨Xi/‖Xi‖,Xj⟩|.

The coordinate-slab bound with c=6logn gives a per-pair failure bound (2/c)n−3≤n−3. Union over unordered pairs therefore implies

P(|⟨Xi,Xj⟩|≤6lognd−1 for all i≠j)≥1−1/n.

If the threshold is at least one, this inner-product condition is already automatic. Combining the two events gives probability at least 1−2/n. These are inner products of ball points; a bound on the cosine of their angle additionally uses their lower norm bounds. Small norms alone would not certify nearly orthogonal directions.

Chebyshev control and the weak law of large numbers · tum-foundations-data-analysis · Type: theorem

Uses variance additivity to bound sample-average deviations and interprets aggregation in a stipulated insurance example.

Chebyshev control and the weak law of large numbers

Let Xi be i.i.d. with finite mean μ and variance v. Centering gives Yi=Xi−μ, and independence cancels cross terms in the squared sum. Therefore

E|1N∑iXi−μ|2=vN.

Markov on this square yields the Chebyshev estimate

P(|1N∑iXi−μ|>ε)≤vNε2→0.

This proves the finite-variance weak law, with an explicit 1/N bound at fixed deviation. It controls probability, not a deterministic outcome for a particular finite sample. Linearity of expectation alone would not cancel variance cross terms; the independence assumption is material.

The review stipulates independent identically distributed device repair costs: 100 with probability 0.05, 300 with probability 0.01 and zero with probability 0.94, hence mean cost 8. A price 6 gives mean return minus 2; a price 10 gives mean return 2. At price 10, returns are −90,−290,10, with second moment 1340 and variance 1340−22=1336. The average return therefore has a deviation bound 1336/(Nε2). A single contract can still lose money despite positive expected return.

The example illustrates aggregation under explicit i.i.d. assumptions. It is not an empirical failure model or a guarantee against common failures across devices. Finite variance gives this bound without an exponential moment, whereas sharper exponential estimates need additional tail information.

Augmented-Lagrangian local exactness through Debreu's lemma · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: method

Uses equality-tangent curvature and Debreu’s lemma to prove local unconstrained exactness at the correct multiplier for large finite penalties.

Augmented-Lagrangian local exactness through Debreu's lemma

For minf(x) with h(x)=0, adding any fixed multiplier term μTh(x) leaves all constrained objective comparisons unchanged. Applying a quadratic penalty to this equivalent constrained Lagrangian problem gives

Pαμ(x)=f(x)+μTh(x)+α2‖h(x)‖2.

This is not simply a nonnegative penalty added to f; the multiplier term can change sign off the constraint set.

Local exactness at the correct multiplier

Let f,h∈C2, (x¯,μ¯) be KKT, and assume Lagrangian Hessian positivity on nonzero equality-tangent directions:

dTHd>0if d≠0,Ad=0,H=∇xx2L(x¯,μ¯),A=∇h(x¯)T.

Feasibility and stationarity give

∇Pαμ¯(x¯)=0,∇2Pαμ¯(x¯)=H+αATA.

Debreu's lemma makes this Hessian positive definite for all sufficiently large α. Hence x¯ is a strict unconstrained local minimizer of Pαμ¯: local exactness holds with a finite penalty once the correct multiplier is fixed. The result is local and conditional on that multiplier and curvature; it does not assert global exactness or supply a multiplier-update algorithm.

Debreu's lemma

If symmetric H is positive on kerA⧵{0}, then H+ρATA is positive definite for all sufficiently large ρ. Otherwise select unit dk with

0≥dkT(H+kATA)dk=dkTHdk+k‖Adk‖2.

A subsequence converges to unit d, with dTHd≤0. Boundedness of dkTHdk gives ‖Adk‖2≤−dkTHdk/k→0, so Ad=0, a contradiction. Monotonicity of the added positive-semidefinite term then extends positivity to every larger parameter.

KKT formulation of the Celis–Dennis–Tapia two-constraint subproblem · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: method

Establishes Slater feasibility and derives KKT equations for a quadratic model with trust-region and residual-norm constraints.

KKT formulation of the Celis–Dennis–Tapia two-constraint subproblem

Consider the quadratic objective with a trust-region and residual-norm bound:

minxxTHx+2bTx,‖x‖2≤Δ2,‖ATx+c‖2≤ξ2,

where H is symmetric, Δ>0, A∈Rn×m, and

ξ>min‖x‖≤Δ‖ATx+c‖.

The minimum on the right exists by compactness. A minimizing y* strictly satisfies the residual bound. If it lies on the trust-region boundary, the scaled points (1−1/(2k))y* satisfy the trust-region inequality strictly, and retain the strict residual inequality for large k by continuity. Thus a Slater point exists for these convex constraints.

At a local minimizer, KKT therefore has nonnegative λ1,λ2 satisfying primal feasibility and

2Hx¯+2b+2λ1x¯+2λ2A(ATx¯+c)=0,
λ1(‖x¯‖2−Δ2)=0,λ2(‖ATx¯+c‖2−ξ2)=0.

Symmetry of H suffices for this formulation; positive semidefiniteness is not assumed. Convex constraints alone do not make an indefinite quadratic objective convex or make every KKT point globally optimal. The exercise derives the system and qualification, not a numerical solver for it.

Elastic SQP feasibility restoration and equivalent l1 model penalties · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: method

Restores feasibility of linearized constraint models with nonnegative violation variables and eliminates them into positive-part and absolute-value penalties.

Elastic SQP feasibility restoration and equivalent l1 model penalties

Let qk(s)=∇f(xk)Ts+12sTHks, rg(s)=g(xk)+∇g(xk)Ts, and rh(s)=h(xk)+∇h(xk)Ts. The elastic model with ρ>0 is

mins,v,w+,w−qk(s)+ρ1Tv+ρ1T(w++w−),
rg(s)−v≤0,rh(s)−w++w−=0,v,w+,w−≥0.

It is always feasible: set s=0, v=(g(xk))+, w+=(h(xk))+, w−=(−h(xk))+. This relaxes incompatible linearized constraints; it does not itself guarantee a bounded objective or a global minimizer for arbitrary Hk.

Eliminating violation variables

For fixed s, the least-cost choices are

v=(rg(s))+,w+=(rh(s))+,w−=(−rh(s))+.

Feasibility alone does not enforce these minima: the two equality slacks can both contain a common positive excess. At an optimum, ρ>0 removes all such excess, and (a)++(−a)+=|a|. Consequently the reduced problem is

minsqk(s)+ρ∑i(rg,i(s))++ρ∑j|rh,j(s)|.

A global solution of either formulation gives one of the other by these formulas. For any feasible elastic tuple, its slack cost is at least this reduced violation cost; that inequality proves the reverse comparison without presuming minimal slacks for arbitrary feasible points.

For f=−x1−x2, g=−x, h=x12+x22−1, Hk=I, xk=(−1/2,−1/2), the explicit model is

min−s1−s2+12(s12+s22)+ρ(v1+v2+w++w−),

subject to 1/2−si−vi≤0, −1/2−s1−s2−w++w−=0, and nonnegative violation variables. The ordinary linearized problem was infeasible; the elastic model has the constructive feasible choice above. The penalty is on model violations, not a claim of exact feasibility for every returned nonlinear iterate.

Local exact penalties and their differentiability obstruction · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: theorem

Shows that local exactness persists above a penalty threshold and explains why smooth nonnegative penalties cannot handle nonstationary constrained optima exactly.

Local exact penalties and their differentiability obstruction

Let π≥0 be a penalty for feasible X, with π=0 on X, and Pα=f+απ. At a constrained local solution x¯, local exactness means x¯ also locally minimizes the unconstrained penalized objective for a finite penalty parameter.

If exactness holds at α^>0, it holds for every α≥α^: on the same neighborhood,

Pα(x¯)=f(x¯)=Pα^(x¯)≤Pα^(x)≤Pα(x).

Nonnegativity of π is needed for monotonicity with the penalty parameter.

If both f,π are differentiable at x¯, then ∇π(x¯)=0, since π attains its global minimum zero there. Unconstrained stationarity of the exact penalty therefore gives

0=∇Pα^(x¯)=∇f(x¯)+α^∇π(x¯)⟹∇f(x¯)=0.

Thus a differentiable nonnegative penalty cannot be locally exact at a constrained solution with nonzero objective gradient. This explains a substantive role for nonsmooth exact penalties; it is not a claim that every nonsmooth penalty is exact or that smooth penalties never converge as their parameter increases.

KKT conditions and first-order directional stationarity · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: concept

Relates Lagrangian stationarity and complementarity to directional optimality, with convex sufficiency and strict-convexity primal uniqueness.

KKT conditions and first-order directional stationarity

For minf(x) subject to g(x)≤0, h(x)=0, define

L(x,λ,μ)=f(x)+λTg(x)+μTh(x).

A KKT triple satisfies primal feasibility and

λ≥0,λigi(x)=0,∇f(x)+∇g(x)λ+∇h(x)μ=0.

Inactive inequalities have zero multipliers. Strict complementarity at a triple means positive multipliers for every active inequality; it is stronger than complementary slackness.

KKT implies nonnegative directional derivative on the linearized cone, without an additional CQ for this implication. For d∈Tl(g,h,x¯),

∇f(x¯)Td=−∑i∈Aλi∇gi(x¯)Td−μT∇h(x¯)Td≥0.

Since T(X,x¯)⊂Tl, it implies the first-order tangent-cone necessary condition. It does not by itself imply a local minimum for an arbitrary nonconvex problem. Conversely deriving KKT from a constrained minimum requires appropriate qualification hypotheses; existence of multipliers is not supplied merely by writing this system.

Convex sufficiency and primal uniqueness

When f,gi are convex and h affine, a KKT point is globally optimal: the convex Lagrangian in x is stationary there, so is globally minimized there, and feasibility with nonnegative multipliers compares it to f on the feasible set. If f is strictly convex, there cannot be two different KKT points: their feasible midpoint would have objective below their common minimum. Primal uniqueness does not by itself imply uniqueness of the multiplier tuple.

Linearized feasible cones, Abadie and Guignard qualifications · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: concept

Compares true and affine-model tangent cones and uses degenerate planar constraints to distinguish Abadie from Guignard qualification.

Linearized feasible cones, Abadie and Guignard qualifications

True geometry and its linearized model

For differentiable constraints X={x:g(x)≤0, h(x)=0} and feasible x¯, let A(x¯)={i:gi(x¯)=0}. The linearized cone is

Tl(g,h,x¯)={d:∇gi(x¯)Td≤0 (i∈A), ∇h(x¯)Td=0}.

Always T(X,x¯)⊂Tl, by differentiating constraints along feasible sequences. The linearized cone equals the true tangent cone of the affine first-order constraint model gl(x)=g(x¯)+∇g(x¯)T(x−x¯), and similarly for hl. For the reverse inclusion, x¯+d/k satisfies the affine active/equality constraints; finitely many inactive inequalities remain negative for large k.

For a cone C, define C∘={v:vTd≤0 ∀d∈C}. Abadie's CQ (ACQ) is T=Tl; Guignard's CQ (GCQ) is T∘=Tl∘. Thus ACQ implies GCQ, while equality of polars need not recover a nonconvex tangent set.

Three diagnostic constraint descriptions at the origin

Constraints g≤0 True tangent T Linearized cone Tl Qualification
g=(−x1,x22) R+×{0} R+×R Both fail
g=(x2−x13,−x2) R+×{0} R×{0} Both fail
g=(−x1,−x2,x1x2) Nonnegative coordinate axes R+2 GCQ holds; ACQ fails

In the first case, T∘=R−×R, but Tl∘=R−×{0}. The zero gradient of x22 loses its exact geometric restriction. In the second case, the cubic feasible cusp has only nonnegative horizontal tangent directions, whereas linearization permits both signs; the polars are respectively R−×R and {0}×R.

In the third case, feasibility forces one coordinate to vanish, so the true tangent is the union of two rays. Both its polar and the quadrant's polar are R−2. First-order inequalities against directions can therefore coincide even though the tangent sets differ. CQs depend on the constraint description as well as the underlying feasible set.

Logarithmic barrier continuation and convergence of global subproblem solutions · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: algorithm

Proves monotonic comparisons and optimal accumulation points for globally solved barrier subproblems when the strict interior is dense in the feasible set.

Logarithmic barrier continuation and convergence of global subproblem solutions

Let f,gi be continuous, X={x:g(x)≤0}, and let the strict interior X∘={x:g(x)<0} be nonempty. Define

β(x)=−∑ilog(−gi(x)),Bτ(x)=f(x)+τβ(x)(x∈X∘).

Choose τ1>0; at each iteration compute a global minimizer xk of Bτk on its domain, then decrease τk+1∈(0,τk). Assume the subproblem minimizers exist and τk↓0. This is an idealized continuation algorithm, not a supplied numerical interior-point implementation.

Monotonic comparisons

Optimality at the two consecutive parameters gives

f(xk)+τkβ(xk)≤f(xk+1)+τkβ(xk+1),
f(xk+1)+τk+1β(xk+1)≤f(xk)+τk+1β(xk).

Adding proves β(xk)≤β(xk+1). Inserting this into the second inequality proves f(xk+1)≤f(xk). No assumption β≥0 is needed; the logarithmic sum may be negative.

Accumulation points and the closure hypothesis

Assume X∘―=X. Every accumulation point x¯ is feasible by continuity and is a global solution of the original problem; moreover

f(xk)→f(x¯),Bτk(xk)→f(x¯).

For any fixed interior y, monotonicity of β and global subproblem optimality bound

f(xk)+τkβ(x1)≤Bτk(xk)≤f(y)+τkβ(y).

Monotone objective values converge to their accumulation-point value. The displayed comparison excludes any interior point with smaller objective; density of the strict interior extends that exclusion to every feasible point. Taking interior points arbitrarily close in objective to the optimum and using the same bounds gives convergence of barrier values.

The closure condition allows feasible boundary minimizers; it does not require X∘=X. Existence of an accumulation point is not proved, nor are rates or guarantees for approximate/local subproblem solutions.

MFCQ strict feasible directions and Slater points · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: concept

Connects strictly decreasing active-constraint directions to Slater points while keeping equality-gradient independence as a separate condition.

MFCQ strict feasible directions and Slater points

For C1 mixed constraints, the full-rank MFCQ conditions used in the multiplier argument are independence of the equality gradients and a direction d such that

∇h(x¯)Td=0,∇gi(x¯)Td<0(i∈A(x¯)).

For inequalities alone there is no equality-rank condition. The direction moves strictly toward all active inequality interiors to first order.

For componentwise convex g and affine h, a Slater point y satisfies g(y)<0, h(y)=0. At any feasible x, take d=y−x. Convexity and affinity give

∇gi(x)Td≤gi(y)−gi(x)<0(i∈A(x)),∇h(x)Td=h(y)−h(x)=0.

Thus Slater supplies the strict-direction part at every feasible point. It does not establish independence of redundant affine equality gradients; a full-rank formulation of MFCQ needs that separate condition.

Conversely the sheet's mixed-constraint qualification construction uses feasible points xk=x+wk+ϕ(wk) maintaining h(xk)=0 and satisfying all gi(xk)<0 for sufficiently large k. This supplies a Slater point when its stated qualification hypotheses apply. The supplied solution refers to a construction in unprovided lecture notes rather than defining ϕ or proving that construction. Its term “generalized MFCQ” is therefore not used here to silently equate the strict-direction condition with equality-gradient independence.

Existence of constrained minimizers and the distinct roles of convexity · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: theorem

Uses compact sublevel sets to prove attainment and distinguishes strict-convexity uniqueness from strong-convexity coercivity.

Existence of constrained minimizers and the distinct roles of convexity

Compactness from coercivity

Let nonempty X⊂Rn be closed and f:X→R continuous. If f(x)→+∞ as x∈X, ‖x‖→∞, then f attains a global minimum. Fix y∈X; its sublevel set Ny={x∈X:f(x)≤f(y)} is closed by continuity and bounded by coercivity. It is nonempty and compact. Minimizing over Ny suffices, since points outside it cannot improve on y.

For compact nonempty X, continuity alone suffices by Weierstrass. A condition concerning divergent sequences inside a bounded X is vacuous and adds no existence guarantee beyond compactness.

What convexity does and does not supply

  • Coercivity without closedness is insufficient: X=(0,∞), f(x)=x, has unattained infimum zero.
  • Convex feasible set and convex objective alone are insufficient: ex on R has unattained infimum zero.
  • The same example is strictly convex on a closed convex set. Strict convexity supplies uniqueness if a minimizer exists, not existence on an unbounded domain.

For nonempty closed convex X, a continuous strongly convex objective does attain a unique minimizer. The sheet's convention is: for some μ>0,

f(λx+(1−λ)y)+μλ(1−λ)‖x−y‖2≤λf(x)+(1−λ)f(y).

To see coercivity without differentiability, fix y∈X and let r=‖x−y‖>1. Convexity puts z=y+(x−y)/r in X. The continuous function has a finite lower bound m on the compact unit-sphere intersection with X whenever such x exists. Applying strong convexity with λ=1/r and rearranging yields

f(x)≥f(y)+r[m−f(y)]+μ(r2−r).

The quadratic term dominates the linear terms, proving coercivity along unbounded feasible sequences. The preceding existence argument applies, and strict convexity excludes two distinct minimizers by their midpoint.

Boundedness, nonuniqueness and strict complementarity of KKT multipliers · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: theorem

Proves multiplier boundedness under MFCQ and uniqueness under LICQ, contrasting these with a nonunique segment and triple-dependent strict complementarity.

Boundedness, nonuniqueness and strict complementarity of KKT multipliers

Closedness and MFCQ boundedness

At a fixed KKT point x¯, the multiplier set M(x¯) consists of all (λ,μ) satisfying stationarity, nonnegativity and complementarity there. It is closed by continuity of those finite-dimensional conditions.

If its elements had unbounded norm, normalize a sequence and take a unit-norm subsequential limit (λ^,μ^). Dividing stationarity by the diverging norm removes the objective gradient, leaving

λ^≥0,g(x¯)Tλ^=0,∇g(x¯)λ^+∇h(x¯)μ^=0.

Under full-rank MFCQ, pairing with its strict feasible direction forces every active λ^i=0; inactive components are already zero. Independence of equality gradients then forces μ^=0, contradicting unit norm. Thus M(x¯) is bounded, and closedness makes it compact. This does not imply uniqueness.

A full multiplier segment

Consider

f(x)=(4−x1)2+x24,g1=(x1−1)2+(x2−1)2−2,g2=(x1−1)2+(x2+1)2−2,g3=x1−2.

At x¯=(2,0), all three inequalities are active, with gradients (2,−2)T,(2,2)T,(1,0)T. The direction (−1,0)T establishes MFCQ. Stationarity with ∇f(x¯)=(−4,0)T gives

M(x¯)={(t,t,4(1−t))T:0≤t≤1}.

The specified multiplier (1,1,0) violates strict complementarity because the third active multiplier vanishes. For 0<t<1, all three are positive. The qualification holds and the set is bounded, yet multipliers are not unique and strict complementarity depends on the chosen triple.

LICQ gives uniqueness

LICQ means that the active inequality gradients together with the equality gradients are linearly independent. At a fixed KKT point let A*=(∇gA(x¯),∇h(x¯)). Subtracting two stationarity equations and using zero inactive multipliers gives A*Δ(λA,μ)=0; independence forces equality of the multipliers. Equivalently, the existing KKT multipliers are

(λAμ)=−(A*TA*)−1A*T∇f(x¯),λI=0.

This is a uniqueness formula conditional on a KKT point, not a guarantee that the formula at an arbitrary feasible point produces nonnegative multipliers. LICQ is stronger information than MFCQ boundedness.

For the separate disk-constrained example minx13 subject to x12+x22−1≤0, at (−1,0) stationarity is (3,0)T+λ(−2,0)T=0. It forces the unique multiplier λ=3/2>0; strict complementarity holds. This contrasts with the multiplier segment above, where some triples have zero active multipliers.

Euclidean projection and projected-gradient stationarity · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: method

Characterizes constrained stationarity as a projected-gradient fixed point and identifies the convexity needed for global optimality.

Euclidean projection and projected-gradient stationarity

For nonempty closed convex X⊂Rn, define

PX(y)=argminx∈X12‖x−y‖22.

The objective is continuous and coercive, giving existence on closed X; its strong convexity and convexity of X give uniqueness. Thus projection is a well-defined map on all of Rn.

For f continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of X and τ>0, let

dτ(x)=x−PX(x−τ∇f(x)).

Applying the variational inequality to the strongly convex projection objective gives

dτ(x¯)=0⟺x¯∈X,τ∇f(x¯)T(w−x¯)≥0∀w∈X.

For convex f, this is equivalent to global constrained optimality. Every constrained global minimizer satisfies the fixed-point condition even without convexity of f; convexity is what makes the condition sufficient. The positive step size cancels from the inequality, so the characterization holds for any τ>0, not a selected algorithmic step-size range.

The equation identifies a projected-gradient stationary point. By itself it proves neither convergence of repeated projected steps nor a convergence rate; no such iteration analysis is supplied by this exercise.

Stationary quadratic-penalty subproblems and limiting KKT multipliers · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: algorithm

Derives scaled-residual multiplier estimates and a limiting KKT pair under primal convergence, diverging penalties and equality LICQ.

Stationary quadratic-penalty subproblems and limiting KKT multipliers

For C1 equality-constrained minf(x), h(x)=0, let Pα(x)=f(x)+(α/2)‖h(x)‖2. The modified penalty scheme is:

  1. Choose α0>0.
  2. Compute a stationary point xk satisfying ∇Pαk(xk)=0.
  3. Stop if h(xk)=0; otherwise choose αk+1>αk and repeat.

The subproblem requirement is stationarity, not a specified minimization routine or a guarantee of global minimizers.

Conditional limit analysis

Assume αk→∞, xk→x¯, and ∇h(x¯) has full column rank (the equality LICQ condition). Set μk=αkh(xk). Stationarity reads

∇f(xk)+∇h(xk)μk=0.

Continuity preserves full column rank near x¯, so for large k,

μk=−[∇h(xk)T∇h(xk)]−1∇h(xk)T∇f(xk).

The normal-equation formula and continuity of matrix inversion give convergence to the same expression evaluated at x¯, denoted μ¯. Consequently

h(x¯)=limkμkαk=0,∇f(x¯)+∇h(x¯)μ¯=0.

Thus the limiting pair is KKT. The argument proves feasibility from scaled-residual control; it does not assume feasibility of every iterate. It assumes convergence of the primal sequence and unbounded penalty growth rather than proving either for every run. No convergence rate or numerical experiment is provided.

Lagrangian curvature on critical directions and local quadratic growth · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: theorem

Uses positive Lagrangian curvature on critical directions to prove local quadratic growth, including an example with a zero active gradient.

Lagrangian curvature on critical directions and local quadratic growth

Positive-multiplier cone and sufficiency

For C2 data and KKT triple (x¯,λ¯,μ¯), set A+={i∈A:λ¯i>0}. The cone used for second-order sufficiency is

T+={d:∇h(x¯)Td=0,∇gi(x¯)Td=0 (i∈A+),∇gi(x¯)Td≤0 (i∈A⧵A+)}.

If dT∇xx2L(x¯,λ¯,μ¯)d>0 for every nonzero d∈T+, then there are α,δ>0 with

f(x)−f(x¯)≥α‖x−x¯‖2(x feasible, ‖x−x¯‖<δ).

In particular the minimizer is strict locally. The curvature condition is sufficient; it need not hold for every possible multiplier at every constrained minimum.

Contradiction proof

Failure of quadratic growth gives feasible xk≠x¯, xk→x¯, and αk↓0 with objective increase less than αk‖xk−x¯‖2. Normalize displacements and extract unit yk→y. Feasibility gives y∈Tl, while first-order expansion bounds ∇f(x¯)Ty≤0. KKT makes that derivative nonnegative, and positive active multipliers force their directional constraint derivatives to zero. Thus y∈T+⧵{0}.

Feasibility and multiplier signs give L(xk,λ¯,μ¯)≤f(xk), with equality at x¯. Since ∇xL(x¯,λ¯,μ¯)=0, the second-order expansion divided by ‖xk−x¯‖2 yields 12yT∇xx2Ly≤0, a contradiction.

Degenerate active gradient with valid sufficiency

For f=x1+x2−2x3, g1=x12/2−x2, g2=ex1−1−x1, h=x32−x1+3/4, the point x¯=(1,1/2,1/2) and multipliers λ¯=(1,0), μ¯=2 satisfy KKT. Although ∇g2(x¯)=0,

T+={(t,t,t):t∈R},∇xx2L=diag(1,0,4).

Its quadratic form is 5t2>0 for nonzero such directions, proving strict local optimality and quadratic growth. A zero active gradient does not by itself invalidate a sufficient curvature test.

Why second-order necessity requires an appropriate curve qualification · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: method

Constructs a degenerate minimum where a required boundary arc does not exist and a KKT multiplier gives an indefinite Lagrangian Hessian.

Why second-order necessity requires an appropriate curve qualification

Consider

min12(x12+x22),g(x)=x14−x22≤0.

The origin is the unique global minimizer, even without constraints. At zero, both objective and constraint gradients vanish, so every λ≥0 gives a KKT tuple. The sheet's cones Ta,T+,Tl all equal R2 there, because the active gradient vanishes. Equality of these first-order cones does not supply the required second-order curve condition.

For d=(0,1)T, the stated CQ2 would require a C2 arc γ with γ(0)=0, γ′(0)=d, and g(γ(t))=0 for nonnegative small t. But boundary equality implies |γ2(t)|=γ1(t)2. Differentiability and γ1(0)=0 give γ1(t)=O(t), hence γ2(t)/t→0, contradicting γ2′(0)=1. Thus the required arc cannot exist. This argument avoids assuming that the sign of the boundary branch stays fixed.

At multiplier λ=1,

∇xx2L(0,1)=(100−1),

which is not positive semidefinite on T+=R2. This does not contradict constrained minimality: the qualification needed for that multiplier-dependent second-order necessary condition fails. In particular first-order qualification information cannot be substituted for the specified CQ2 arc hypothesis. The example establishes this obstruction without requiring the unavailable lecture's complete CQ2 formulation.

Preserving LICQ when introducing nonnegative slack variables · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: theorem

Proves that replacing inequalities by equalities with ordinary nonnegative slacks preserves independence of active constraint gradients.

Preserving LICQ when introducing nonnegative slack variables

For inequality constraints g(x)≤0, introduce s∈Rm:

g(x)+s=0,−s≤0.

At feasible x¯, set s¯=−g(x¯). The transformed point is feasible and the active slack bounds are exactly the original active inequalities.

If the original active gradients are independent (LICQ), the transformed active inequalities and all equality gradients are independent. The equality-gradient columns are (∇gi(x¯),ei)T; active bound-gradient columns are (0,−ej)T, j∈A. In any zero linear combination, the inactive slack coordinates force the corresponding equality coefficients wi=0. The x-coordinates then give ∑i∈Awi∇gi=0, so original LICQ forces all remaining wi=0. The active slack coordinates finally force the bound coefficients to vanish.

Thus this reformulation preserves qualification at the corresponding point, not just feasibility. The statement concerns ordinary nonnegative slacks; it does not establish an analogous result for squared-slack transformations.

Finite identification of the limiting active set in SQP · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: theorem

Proves eventual identification of the limiting QP active set under convergent SQP triples, positive step-size bounds and strict complementarity.

Finite identification of the limiting active set in SQP

Assume a globalized SQP sequence (xk,λk,μk) converges to KKT triple (x¯,λ¯,μ¯), with C2 data, QP KKT multipliers chosen as (λk+1,μk+1), and

xk+1=xk+σksk,0<σ¯≤σk≤1.

Then sk=(xk+1−xk)/σk→0. A vanishing step-size sequence would not justify this inference from convergence of xk alone.

Define

AQP(sk)={i:gi(xk)+∇gi(xk)Tsk=0}.

For any inactive limiting inequality, gi(x¯)<0, its model value tends to that same negative number. Hence eventually AQP(sk)⊂A(x¯). QP complementarity also gives

λk+1T[g(xk)+∇g(xk)Tsk]=0.

If strict complementarity holds at the limiting triple, each i∈A(x¯) has λ¯i>0, and thus λk+1,i>0 for all large k. With nonpositive model constraint values, complementarity forces each such value to be zero. Therefore eventually

AQP(sk)=A(x¯).

This is conditional finite identification of the QP active set. It does not prove that the nonlinear iterates lie exactly on the limiting active surfaces, or establish global convergence of an arbitrary SQP implementation.

SQP quadratic models, feasibility and exact quadratic special cases · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: algorithm

Builds quadratic Lagrangian models with affine constraints and analyzes infeasibility, exact convex-QP steps and an equality Newton example.

SQP quadratic models, feasibility and exact quadratic special cases

Local subproblem

At (xk,λk,μk), exact-Hessian SQP uses

mind ∇f(xk)Td+12dTHkd,g(xk)+∇g(xk)Td≤0,h(xk)+∇h(xk)Td=0,

with Hk=∇xx2L(xk,λk,μk); variants may supply a different Hk. The model retains Lagrangian curvature while replacing constraints by affine models. A globalized update uses xk+1=xk+σkdk and QP multipliers. The sheets analyze this structure, not a fully specified merit function or line-search implementation.

If the original feasible set is nonempty, each gi convex and h affine, any feasible x^ gives subproblem-feasible d=x^−xk, since g(xk)+∇g(xk)Td≤g(x^)≤0 and the affine equality is exact. This establishes feasibility, not boundedness below or existence of a minimizing QP direction.

Without these assumptions the subproblem can be infeasible even when the original problem is feasible:

  • For g(x)=−x, h(x)=x12+x22−1, xk=(−1/2,−1/2), linearization requires d1,d2≥1/2 and d1+d2=−1/2, impossible.
  • For scalar f=x3, g=1−x4, xk=0, Hk=1, the constraint model is the impossible 1≤0, despite the positive quadratic model Hessian.

Convex quadratic exactness

For q(x)=12xTQx+cTx, Q⪰0, with Cx≤bg, Ax=bh, KKT is necessary and sufficient at an existing solution:

Qx+c+CTλ+ATμ=0,Cx≤bg,Ax=bh,λ≥0,λT(Cx−bg)=0.

Affine constraint geometry supplies the qualification, without requiring LICQ. The exact-Hessian SQP model has Hessian Q; its objective differs from q(xk+d) only by q(xk). Its constraints are those of the original QP at xk+d. Hence any global subproblem solution gives an original global solution in one full step. This does not assert that arbitrary damped steps terminate in one iteration.

Equality-constrained Lagrange–Newton step

Newton's method for equality KKT equations solves the block system with Lagrangian Hessian and equality Jacobian. For f(x)=x2, h(x)=x, at (x0,μ0)=(1,0),

(2110)(δxδμ)=(−2−1).

It gives δx=−1, δμ=0, reaching the KKT pair (0,0) in one step. This scalar exact example is not a general one-step or convergence theorem.

Strict tangent-direction positivity as a local sufficiency condition · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: theorem

Proves strict local minimality from positive gradient pairing with every nonzero tangent direction without assuming convexity.

Strict tangent-direction positivity as a local sufficiency condition

Let X⊂Rn be nonempty, f:Rn→R differentiable and x¯∈X. If

∇f(x¯)Td>0∀d∈T(X,x¯)⧵{0},

then x¯ is a strict local minimizer. Neither feasible-set convexity nor objective convexity is required.

If this failed, there would be distinct feasible xk→x¯ with f(xk)≤f(x¯). Put tk=‖xk−x¯‖>0, dk=(xk−x¯)/tk. Compactness of the unit sphere supplies a subsequence dk→d, where d∈T(X,x¯) and ‖d‖=1. Differentiability gives

0≥f(xk)−f(x¯)=tk∇f(x¯)Tdk+o(tk).

Division by tk and passage to the limit contradict strict positivity. The finite-dimensional unit-sphere subsequence is central to this proof.

This is stronger than the nonnegative first-order necessary condition. It is a sufficient test, not a characterization of all strict local minimizers, and it does not imply global optimality in a nonconvex problem.

Tangent cones and convex feasible directions · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: theorem

Represents convex tangent cones by closures of rescaled feasible displacements and establishes closedness, conic structure and interior-point behavior.

Tangent cones and convex feasible directions

The Bouligand tangent cone at x∈M⊂Rn records limits of positively rescaled feasible displacements:

T(M,x)={d:∃xk∈M, xk→x, ηk>0, ηk(xk−x)→d}.

For nonempty convex M,

T(M,x)={η(y−x):η>0, y∈M}―.

The closure matters: a limiting feasible direction need not itself be a positive multiple of a single feasible displacement.

Every tangent direction belongs to the displayed closure directly from its defining sequence. Conversely, for d=η(y−x), convexity gives xk=x+(y−x)/k∈M, and (kη)(xk−x)=d. For a limit dk=ηk(yk−x)→d, choose

αk=k(‖yk‖+1),xk=x+(yk−x)/αk,η~k=αkηk.

Then xk∈M, xk→x, and η~k(xk−x)=dk→d. This proves the reverse inclusion without assuming closedness of the original displacement cone.

The representation describes the local first-order geometry through the globally available convex segments. It does not extend unchanged to a general nonconvex feasible set or replace a constraint qualification for nonlinear inequality descriptions.

General properties

The tangent cone always contains zero and is a cone: take the constant feasible sequence, or multiply the positive rescaling factors by a positive scalar. It is closed. For dk→d with dk∈T(M,x), select one realizing displacement for each dk, with both the position error and the rescaled-direction error at most 1/k; the selected sequence realizes d. At an interior point every direction is realizable by sufficiently short segments, so T(M,x)=Rn.

For convex M, the tangent cone is also convex. For directions di=ηi(yi−x), combine the two rescaling factors: λd1+(1−λ)d2=η~(y~−x), where η~=λη1+(1−λ)η2>0 and y~ is the correspondingly weighted convex combination of y1,y2. Closure preserves convexity. For nonconvex sets, tangent cones need not be convex.

Variational inequalities for constrained first-order optimality · tum-nonlinear-optimization · Type: theorem

Derives nonnegative gradient pairings along feasible segments and shows their global sufficiency when the objective is convex.

Variational inequalities for constrained first-order optimality

Let X⊂Rn be nonempty and convex, and f continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of X. If x¯ globally minimizes f on X, then

x¯∈X,∇f(x¯)T(w−x¯)≥0∀w∈X.

For fixed w, the feasible segment v(t)=x¯+t(w−x¯), 0≤t≤1, gives f(v(t))−f(x¯)≥0. Divide by t>0 and let t↓0. No convexity of the objective is needed for this necessity argument.

If f is convex on X, the inequality is also sufficient for global optimality: its supporting-plane inequality yields

f(w)≥f(x¯)+∇f(x¯)T(w−x¯)≥f(x¯)∀w∈X.

Thus the gradient need not vanish at a constrained minimizer; it must pair nonnegatively with all feasible displacement directions. Closedness is unnecessary for this characterization at an existing feasible point; it becomes relevant when constructing projections or proving existence.
